THE DREASIB OF EARLY DAYS. The earth is glad and beautiful, I hink and feel it yet ! The happy dreams of early days I cannot floss- foraet. Loud sing the bird in joyful notes Upon the booming tree, Rejoicing in the sunny sky In simple love and free. Delightful is the rippling wave As e'er it was before, And murmurs peaceful music Upon the tranquil sla,-:re. Snb'ime the rugged rm)untains, That look so dark and high, And seem, when evening sh tdo w s fall, To reach the mantled sky. Hew pleasant a‘"e the crystal lakes, When balmy z,nhyrs And, all the little fa!ry isles, Where trees of beauty grow. When rushing, splashi,,g, waters Resounoing onward go. They echo iii the mountai is, 'through fertile valleys flow. Sweet is the dawn of early spring, With all her budding flowers, And sweeter summer'- perfumed breath, Amid her gorgeous bowers. Oh, yes! the earth is beautiful, Sr very lovely yet; The happy dreams of early days We Lever can forget.
B. KrNYON.
Warzington..

THE SEVEN AG.ES OF WOMAN. (By a Cantankercus Old Curmudgeon.) All the world's a Wardrobe. And all the girls and women merely wearers; They have their fashions and their fantasies, And one she in her time wears many garments Throughout her Seven Stages. First, the baby, Befrilled and broldered, in her nurse's arms. And then the trim-hosed schoolgirl with her flounces And smail-boy-scorning face, tripping, skirt-waggling, Coquettishly to school. And then the flirt, Ogling like Circe, with a business reillade Kept on her low-cut corset. Then a bride Full of strange finery, vestured like an angel, Veiled vapourously, yet vigilant of glance, Seeking the Woman's heaven, Admiration, Even at the Altar's steps. And then the matron, In fair rich velvet, with suave satin lined, With eyes severe, and skirts of youthful cut, Full of dress-saws and modish inst?.nces, To teach her girls thcir dart. The sixth age shifts Into the gray yet gorgeous grandmamma, With gold piece-nex on nose and fan at side, Her youthful tastes still strong, and wordly wise In sumptuary law, her quavering voice Prosing of fashion and Le Fullet, pipes Of robes and bargains rare. Last scene of all, That ends the sex's Mode-swayed history, Is second childishness and sheer oblivion Of youth, taste, passion, all—save love of dress I—Punch.

A plate, please." &cm Lross.—A native of likaranga asserted that in the village next to that in which he lived the people were On the most friendly terms with the lions, which to walk In and about the village without attempting to injure anyone. On great occasions they were treated W honey, goats, sheep, and ugali, and sometimes at these afternoon drums as many as ZOO lions assembled.' Each lion was known to the people by name, and to these they responded when called. And when one died the inhabitants mourned for him as for one of themselves. This village was reported to be situated on the shores of Lake Tanganyika, not very far distant from Jumah Merikanies house; and he also told me that his friend- ship between the natives and lions was commonly :Token of, ' but he had never been present at one of the gatherings. The Mkananga, however' weeded that he had often witnessed this friendly intercourse bet ween man and beast, and brought several of his tribesmen to testify to the truth of his state- ment. Certainly, if this be true, our most famous lion. tamers have yet something to learn from the natives of Africa.—Across Africa. ExEctITIM; OF THE MARQUIS OF ARGYLE.—On Satur- day, the 2'dth of May, 1661, Argyle was sentenced to be beheaded on the Monday following. He was the most pro- minent Protestant in Scotland, and therefore he must die. Argyle shrank from physical suffering; but now, sentenced to the axe, he conquered his constitutional weakness, and rose above the fear of death. A deep serenity filled his mind, which imparted a calmness, and even majesty, to his demeanour daring the hours between his sentence and its execution. In his prison be had a ravishing sense of God's love, and a firm assurance of his admission into the heavenly joys. All night through he slept sweetly, and rose re- freshed in the morning. He dined with his friends on the day of his execution, discoursing cheerfully with them, and retiring after dinner for secret prayer. The procession to the scaffold being formed, "I could die like a Roman," said ' he, "but choose rather to die as a Christian. Come away, gentlemen; he that goes first goes cleanest." He stopped a Moment on his way to execution, to greet James Gathrie, now under sentence of death, and confined in the same prison. They embraced. "Were I not under sentence of death myself," said the minister to the marquis, "I would cheerfully die for your lordship." They parted as men do who are soon to meet again and Argyle, his step firm, and the light of triumph on his brow, went on his way. On the scaffold he addressed the people with great composure, bid- ding them prepare for times which would leave them only this alternative, to "sin or suffer." When about to lay his head on the block, his physician approached him and to uchee his pulse, and found that it was beating at its usual rate, calm and strong. Be kneeled down, and after a few minutee prayer, he gave the signal, the axe fell, and that kingly bud rolled on the scaffold. It was affixed to the west end of the Tolbooth, "a monument," rays Wodrow, "of the Parliament's injustice and the land's misery."—History .Peotestantism,by the Rey. Dr. Wylie.

A. large lacustrine canve, in excellent condition, has been found near Beet, 4,000 feet above the sea level, and nearly 3,000 feet ab eve the valley of the Rhone. No lacustrine relics have ever before been met with in Switzerland at such an elevation. Dr. J. Pili3l has discovered another small planet, his fourth for the present year, making 224 in all. It was dis- covered on March 30th, whilst seeking for Callisto, and is described as very faint—less than the eleventh magnitude. its electric railway is to be made in the picturesque val- ley of the Brithl, near Vienna. It will extend from the railway station of the sulphurous baths of Merdling to the hotel known as the Zwei itaben, near Meierei, in the Hin- terbrilhl, which is annually frequented by thousands of tourists. The length will be nearly two mile. THE OBSERVATORY ON THE PCrY DE DOME.—For moun- tain observation of meteorogical and other phenomena, a recent arrangement at the top of the Puy de Dome seems ' well adapted. Round the ob ervatnry tower, a continuous circular terrace, with balustrade about 40in. high, has been formed, giving a full view all round. The balustrade is divided into 360 dege., the numbers being cat in 'stone. North is 0 deg., east 90 degs., and so on. More than 300 localities have already been referred to this gradation. Two teleecapes are mounted on chariots, which run on rails, and may be brought to any divisions of the circle, facilitating the view, which embraces some seven departments. Mont Blanc can sometimes be seen, at a distance of 230 km. (say, 175 miles). A vocabulary gives all the places visible from the summit, and the places in each vertical plane passing threngh a degree are indicated. Further, geographical maps are constructed, having Pay de Docue as centre, and a number cf concentric circumferences with radii, indicating distances. With this system the path of thunderclouds, and varions other phenomena, can be easily observed with great precision. A WONDERFUL TELEFuoNE.--A very remarkable im- provement in the telephone, by means of which vocal mes- sages can be transmitted over the wires thousands, instead of tens and hundreds, of miles, as heretofore, is reported to have been recently demonstrated in Boston, where the main office of the Bell Telephone Company is situated. The report has created some impression among electricians in this cite", as it seems to open, if verified in all its details, a future for the speaking telephone not second to that of the telegraph itself, indicating, indeed, in the opinion of the most sanguine, that vocal transmission will ultimately supersede the written message for many practical purposes. It appears that Mr. C. E. Chinnock, who is employed by the Metropolitan Telephone Company, of this city, in the capa- city of electrician, had occasion, a couple of weeks ago, to pay a visit to Bostsn in order to confer with the Bell Tele- phone C nnpany. While there be was shown by Mr. Jaques, the electrician of that company, the workings of an iaven• tion by the use of which parties as distant from each other as New York aad Boston can converse with each other intel- ligibly and rapidly. It is stated that the only alterations required in the construction of the telephone as now in use in this city consist in the substitution of batteries of four cells each for the feeble ones employed for telephcning in the present state of the science, and in the substitution of carbons treated in a particular manner, which is kept secret as yet, in place of the simple carbon vibrating surfaces %ith which even the ordinary observer is familiar.—Neto York Times.

I THE NEW ELECTRIC RAILWAY AT BERLIN.—The Daily News Berlin correspondent, describing the new electric rail- way there, already referred to in a telegram, says that the system, which has been in use.in Berlin for more than a year, has not proved a financial success. It has also been found that there is some inconvenience attending the transmission of the electric current through the rails. A horse while crossing this line, striking it with his shoe, received a severe shoctc. It is impossible, moreover, to repair or remove the rails without causing a suspension of traffic over the entire route, sitice such removal interrupts the current. Herr Siemens, to meet these and other objections, devised his new system, which is far more practicable than the first. Over the entire line two cables are suspended parallel to and about tirelve inches from each other on poles approximately 16 feet above the ground. Along these cables a system of wheels pase-s, connecting with the tram-car by another cable which cm be detached from the car at pleasure. The cables are charged with electricity, which is generated at a station about the middle of the route, and which is taken up by the sop 'rattle as it runs over them. It than passes through the conneeting cables down beneath the tram car over a system of drums which unites with the running-gear. The appara- tua passing along the suspended cables either precedes or follows the car. The speed of the vehicle is regulated by a crank, and a complete stop can be made as readily as if it be drawn by horees. On Saturday, during the trial, two cars were run, first separately and afterwards together. In the first case two distinct connecting cables are necessary, while in the second one answers the same purpose, the electricity peeling the car couplings, the only difference being a diminution of velocity, owing to the additional weight. The length of the route run over on the trial trip is about three miles, a portion of the:distance being uphill, an inclina- tion of Ito 28. A car can be run up this grade at the rate of from 15 to 20 miles an hour, while on a level it will make 30 miles to the boon. :After haying thoroughly tested the working of the railway, visitors were driven to the country to witness the operation of a road car which Herr Siemens has invented. It also is propelled by electricity on the same principles as those described for the tram-cars. It runs as smoothly as a common carriage, and is perfectly manageable. It is directed by the driver, who sits in front, by turning a wheel very similar to those used in steering ships, and is started or stopped by simple pressure made upon a lever. This car is intended to run between towns whose population are too small to make a railway profitable pecuniarily. "It appears to me." adds our correspoedent, ' "calculated to meet this end when once the question of its economy over the running of stage-coaches has been demon- strated." THE PROBABLE. DURATION OF OUR COAL FIELDS —The importance of our coal and iron industries is strikingly shown in "The Coal and Iron ledustries of the United Kingdom," just issued by Mr. Richard Meade. In 1880 the qu ,ntity of coal raised in these islands amounted to 116,969,409 tons, havine a money value of £62,395,414 sterling at the pit's mouth. In the same year were raised f,cm enr own mines 13,026,409 tons of iror ore, from which, ei h the addition of some 2,634.400 tors of imported ore, by the power of 567 blast furnaces, were made 7,749,233 tone of pig iron, with a vales of £19,373,082. The probable du- ration of oar coal supply is a question invested with addi- tional interest owing to the greatly increased quantity drawn from the collieries in the last two years. The in- crease in 1330 over the previous year amounted to 12,810,394 tons, while we find from a non-official seurce that the quan- tity of coal raised in 1881 was 151,184,300 tons, or 7,214,:591 toes increase upon the yield of eur collieries in 1880. This question has been examined by M. Meade with all the ad- vantages of our new light; and he gives exelatively the fellowine results _ .

Although there has been an in- ereass of more than 7,000,000 tons last year, it does not seem likely that the future increase will continue in a correspond- ing ratio. Checks will, from various causes connected with the many uneertaintise attendaat en manufacture and com- merce, be continually arising; and,examining the results of the het t venty years, we find that the rate of increase has been less thin 4,000,000 tons in each year. A NEw Tdit,Panaa 2/7.??2°/ Vrem.ya gives an account of a new submarine boat, the inveebis of M. Dgevetsky, which has recently been submitted to trlale at Cronstadt. Same previous experiments had already been condanted in the Black Sea, and the Ministry of Marine considered the result so important that they assigned a sum of money to cover the construction of 50 boats of this design. These boats are now completed, and some of them have been despatched to the Black Sea and the rest are re tamed for service in the Baltic. The proportions of these, vessels are very small, being from about 151 t. to 201 t. in length, but of sufficient weight and bulk to effect their pur. pose of subaqueous attack. The weight of each it not more than 150 poods, and is such, therefore, as to ;admit of every man-of-war having several of them on board. The last examples have been fitted with appliances by means of , which they may be hoisted on deck like ordinary ships' boats. The subaqueous boat of M. Dgevetsky has the form of a cigar, its screw propeller is moved by the feet of four men placed in the central part of the vessel beneath a small glass dome, through which the officer in command can see the submerged portion of the enemy's vessel, and accord- inely direct the attack. The speed attainable by these boats i= four miles an hour, which, it is considered, is amply sufficient to enaole a subaqueous attack to be made upon vessels lying at anchor or approaching. The steerage of the boat presents no difEculty. To lower it to the dis- tance of 50ft, and to raise it again to the surface of the water is rendered an easy operation by a very ingenious device. This elevation or depression is effected by means of weights made to slide upon longitudinal, horizontal bars or guide rails. When the boat is fully stored, charged, and equipped, its normal position is just beneath the surface of the water, the upper portion of the glass dome alone slightly emerging. When it is desired to sink to a certain depth the weights are slid forward to the prow of the boat, which, upon the propeller being set in motion, immediately begins to deecend. The depths attained are shown by a specially-constructed manometer. As soon as the boat has reached the desired depth, the weight is moved back to the centre of the boat, and the latter now takes a horizontal direction. In order to rise to the surface the weight is slid back to the stern, and thus an upward direc- tion is communicated to the motion of the boat. Each of these boats is provided with a couple of mines or torpedoes, attached by means of levers. As soon as the boat passes underneath an enemy's ship these can be instantly detached, and are so constructed as to mount upwards, and, by means of a gutta-percha appliance, attach themselves pneumati- cally to the enemy's hull. The attacking boat then retires , to a safe distance, paying out at the same time the electrode wires in connection with the torpedo, which is then ex- ploded. A supply of air compressed to a 50th of its normal volume is kept in a strong reservoir for the inhalation of the crew manceuvring the subaqueous vessel, and is emitted ,by valves of a particular construction. Sufficient air is stored in this way to last 24 hours; the exhaled gases are at the same time absorbed by chemical means. Such are the general features of this new invention. M. Dgevetsky, who is at present in Paris, is said to be devising means of applying electricity as the motive power in these boats, and thus considerably increase their speed.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c. An agricultural school at Mangra Nowa (Oleska), which completed ha first year this Easter with 75 scholars, has in- creased since then to 113. The two lower classes and the 4th, sth, and 61t are conducted on the same principle as in the ordinary gymnasiums and there are eight superior masters under the manar2ement of a director. A new schooll is being erected, which will be taken possession of at ' Michaelmas this year. It is stated that quite recently stablemen throughout the city of Philadelphia have been surprised at the appearance of a peculiar disease among many of the horses under their charge, affecting the feet and ankles of the animals in a most unusual way. The first symptoms are fever and in- flammation upon the parts around the pasterns and below the fetlock. The following morning there are running dis- charges of a thick yellowish matter, and afterwards pus begins to flow freely. The horse becomes lama and dispirited, and is totally unlit for work. Experienced horsemen and veterinarians apJear to be at a loss to comprehend fully the nature of the disease, but all are united in the opinion that it his been caused by the salted railroad tracks. A few of the street railway horses are afflicted, but the drivers are _ _ _

reticent in speaking of the matter. After examining with great care 710 plans and models of stock cars, submitted for their endorsament, a committee of the American Humane Society make the following state- ment :—" It is our deliberate conviction, forced upon us against our will, that it is hardly possible for any inventor, no matter how skilled he may be, to invent a successful stock-car, in which stock may be properly separated so that they can lie d )wn and rest, and in which they can be fed and watered, while in motion, without such car infringing on some one or more of the patents granted previous to Feb. 1, 1881, of even previous to Jan. 1, 1881." This is pre- cisely how the matter stands in this country. The only remedy for the necessary evils connected with the convey- ance of animals by railway lies in rapid transit and in the extension of the dead meat trade to its fullest workable limit.

The list of candidates for the Royal Agricultural Benevo- lent Institution, recently sent to subscribers in preparation for the election in June, is a melancholy document. The number of candidates, counting each married couple as one, as in the list, is 314; and out of these cnly 52 can be elected, leaving 322 unfortunates disappointed. .No wonder that Lord C arington, as chairman of the Executive Council, has appealed to the public for additional help in this time of almost unexampled distress among farmers He states that since the foundation of the society 900 cases of real agricultural distress have been permanently relieved, at a cost exceeding £93,000; and 550 necestitotts farmers, their widows and orphans, now swell the list of pensioners, at an annual cost of £12,600. To meet the present demands upon the Institution a further sum of £B,OOO to £9,000 is re- nuked. Could not the Lord Mayor of London be induced to open a fund for the purpose? Celery trenches ought to be prepared in good time, and not, as is so often the case, be deferred until the plants have really become week through overcrowding. In a small gar- den it is never advisable to have celery very forward, for the simple reason that trenches cennot be made for it until peas come off and other early crops are over. The less check to the plant the better, and to ensure fine celery the cultivator must be in advance of events rather than lag be- hind them. Plenty of manure must be used; it is scarcely possible in fact, to employ too much, and liberality is not waste, because the ground will be in capital condition for the next crop. There are many modes of planting celery, but the simplest is to make the trenches four feet apart and a foot and a half wide, and put the plants nine to 12 inches apart, according to the sorts. In planting take off suckers and observe if any of the leaves are blistered, and, if they are, finish by dusting the plantation with soot. THE LATE STORMS AND THE FRUIT TREES.—Oat-door fruit prospects are by no means so bright as they were pre- vious to the hurricane that did so much damage a fortnight ago. The windward side of thousands of trees is almost as hare as in winter, and they will not recover from the check they have received for a long time; indeed, some trees are apparently ruined. It is curious to ebserve that the young fruit on several trees resisted the wind much better than the foliage did; but it will be very unwise to permit the injured portions to be further exhausted by a heavy crop. The crop, where there is one, should be heavy on the healthy side, and light on the weak one; the trees may then in some measure recover their lost balance. Where young or recently planted trees have had the growths cut off on one side, be- ing healthy on the other, it will be worth consideration whether the points should not be pinched off some a the free-growiog shoots, to slightly check their progress and enable the weaker side to gain strength. If trees are allowed to be " one-sided" in a young state, symmetrical and well- developed specimens can never be produced. There is no better nor safer mode of regulating the growth of trees and distributing the sap equally, and thus producing equal growth on all sides, than by taking the tips off any shoots , that are seen to be growing grossly. The sap is then di- ' verted into other channels where it is needed, and the weak parts are strengthened. This pinching and regulating may be done now, but it must be done thoughtfully and judi- ciously. These remarks apply to trees of all kinds whether they have been injured by the storm or not, for undoubtedly one of the most essential points in fruit culture is to secure well-balanced trees, and it is a great fallacy to think that , malformed trees can be made symmetrical, and kept so, by winter pruning alone. A BARLEY GRUB.—F. J. Hammond, Adlington, West Mailing, Kent, writes to the Agricultural Gazette as tot- lows:—This afternoon, when hunting fotfrevireworm in a field of barley which appeared affected by that plague, I found what I have never heard of or seen before. Having always understood that patchiness and yellowness showed wireworm, and having frequently found it at the roots of yellow plants of corn, I deg up several such roots with my knife, but only to find the seed black and withered; in some cases entirely devoid of the nutritive matter, in others only partially so, as at this stage of growth might reasonably be expected; but in the former case the seed, or rather skin, contained a very little black dust and a minute violet- coletered worm. The worm, when examined under a micro- scope, is apparently no more than a worm —i.e , has no legs, is of a pale violet hue, with a brown head, and is about the eighth of an inch in length. As I found several such, I would ask, through the medium of your paper, whether any of your readers have found a similar thing in their own bar- ley crop, and I should also be glad to know what it is, and how it may possibly be prevented ?—Miss Ormerod has kindly reported as followe :—" I never met with the attack described, and the only one resembling it that I am aware of is that of the 'little corn moth,' scientifically the Butane unrealella. The grub of this moth is about the length named, it has a brownish head, and is described as'smooth,' the legs being so small as only to be distinguishable with the help of a strong magnifying glass. It is characteristic of , this larvae to clear out all the inside of the grain (barley or or other corn) thus reducing it to the mere skin described, and also the very little black dust,' found together with the grub agrees with the note by Curtis of the grub being found in the grain along with some little brown and yellow grains,' which are its excremennand which, from their being ' fewer in number with old than young larvae, and also from there being no aperture in he in)ared corn' are supposed to be re-eaien onai or twice. The grea, if of this kind, will probably turn to the moth during the month of May er eery I in Jane, and if some of the infested corn were forwaided to ! me, I would do what I could to rear the creatures and get I them identified. This moth has sometimes caused great de- I struction in the warmer parts of France; also was trans- ported to the United States, where it was naturalised in the more southerly parts, and is frequently brought thence in cargoes to New York; but the climate there is too cold for it to thrive, so that (in case it should prove that the grub is! of this kind) it is not likely to establish itself as a perma- nent attack."

VISIT OF ENGLISH FARMERS TO A DUTCH FARDL-Mr. farm is called, " graan voor Int'ui2:tt.ll:lu sit,;; for Only a few ytmrs ago Alia fertile spot was covered with water. The farm is his own pro- perty, and contains 750 acres, half pasture and half arable, and is worth £3 per acre per annum to rent; 200 are kept, the whole of the milk being made into cheesa. We saw the milk of 180 cows in two large vats. These make from 21 to 26 cheeses a day, each being worth 13s. 6d. They are sent to England, and are sold as "Factory Darby." Mr. Vanderbreggen also buys milk of his neighbours, the present prices being sd. per gallon. We saw a great many bags filled with goods for the workmen; these we were told contained cone and tea, tobacco, sugar, rice, the., bought in quantity and retailed to the men on co-operative principles. Twelve pens, each containing five pigs, were next inspected; these are sold when fat at about 20 stones (14 lbs.) for about £7 etch—they were of very useful quality, a cross between a Yorkshire sow and a Berkshire bog. Maize meal and pea meal, mixed and scalded, and whey, is the food on which these pigs are fatted, the cows receiving, in addition to the hay, a soup of decorticated cotton cake nasal and a pudding of boiled meal, a mixture of beans, linseed, and maize. Fifty horses are tied up all under one roof, thirty of them workers, the others yearlings, two-year-olds, d:c The horses are all of the hackney type; they stand 3 feet 6 inches apart, and are awfully hot. The stabling, cow-houses, pig. genes, muck heap, and dairy are all in remarkable proximity to one another. There are 300 lambs, 200 ewes, and 100 yearlings on the farm. A fine bull was paraded for us, and a very useful stallion, lately purchased for £33, a very cheap animal indeed. A great number of store pigs and sows are kept in houses opening on to the pasture, where they roam at will. We were shown a boar and two sows from Mr. Spencer's herd, but we thought them rather poor specimens. We were much taken with the grass ensilage practised here. The grass is cat, and at once taken home, wet or dry, salted, and well trodden by men and boys; finally it is covered over with planks and a thick layer of sand. This is done in June or July, and in November is ready for use. Cows prefer it to any other food, and it adds largely to the quantity of milk they give. The hours of labour are here from five to seven, 7 30 to 12, and one to seven, resting for a short ;time for tea, and the wages are 2s. a day. A teamsman has six horses to attend to, working three of them half a day and three the other half day. In harvest the men get 3s. a day, and something extra at haysel. Mr. Vanderbreggen then invited us to luncheon, and we inspected prizes for early beef-making, and a silver epergne for the best farm in Hol- land. Sir T. Fowell Buxton proposed the health of our host, regretting that this was the last tune we should meet our Dutch friends. He referred in felicitous terms to his chil- dren and grandchildren, and hoped that everything would prosper them, and for the last time we gave our musical honours. Mr. Vanderbreggen's reply was translated by his son to us, "It is happy to have gentlemen coming from a great country such as England is to see what is useful in Holland. It is still more happy because it is well known that England is far beyond Holland in all that is agricul- tural. It is a proof that he thinks so because he thorght I.

very good for his son to go to England to learn farming, and he is delighted you approve of what you have seen." Mr. Crommelin (whose son is a pupil of Mr. Vander. breggen's) also expressed the pleasure it had given him and his friends to see us in England, and he wished us a good passage and safe return. AGRICULTURAL PROSPECTS IN CEIESHIRE. A correspondent writes :—"I have just had a run through a portion of Cheshire, taking Northwic'n, Acton, and the line from Warrington via Lymm. I was scarcely clear of Old Trafford before the evil effects of the cold and wet weather became painfully visible. The grass has suffered a severe check and does not realise the expectations raised when I visited the district six weeks ago. But it looks worse, per- haps, than it really is in places, owing to the sorrel which has sprung up amongst it. Grain looks very sickly and yellow. Oats, besides looking dull, have apparently in several places got the grub. Wheat has lost root as well as colour. A little further west and grain looks much better, koth in colour and root. Oats are in want of genial weather. One can readily imagine how the few fine days at the end of last week have told favourably both upon oats and grass. Beyond Peel Causeway there are some good beans, but beans are almost invariably good this season, About the Bollin banks are some potatoes which have come up nicely, _ _ _ _ _

and some fields which are planted with the tuber in that locality seem to have a very comfortable tilth, and are appa- rently very free from weeds. There is a moderate bite of grass in the pastures, and the meadows have made a storing, thanks to the few warm clays. Oats look dull, but are evenly rooted. Farther west, approaching Knutsford, pastures are bore and meadows late. There are some luxuriant rushes in this neighbourhood, which is a bad sign. Beyond Knutstord wheat i:nproves, and good fields are not at all difficult to find, but very few are entirely free from the cold blight, though most of them would soon recover with genial weather. I only saw one really bad field of wheat, but it was the worst I have seen this season or expect to see. Oats, of which there is a large area, have suffered very consider- ably here, but there is plenty of root and there are some good fields. From Knutsford to Northwich there are some pretty good fields of clover and artificial grasses, but they

are not so forward as might have been expected, considering that "grass day " has been reached. The cattle that one sees in the fields are looking well, and several very nice lots are visible. Beyond Northwich natural and artificial grasses are fairly forward. Wheat has been sorely tried and weakened. From Acton to Warrington wheat is mixed ; • oats are com- paratively good. In this length there are plenty of potatoes up. I saw some in Acton eight or ten inches high, and plenty up in the row. Towards Preston Brook and Moore potatoes are looking very well, and are in the broad leaf by the acre together. I don't remember seeing a better look- out for potatoes. I had the opportunity of examining one field which I went to visit, and I could not see a single damaged leaf. The potatoes are also coming on well about Latchford, Thelwall, and Lymm. There is no sign of their being frost-bitten. Some of the wheat looks admirable, and presents a good colour. Wherever the ground is wet the wheat blades are yellowest and thinnest, and a little more careful attention to draining the wet spots would well repay the outlay. One of the best practical tenant farmers that I know, whose contract is to do his own draining, never allows a wet spot in a field to continue two years together. As soon as a drain ceases to do its work he cuts another and keens the arable soil dry, and although he has over a hundred acres under the plough there are none of those bare patches and none of those very yellow blotches in his grain which one encounters in so many places this season. On the way from Warrington to Manchester is some capital clover and ryegrass, but there are some bare pastures for the fine herds of cattle that graze there. I heard favourable reports of cattle generally, milkers doing very well. Pos- sibly the growth of grass during the winter months when the ground is usually at rest may account for the scar city in places now. Cattle, however, look well."

In 1323 O'Connell met Shiel among the Wicklow hills, and the two entered into earnest conferences on the pros- pects of Catholic Emancipation. "After exchanging their opinions," says Mr. Shiel, "on the deplorable state to which the Catholic mind had been reduced, and the utter want of organisation in the body it was agreed that they should both sign an address to the Irish Catholics, and enclose it to the principal people of that religion." The result of this pro- cedure was for the time not very encouraging. A very thin meeting which did not consist of more than twenty indi- viduals was held at the tavern in Sackville•street, and it was there determined that something should be done. Out of this minute germ arose the world-famous Catholic Associa- tion. The response to the appeal of O'Connell and Shiel came slowly at first, but it came. The association from a mere mustard seed grew apace, and in the couree of the following year attained a magnitude and importance of which its sanguine authors hardly dreamed. It drew into its net, circle after circle of Irish society. The people, the clergy, the gentry, the nobility.; of Catholic Ireland were embraced in its ample folds, and even many Protestants of distinction and influence were enrolled as members. To carry on the costly business of agitation, steady supplies were indispensible. The donations of opulence would soon have fallen short, and the middle class it was feared would grow weary of contributions. O'Connell invented a device which solved the difficulty. Membership of the Association was founded on the payment of a penny a month or a shilling a year. In every parish collectors were appointed to gather from the humble and the well-ter-de their c Amon. quota, and to enrol thele subscriptioete " The pence of the poor," said O'Connell, "will do more to emancipate the peer than the pounds of the peer will do to emancipate them, for whenever a man gives his money he gives his heart, and whenever ascendancy finds that enough of hearts are beating together, it will give way." The Catholic Rent was the fruit of this sagacious counsel, and by the end of 1824 it had reached £5OO a week. The Government became seriously alarmed. Despair of redress had worked a miracle of union in the people. Early in 1825 Mr. Goulburn, then Secretary for Ireland, brought into Parliament and carried through both Houses "a Bill for Suppression of Unlawful Associations in Ireland." This law was of course aimed against the existing Catholic Association, which was not at all unlawful. Imitediately it was passed, the Association, under the legal advice of O'Connell, dissolved itself. But the agitation burst forth anew, and O'Connell redeemed his promise of "driving a coach and six through the Suppres- sion Act" by devising a new association for charitable pur- poses, such as was not forbidden by the Statute. While the Government thus made a show of coercion on the one hand, they had on the other prepared a bill for granting the Catholic claims in a certain stinted and very guarded manner. The Bill, which was prepared under the inspiration of Sir Robert Peel, proposed to admit Catholics both in England and Ireland to Parliament and to Municipal Corporations, but provided for Ireland two very imperteet safeguards for the perpetuation of English supremacy in that island. In the first place the entire class of comity voters having freeholds worth 40s. were to be disfranchised. These made the great bulk of the rural voters. The other measure was to pension the Catholic clergy. The bill pro- vided that they were to be paid out of the Treasury at the rate of £l,OOO to each Bishop, £3OO to a Dean, £2OO to a parish priest, and £OO to a curate. O'Connell, who was in London as one of a deputation, had much conversation with leading Whig politicians upon the terms of the proposed mealure, and upon the way in which it might probably be received in Ireland as a fireal settlement, and he expressed his willingness to take the bill as it stood with the two con- ditions—called "the wings of the bill." On his return to Ireland he found that both priests and people were resolutely opposed to both of "the wings," and "when O'Connell found," seys Mr. Mitchell, "that his complying disposition was very likely to injure his popularity and his power for good, he very promptly and frankly retracted, and took his position again with his countrymen." Fortunately the bill itself was defeated. After passing the Lower House, it en• countered most infuriated opposition in the Lords. The Duke of York distinguished himself by a speech against the measure of the iatensest malignity, which threatened to have a most serious effect, as he was heir presumptive to the Crown of England. In presenting a petition from the Dean and Canons of Westminster against the bill, his Royal , Highness took occasion to declare his own opinions on the Isubject, and his own intentions in case of his succeeding to the Crown. He laid before the House the case of the late King—the severe illness and ten years of misery which had clouded the existence of "his illustrious and beloved I father" on account of the scruples of his conscience about the coronation oath, he declared that his principles were the same, and "that these were the principles to which he would adhere, and which he would maintain and act up to the latest moment of his existence whatever might be his situation of life—so help him God." The Lord Chancellor Eldon listened with delight, and wrote out the speech in his anecdote book before he slept. The bigots on his side got it printed in gold letters, and framed it for their draveing•roam walls, and circulated it through the country. The " dalo-me•God Duke" fell ill, and O'Connell treated his ill- ness in the following style: "I wish no physical ill to the royal duke, bat if he has thrown his oath in the way of our libertiee, and that as long as he lives justice shall not be done to the people of Ireland, it is mockery te tell me that the people of Ireland have not an interest in his ceasing to live. Death is the corrector of human errors; it is said to be man's hour for repentance, and God's opportunity. If the royal duke should not become converted from his po- litical errors I am perfectly resigned to the will of God, and shall abide the result with the most Christian resignation." Clearly the effect produced by this " Help-me God speech" was somewhet different from whet was intended and ex- I pected. It showed that an effort must ba ,made to secure Catholic Emancipation during the life of the present King, aad exertion was stimulated accordingly. Simultaneous meetings to petition were organised. Tee rent was collected more amply and expended more boastfally than ever. Moderate men, exasperated at the royal declaration, joined the Catholic Association, and the Irish Executive were de- I fied openly by O'Connell aed Shiel to put it down.

BY 11 ILLIAM FRANCIS. No. XXI.—DANIEL O'CONNELL. To side with truth is noble, When we share her wretched crust, 'Ere her cause bring forth fame and profit, And 'tis prosperous to be just.—Anon.

In the October of 1810 George 111. sank into drivelling idiocy—a condition in which "the once feared monarch" continued until the day of his death. While he possessed what little stock of wits he had, the Catholics had no hops of relief. But now when his son, the Prince of Wales, be- came Regent, the hopes of the Catholics suddenly revived. The Regent had not only m Ade repeated professions of good will to the Catholics and their cause—he was even known xo have pledged himself expressly on more than one occa- sion "that as soon as he should enjoy the regal authority he would do all in his power to secure Catholic Emancipa- tion." No sooner, however, did the "first gentleman of his age" take the reins into his own hands than he convinced the Catholic that he certainly had not that which his father professed to have had—a conscience. Under the in- fluence of the Marchioness of Hertford, a lady who not only hated the seven sacraments of the Church of Rome, bet who found the two sacraments of the Church of England too many to observe—the Prince Regent violated all his pledges and treated the Catholics with the utmost contempt. Great indignation was felt in Ireland in consequence thereof. At a public meeting resolutions were adopted in which the Catholics expressed "their deep disappointment and anguish on learning how the promised boon of Catholic freedom had been interrupted by the fatal witchery of an unworthy secret influence, hostile to their fairest hopes, spurning alike the sanctions of public and private virtue, the demands of per- sonal gratitude, and the sacred obligations of plighted honour." The Catholics also spoke of a certain "impure source" to which all their immediate grievances could be traced. They expressed their just contempt for "fickle courtiers or the pompous patronage of men who would sacri- fica at the shrine of perishable power or to the blandish. meats of a too luxurious Court the feelings and interests of millions." They also expressed their resolution never to "abandon the pursuit of equal constitutional rights—uncon- ditional, unatipniated, unpurchased by dishonour." These resolutions, which were brought forward by O'Connell, were known as "Witchery Resolutions," and were levelled against the influence hostile to the Catholic cause supposed to be exercised over her royal paramour by the Marchioness of Hertford. They caused a considerable fluttering of wings among all the butterflies and gadflies that haunted Carlton House, and their stinging sarcasms sank deep into the Regent's breast, and they were never forgiven nor forgotten. Almost the first act of any consequence done in Ireland after the Prince became Regent was a State prosecution instituted against the Catholic Committee in the person of two of its members, Mr, Kirwan and Dr. Sheridan, who were delegates, for breach of the Convention Act. The Government hRd long been watching for this chance, and now the Castle strained every means to ensure a conviction. A cmviction was obtained, and the Catholic Committee in that form ceased to exist. "A great blow," says Mr. Shiel, "had been struck at the cause, e and a considerable time elapsed before Ireland recovered from it." Bat although that or- ganisation was at an end, many angry meetings were held; and the Catholic fress assumed a tone of .agaression and defiance which had not been usual with it. O'Connell, in conjunction with others, both by tongue and pen, on the e‘tet'orm aed throtreh the press, still carried on the agita- te • tion with baldness, ability, r 4 vigour. Godlike 1812 the " odirse Mr. the "No-Popery Prime Minister," was assassinated by a maniac in the lobby of the House of Commons, and a change of Administration became necessary. Bat the new arran rements had little in- terest for Irishmen, and presented no i'tope of any approval to justice in the treatment of that country. Lord Liverpool was Prime Minister, and both Canning and Castlereagh were members of the Cabinet. This Cabinet was nicknamed by Tierney as "Liberty Hall," beceuee the members thereof were at liberty to act t th.Ty pleased in reference to the Catholic quellon. Six years after this George 111. died. The "first gentleman of Europe" had virtually reigned eight years when the death of his father gave him the crown. He exchanged the title of Regent for that of Ktng, and no other alteration was expected by the public. "Liberty Hall" appeared to red t upon a stable foundation, and its efforts for crushing the liberties of the people both in England and in Ireland were •supported by a powerful majoritv in P4rliamout, In 1821 a measure of Catholic Emancipation as carried through the Horne of Commons, but defeated in the Lords chiefly through the influence of the Duke of York, heir presumptive to the throne. This was 1 followed by the Coronation of the King—a cold and costly ceremonial, rendered melancholy by the exclusion of the unfortunate Queen who retired home to die of grief and mortification. Immediately afterwards the King visited Ireland.

'Ere the daughter of Brunswick is cold in her grave, And her ashes still float to their home o'er the tide, Lo George the triumphant speeds over the wave To the long cherished isle which he loved like his bride.

Sir Benjamin Bloomfield had already been sent over, and had intimated the royal anxiety that "all differences and animosities shbuld be laid aside." Accordingly it was agreed that a public dinner should be held, where the leaders of both parties should pledge each other in libations' of ever- lasting amity. "This national festivity," says *Shiel, "took place, and from the vehement protestations on both sides it was believed by many that a lasting reconciliation had been effected. Master Ellis and Mr. O'Connell almost embraced each other." The King was the only person who reaped any benefit from this procedure. The Catholics deter- mined not to obtrude their grieraves upon him, and accor- dingly he passed rather a pleasant time in Dublin. He was hailed with tumultuous hurrahs wherever he passed, and in return for the enthusiastic reception which he had received he directed Lord Sidmouth to write a letter recommending it to the people to be united. His Majesty shortly after- wards set sail with tears in his eyes from Danleary. An obelisk marks the spot where the King stood previous to going on board, and the name of Danleary was changed or degraded into Kingstown. So ended the visit of "the first gentleman of Europe" to his loving subjects the Irish. Clearly on this occasion the Irish of George IV. deceived each other. It was expected that the King would in some way put an end to the civil and religious differences which had so long distracted Ireland. O'Connell seems to have shared this belief. His fervour of loyalty to the corrupt- hearted King was carried to the utmost excess of servile adulation, and the Catholics professed a personal devotion to their sovereign that passed the limits even of passive obedi- ence. This humiliation was most disastrous. The King hearing no complaint of grievances, and receiving no pe- tition for redress, sagely concluded that the Irish were well satisfied with the existing state of things, and that Eman- cipation was sought only by some obscure faction. The Irish looked upon the King's theatrical embrace of the shamrock and the unmeaning letter of farewell, prepared by Lord Sidmouth, as certain signs of an approaching change

div.head: POLITICAL ITEMS.
div.p: POLITICAL ITEMS.

The Prime Minister has consented to receive a deputation from the Scottish Farmers' Alliance upon the subject of a I reform of the Land Laws in Scotland. The interview will probably take place early in June. The report that Mr. Parnell contemplates resigning his seat in Parliament is inexact. The hon. gentleman may possibly take a short leave of absence from the house after the passing of the Prevention of Crime Bill, but he does not intend wholly to retire from public life. It is stated that when the Procedure Rules come on for consideration after Whitsuntide a determined effort will be made from the Opposition benches to stop further progress for the §cr7s;oll, Mr, To c9llinS will move that the order for the arilo'irrned debate be tiltc.' begat Mr. Thomas Baring Was the only Conservative who voted with the majority on Tuesday night in both divisions on the Arrears Bill. Mr. Bellingham, Conservative Home Ruler; voted, however, with the Government in the first division. Two Liberals, Messrs. Albert Grey and Montagu Guest, voted in both divisions with the Opposition. There are now eight pages of amendments on the Preven- tion of Crime Bill on the paper, and several fresh amend- I ments were given in on Tuesday night. It is at present impossible to say how long the committee on the bill will last, but it is now hardly possible that the committee stage will close this week. The Irish members are determined to fight several of the clauses of the bill more obstinately than was at one time anticipated. Addressing a meeting of. the Kensington Conservative WorFing Men's Clubs on Saturday, Lord H. B. Bruce said , that when the Government released Mr. Parnell they ought ' to have replaced him in Kilmainham by Mr. Gladstone, and Mr. Parnell, in his opinion, ought to have gone to Downing- street. With regard to the Kilmainham compact, they would never get to the bottom of the matter ; but, for their information, he would tell them that Mr. Chamberlain, that political Mephistopheles, was deeply concerned in it. The public interest in the proceedings of the House of Commons has reached a pitch somewhat embarrassing to the authorities. Night after night, whatever may be the busi- ness before the house, all the galleries open to strangers are filled. In the last Parliament it was rare to see more than half a dozen persons in the Distinguished Strangers' Gallery. The overflow from the other galleries filled on Monday night, as on all recent occasions. Lord Carnarvon was present on Wednesday at a Conser- vative gathering at Hanley, and moved a resolution, "That this meeting, whilst anxious to support the Executive Government in the enforcement of order and the repression of crime in Ireland, desires at the same time to record its emphatic protest against the vacillating and revolutionary policy pursued by Her Majesty's Government, which has resulted in bloodshed and sedition, and threatens to bring about the dismemberment of the Empire." He charged the responsibility for the present condition of Ireland upon Her Majesty's present Administration, which, he said, had been a gross and manifest failure. Accordiug to the picture pre- sented by the noble lord, the Government is in a deplorable plight. Supporters in and out of the Cabinet are withdraw- ing their allegiance. "Literature, science, and art, the pro- fessional classes, property, education, intelligence, are all crying off from the Government, and are seeking their true home where it ought to be, namely, under the shadow and shelter of the constitutional cause." Meanwhile, the ship of the State, "swept onward by extravagant floods of rhetoric," seemed in danger of foundering: This might be attributed to the Government's incompetence or ill luck, but in either case the Government were "not the persons to whom the great fortunes of historic England should be entrusted." He declared that the Conservative party had no desire for office—what they desired was to make the Government do their duty. The most wholesome and nutritious of confections is far less consumed than it would be were It not for the greatly adulterated articles sold under the name of chocolate. Every cake of Chr;colate bearing the name of Cadbury is guaranteed to consist solely of pure Cocoa and white -sugar, and may there- fore be given to children with perfect safety. Chocolate makers by special appointment to the Queen.—Advt.
THE STATE OF IRELAND.
Major Clifford Lloyd arrived at Foynes on Saturday, and proceeded by the gunboat Banterer on a tour of in- spection.

The boy Meloly shot at Ballina by the police on the night of the 6th inst., during the affray there, died on Sunday morning. This is the only death. On Monday night, at Athenry, County Galway, the house of a man named Madden was fired into. He was wounded while sitting at his fireside. A Parliamentary return issued on Wednesday shows that during April last 519 families were evicted in Ireland. Of these 237 were readmitted as tenants or caretakers. Dr. Butler, Roman Catholic Bishop of Limerick, has re- fused to sanction the reappointment of the Rev. Eugene Sheehy, of Land League notoriety, to a curacy in his diocese.

The Rev. Father Doyle, whose speech denouncing Dublin Castle as "a nest of vipers which should be burnt to the ground," and was referred to by the Irish Solicitor-General in Parliament, has arrived in New York.

The Feeeman's Journal says that the members of the Irish Metropolitan Police Force have during the last few days resumed their side swords, which were introduced some yEars since during the Fenian agitation, but were shortly afterwards dispensed with. They have not bcen worn since until .now.

The secretary of the Liverpool branch of the Land League has received a letter from Mr. Davitt, accepting an invitation to visit Liverpool in the course of the next two weeks. Preparations are being made by the League for a demonstration on an extensive;scale, to give him such a re- ception as they think him entitled to. The farmer.O'Donnell, who was found insensible on the railway line about five miles from Trate° four days since, died on Tuesday morning. He is believed to have been murdered from agrarian causes. Sticks bespattered with blood have ben found about 400 yards from the place. Tbree arrests have been made on suspicion. At the Dublin Police Court, on Wednesday, Thomas Caffrey was committed for trial for being concerned wr.1.1 three others in stabbing a young man named Duffy, who had given information to the police in reference to a shoot- ing —••— in the citT. The men entered Duffy's room , and stabbed him.

On Saturday night an armed party visited Crag House ant fired at the caretaker, a pensioner named James •Forde. The men then decamped, but Forde fired after them and shot one of the party in the back. He then informed the police, who on Sunday arrested a shoemaker named John Tubbridy, who was found to be wounded, though not fatally. In Dublin, on Monday morning, shortly before six o'clock, a policeman on his rounds found a loaded gun at the door of Dr. Lyons, one of the members for Dublin City, at 8.5, Merrion,,quare West. The weapon was taken to the police station. It is supposed the gun was placed there as a sigtificant warning to Dr. Lyons, who is unpopular with the Parnel I ite section. .

A series of outrages on tenant farmers was committed on Tuesday in daylight at Ilighwood, near Boyle, by three armed disguised men. The houses of four men, named Mullany, Flynn, Coulon, and Connaughton were attacked. Mullany was so badly wounded that his life is despaired of. Flynn's family were going to dinner when the shot broke the pot on the fire into splinters, severely wounding Flynn's son. The men attacked had cattle grazing on boycotted farms.

A special correspondent in Ireland describes the condition of that part of Connemara which has been the scene of recent evictions. About 300 families have been turned out of their holding 3 within a fortnight. Many of the evicted tenants have been re-admitted as caretakers; but in a large proportion of cases there is neither shelter nor means of subsistence. The people would welcome emigration as an escape from their present miseries, which are due to a sheer inability to pay rent, owing to the poverty of the district and the badness of the seasons.

One of the results of the Phcenix Park tragedy may pro- bably be the construction of a new detective force for all Ireland, the Metropolitan detectives' being absorbed into the extended constabulary department for the detection of crime. The Dublin Detective Division comprises only 44 !non, but the multinudinous duties put upon them leaves, at the outside, about a dozen at the disposal of the inspector for actual detective work. The proposition has been made to organise a completely new system, having a special director—a man of experience and position—and that a very superior class of men should be asked to join. _ A VINDICTIVE TENANT. _

A man named Kennedy, a tenant of Mr. Benjamin Going, of Ballyphillips, County Tipperary, has made a determined attack upon his landlord's residence. Late on Tuesday night he visited the house armed with a hatchet, uttered violence denunciations against all landlords, and sought to burst in the door; fail ing in this he attacked and killed two valuable setter dogs. He and three other men, with whom he was drinking, were afterwards apprehended in a public-house. BRUTAL MAIMING OF ANIMALS AT CORK. The other night several cows, the property of Frederick Harrison, County Cork, were brutally mutilated. The tails of two were completely severed within one foot of the back- bone, and the tails of some others were so chopped as to remain suspended by only tha skin. The herd, which con- sisted of valuable heavy milk animals, were much injured by cuts and scars. Mr. Harrison has always opposed the Land League movement. A CLERICAL MOONLIGHTER. The Rev. Thomas Rice, a near relative of the Attorney- General, was on Monday sent to eaol for six months on the complaint of his wife, who charged him with having threatened to hang her. This gentleman gave a great deal of trouble in Dublin recently, and since his sojourn in Cork has given the aulhorities a great deal of annoyance. Ills practice is to go about the country as Captain Moonlight demanding. arms from farmers and others.

ARCHBISHOP CHOKE AND COERCION. In replying to an address presented to him at Galbally, County Limerick. Archbishop Croke said it would have b-?en well for the Government if they had last year adopted the suggestions of the Catholic bishops in Ireland as to the amendment of the Land Bill. He earnestly called on the Cabinet to pause in their coercive career, and to consult the friends instead of the enemies of the country.

div.head: RIOTING AT LIMERICK.
div.p: RIOTING AT LIMERICK.

Another serious riot took place at Limerick, on Saturday. Three constables, whilst on patrol, arrested a man for being drunk and disorderly, when they were set upon by a mob of over a thousand people and stoned. Acting-constable Scully and Sub-constable Stewart, who assisted in the arrest, are bath severely wounded, their lives being endangered. The police drew their revolvers, but did not use them. Several priests endeavoured to quiet the mob, but were unable to do so, and one of them was struck and knocked down with a large stone. One of the clergymen then went to the police barracks for assistance, when 40 constables, armed with loaded rifles, turned out and charged the mob, scattering them. The wounded constables retained their prisoner, and lodged him in the police barracks. No magistrate was present,.

The Chief Secretary for Ireland has ordered that in cones- einence of the lawlessness that prevails in the city the police force shall be increased by thirty men. Two constables have been appointed to the new detective department lately formed, with Colonel Brackenbury at its head, and each stipendiary magistrate will have a detective to protect him, and be in his vicinity at all times. Some of the stipendiaries have protested against this, but are compelled to accept pro- tection.

div.head: DUBLIN ASSASSINATIONS.
div.p: THE DUBLIN ASSASSINATIONS.

The belief is now generally accepted that the murderers of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke have succeeded in leav- ing- Dublin. All the clues obtained have been followed up and have led to nothing. Discussing the failure of the attempts to discover the Dublin assassins, the Daily Noes contends there is little to show that many parsons outside the society of the murderers know much of the affair. There is but one hope, not so much of arresting the criminals as of acquiring some faint knowledge of the workings of their system. Some one my be tempted to inform, but the chances are extremely remote.
The Daily News understands it is the intention of the Irish exi:cutive to permit the provisions of the Coercion Act to lapse horn the moment when the Prevention of Crime Bill becomes law,

The Standard sAys Mr. Parnell's contemplated resignation of his seat in Parliament is opposed by the Laud League Executive, though the member for Cork has strongly urged his desire to reside for some time on the Continent.

The Lord-Lieutenant having requested that the manu- script of the story published in the l'reenzan's Journal, pur- porting to be a confession by one of the Phocenix Park assassins, a reply was sent that the document might be seen at the office of the Journal on Saturday. An official of the detective department inspected it, and it is understood has furnished a report to his Excellency. The Mayor and citizens of Cork offer, by the means of numerous placards, a supplemental reward of £l,OOO for the apprehension and conviction of the murderers of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke. It will be remembered the offer was made to the Lord-Lieutenant, who advised that it should be independent of the Government reward.

div.head: COLONEL BRACKENBURY.
div.p: COLONEL BRACKENBURY.

Colonel Brackenbury has been appointed Director-General of the new Criminal Investigation Department for Ireland. The Pall Mall Gazette says that Lieutenant-Colonel Brackenbury will have his head office in Dublin Castle, ani all resident magistrates throughout the country and the Commissioners of the Metropolitan Police will have to re• port every case of crime to him. The Dublin detectives will be included in the organisation, and they will have a power which they at present do not possess of following the investigation of cases into any part of Ireland, and arrest- ing the prisoners outside the metropolitan district without being compelled to get the permission of the constabulary authorities in the respective counties, as they were hitherto obliged to do. Men of superior education who have not undergone police drill or barrack discipline will be employed as detectives.

div.head: FENIAN MANIFESTO.
div.p: A FENIAN MANIFESTO.

The Council of the "Fenian Brotherhood " at New. York has issued a manifesto to Irish revolutionists at home and abroad. The following is an extract from this document:— "The spirit of revolution is abroad. Every effete, gouty monarchy in Europe totters on its rotten foundations. Brethren, awake! arise! and labour with us new. Thus shall we, with solemnity and secrecy, continue with aug- mented force, to give the emphasis of the dagger, tire, and sword, and of other available resorces of civilisation,' to our ancient, merciless, unrelenting enemy; to destroy whom we shall use, while life endures, every means within the reach of human effort.
