div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNEspAy.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNEspAy.

A PERSONAL EXPLANATION.—Mr. FORSTER made a personal explanation arising out of a statement made by Mr. J. Low- titer in one of his recent Yorkshire speeches, to the effect that the ex-Chief Secretary's colleagues had conducted " clandestine negotiations " to a great extent utterly un- known to him. Mr. Forster declared that the member for North Lincolnshire had been absolutely misinformed, as he was cognisant of the negotiations, although the time came when be was no longer able to share in the responsibility connected with them. It was entirely contrary to his belief that there was anything clandestine connected with the negotiations. Mr. Gladstone explained that he and his col- leagues were compelled to deny entirely that the word " negotiations " was applicable in any manner to what was done. THE PREVENTION or CRIME BILL.—The debate on Mr. Cowen's amendment to the motion for going into Committee on the Prevention of Crime Bill was resumed by Mr. DILLON, who said he looked forward to a gradual settlement of the land question in three or four years. The members of the Land League were now anxious to conduct their movement without outrage, but outrages could not be put down so long as evictions prevailed. He had never denounced outrage in Ireland, and never would denounce it until the English Par- liament denounced evictions. The weapon he had pointed out, which could take the place of outrage, was" boycottirnr," and he openly advocated that because he saw in it the means by which he could convince the people that they could pro- tect their rights Erore effectually than by violent outrage. He predicted that the bill before the House would have a most injurious effect in rendering the people more opposed to law and in creating secret combinations.—Mr. QLADSTONE asserted that the speech of Mr. Dillon was a heart-breaking speech. That his declaration that he should refuse to denounce outrage should be made in the name of liberty, in that great temple of liberty, was amongst the gravest facts which could carry sorrow to the depth of his heart. In his defence of " boycotting " the hon. member for Tip- perary appeared as the apostle of a creed of force, of op- , pression, of the destruction of all liberty, and of the assertion of a despotism detached from all law, from all tradition, and all restraint. The right hon. gentleman having replied to the objections of Mr. C. Russell appealed to all members of the House not to prolong the debate and to restrain discussion at the present stage as much as possible, as the result of preventing progress in Committee would be 1 to delay the Arrears Bill. One or two insignificant Tory members who endeavoured to make capital out of this inci- dent were promptly snubbed by Sir Stafford NORTIICOTE, who declared it would be a misfortune if there seemed to be any uncertain sound from the Conservative side of the House when the Government were engaged in a task which was enough to try the strength of the strongest Government that England had ever seen. They had a right to criticise fear- lessly any measures that might be brought forward, but in face of the language that bad been use in the House that day, and in the face of the acts in the sister island, it was their duty to stand up manfully for the Government, and to support them as far as they were able in the legislation they had submitted. Mr. BORLASE declared that after hear- ing the speech of Mr. Dillon he and other Liberal members who had been preparing proposals for modifying the bill would now support the Government through thick and thin in passing the measure. On the motion of Mr. PARNELL the debate was adjourned. Mr. STEVENSON obtained leave to re-introduce his Sunday Closing Bill.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-THURSDAY.

POLICE PROTECTION IN IRELAND.—Mr. TREVELYAN in- formed Mr. Redmond that police protection was given to Mr Forster often against the right hon. gentleman's wishes. Bat when Lord Frederick Cavendish arrived unexpectedly in Ireland he was regarded as one of the Lord Lieu- tenant's party, and no official steps were taken to protect him. On censidering the matter with reference to the police, the Lord Lieutenant was obliged to take into account the fact that police protection had been objected to, and even forbidden, by Mr. Forster and Mr. Burke. EGYPT.—In answer to Mr. Bounce, Sir CHARLES DILUE said he WaS always anxious to answer-questions put by re- presentatives of the foreign policy of the late Government, but lea could not, in the interests of the public service., give any reply to the question now put as to whether the -des- patch of the fleets to Alexandria it met with the assent of the Great Po';' ors and the Porte, and whether the Govern- ment of France had objected to the despatch of Turkish troops to Egypt. With regard to the other questions, he could sey that the two Western Powers still felt confident that the. course agreed upon with regard to Egypt would meet the assent of all the Great Powers and the -Porte.! MICHAEL DAVITT.—Mr. GOIIST inquired what steps the 'Government intended to take in consequence of Mr. Davilt's speech at Manchester.—Sir Wm. Hancouna. said he had not seen the speech, and he did not feel hound to pass a com- mentary upon it. Till: PREVENTION OF CRIME BfLL.—The adjourned de- bate en the motion for going into Committee on the Preven- tion of Crime Bill was resumed by Mr. PARNELL, who, re- ferring to the speech of Mr. Dillon on the previous day, asserted that the deductions drawn by 'the Prime Minister from those remarks were not warranted. Alluding to his Ennis speech, in which he recommended " boycotting," the hon. member said that the practice had been much abused, and had been used for purposes for which it was never in- tended. He agreed that the system he then recommended would not have been perrnissabie in a self-governed country. It was a rough method, but it, was necessary that it should be employed. The introduction of the Arrears Bill was an snot-mons advance, hut the situation had been changed by the introduction of a Coercion Bill, and he thought much of the. character of the speech of Mr. Dillon was due to the despair he felt at the prospect before Ireland on account of that measure. He admitted the difficulties of the Ministers, but he did not admit that there was any justification for them to turn aside from ameliorating: measures and to enter upon fresh coercion. He feared that the passing of this bill would throw everything in Ireland into the hands of the secret societies.—Mr. G. Rus- SELL was in favour of some modification of the bill, but he should support it ha its entirety rather than seem by half- hearted approval to weaken the hands of the Executive.— Mr. A. ARNOLD said the Government had made important proposals for the modification of the bill, which led him to hope that when the House went into Committee they would consent to further modifications. He congratulated the Government that they had abandoned the crime-producing anct-exasperating policy of the Act of last year.—The bill was supported by Sir J. Hay and Mr. Mellor, and opposed by Mr. A. O'Connor, Mr. Redmond, and Mr. Synan.—Sir I". O'Brien said he would not support the bill, but would endeavour to give force to those amendments which tended to mitigate its severity.— Mr. TREVELYAN remarked that the speech of Mr. Parnell was a most remarkable one, and speaking of the distinctionsl he had drawn as to Boycotting, s.id the Government could draw no such distinctions. It was their bounden duty to ensure obedience to the law. During the first four months of this year there had been upwards of 1800 outrages the average for the present month being the same as in these preceding it, and while the increase on the outrages during the corresponding period of last year had been very large, the comparison made by Mr. Parnell between 1833 and the present time was hardly warranted, because, calculated according to the population, the result assumed a very different aspect, the number of inhabitants now being three millions more than in 1833. Alluding to the speech of Sir S. Northcote, he said the Government recognised in it the main attitude of the Conservative party, and had every , reason to be satisfied with the circumstance it indicated. As p4triots and Englishmen they should be very glad of the support of the right hon. gentleman (ironical cheers from the Parnellites). The member for Newcastle brought a very serious indictment against England for her treatment of Ireland (Land League cheers.) The hon. member's speech was very powerful, but it was not quste new; but whether it was new or not, it was very true and very painful, but the withers of the present Government were unwrung (cheers). There was no parrallel to be drawn between Ireland under the present administration and that of France under Louis Napoleon. In whatever shape the Press clauses were passed, any editor in Ireland might write exactly what he liked (" Oh, oh," from the Land Leaguers), if he would only ab- stain from putting in the advertisement of Captain Moon- light, or the invitations to private murder. (Cheers.) It had been said they were sending a message of conciliation and a message of coercion, but they were not sending them to the same address. The message of conciliation, what- ever hon. members might think of the method of it, was a very well meant message, and it was being sent to the hard working and struggling farmers of Ireland, but the message of coercion was being sent to a much smaller, he hoped a very small class, who were the worst enemies that those farmers could have (cheers). The Government placed very considerable reliance on the scheme which was being carried out for remodelling the in- telligence department in the Irish police. They had ap- pointed a special assistant secretary to keep in his hands all the threads of the police system of Ireland, and to apply his undivided attention to the business of detecting crime. The hon. member for Dundalk had said that there was nOthing in the bill which would enable them to procure satisfactory evidence. He believed, however, that the search clauses would bring evidenee forward. The proposal against which he had heard nothing from Irish members was the jury sys- tern as it was at present. (Hear, hear). That system was one under which thirty successive agrarian murders had been committed with impunity. (Cheers, and cries of" Not tried " from Irish members.) The clause for giving sum- mary jurisdiction to magistrates was essential to the bill. Great apprehension had been expressed at the powers being given to Major Bond and Mr. Clifford Lloyd. (Hear, hear.) He thought Major Bond's term of appoint- ment expired on the 3rd July, and would not be renewed. (Irish cheers, and cries of "Oh, oh," from the Opposition). If hon. members heard the whole case they would find Major Bond had not been thrown over. Mr. Clifford Lloyd had endeavoured to support the law by giving short but certain sentences, believing that the best course to be adopted, but for six months he had never sat in petty sessions, except in two or three trivial instances of vagrancy and drunkenness' and in the well-known cases of the Land League huts. Lord Spencer had determined that all cases of interference with the erection of huts ostensibly raised for the shelter of evicted persons should be submitted to his own eyes and judgment before action was taken by the police. (‘• Oh " from the Opposition and Irish cheers). After some further observations, the House divided with the following result :—Against Mr. Cowen's amendment, 344; for, 47; majority against, 207. The House soon afterwards adjourned.
WARRINGTON CEMETERY.—Returns of inteunents in the Warrington Cemetery during the week ending yesterday : Adults, 6 children, 3; total, 14.

div.head: TUE EXAMINEP, SATURDAY MAY 27, 1882.
div.p: TUE EXAMINEP, SATURDAY MAY 27, 1882.
MISOELLAN EOU S.

At ‘Vcdneshurv, on Tuesday, Jemima Hole, an inmate of West Bromwich 'Workhouse, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment for a brutal assault on her child, seven • months old. The prisoner had frequently beaten the child until it was black and blue, and on '1 uesclay morning she beat it until blood oozed from its ears. Had not the child been rescued, the prisoner would undoubtedly have murdered it. . At Bradford, on Tuesday,John Sydney Green was charged with being concerned in the illicit manufacture of spirits. On Saturday mornicg last the police and some excise officers seized an illicit still in an unoccupied house in Brad- ford, which they believed to belong to the prisoner. Subse- quently they arrested the prisoner, and found at his resi- dence the apparatus used in the manufacture of spirits. The prisoner, who had been previously convicted, was fined £6O. Lord Derby will preside at the approaching banquet of the Cobden Club. The presence of representatives of the Free Trade party in France, Holland, and the United States is also anticipated. The committee of the Club have decided that the following shall be the subject for the Oxford Prize Essay of 1883 :—" In what respect, on purely economical grounds, is the further application of a Free Trade policy required in the legislation of this country ?" A Conservative demonstration was held on Wednesday at Stratford. Lord Salisbury was the chief spokesman, con- fining his remarks to Irish affairs. He strongly condemned the policy of the Government, who, he said, had been bar- tering away the interests of the empire. The noble marquis denounced the policy of "conciliation," and declared that in the presence of .social revolution either the revolutionists or the Government must be struck down. THE SEE OF NEWCASTLE.—The London Gazette contains an Order in Council declaring the Bishopric of Newcastle founded. The diocese comprises the county of Northumber- land, the counties of the towns of Newcastle and Berwick, and also the ancient common law parish of Alston, with its chapelries, in the county of Cumberland. The parish church (St. Nicholas), Newcastle, is to be the cathedral church. _

Mr. Spurgeon has so fer recovered from the effects of rheumatic gout as to be able to resume part of his duties. In the erraordinary charge of conceaimcut. of birth at Tranmere, the accused, Emma Ferguson, was the other day committed for trial at the assizes.
The Lord Mayor of London (Mr. Ellis) bas received the honour of a baronetcy in recognition of the preservation of Epping Forest to the people by the exertions of the London Corporation.

Threeipolice officers were severely handled in attempting ti capture six poachers on Lord 6tamford's preserves, at Swindon, on Saturday. One of them is in a critical condi- tion. The poachers escaped, but they are known. Fifteen children have been treated in one of the Liver- pool hospitals as suffering from poisoning of the system owing to eating Calabar beans. The children found the beans in a receptacle for rubbish in a stable yard. The symptoms in one case assumed a serious character, but all the patients are now expected to recover. Late on Saturday night, Richard Wyatt, farmer, of Pitch- ford, Salop, was taking a bull out of the fold-yard, when the pole by which he was leading it boke. The infuriated animal made for Wyatt, who tried to escape by climbing over a gate. The bull, however, caught him, knocked him down, and gored him so frightfully that he was killed on the spot.

Many speculations have been rife, says the City Press, as to the cost of the proceedings on the day on which Her Majesty declared Epping Forest free for the people for ever. To correct these wide assertions, we may state that the whole cost of the celebration will fall short of £lO,OOO, and may possibly be as low as £B,OOO. During a thunderstorm which passed over Dudley and Netherton, on Monday afternoon, a boy named Elijah Ray- bould was killed by lightning. A storm also swept over Aylesbury, and the lightning struck the vicarage at Stoke Madeville, two miles distant, shattering the chimney. One of the agricultural journals says the prospects are very encouraging, much more so than has been the case for some years past, and, should the weather remain as propi- tious as at present, the result of the harvest can hardly fail to be very ageeeable to the agricultural interest. William Mertens, a German compositor, residing at 54, Whitfield-street, was charged on remand at Bow-street, Lon- don, on Wednesday, with publishing in the Freiheit a libel concerning the late Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke, and thereby inciting to murder. The prisoner was committed for trial, bail being refused. Mr. Mundella, the Vice-President of the Council, in presiding at the annual meeting of the Church School- masters' arid Schoolmistresses' Benevolent Institution on Saturday, said that during the past ten years there had been an increase of 20 per cent, on the average annual earnings of teachers employed by the National Society. He mentioned this to show that not only was education more appreciated, but that teachers were now better paid than formerly. • A CRUEL SISTER.—The Newcastle-under-Lyme magis- trates, on Wednesday, committed Rose Jackson, a married woman, to jail for six months for cruelty to her half-sister, a girl nine years old. The prisoner has been in the habit of beating the child till she was discoloured all over her body, and after renewing her attacks on Sunday, she kept her in a room for three days without food. The police re- moved the child to the North Staffordshire Infirmary, where she lies in a shocking condition. THE TEL RACE FROM CHINA.—A Lloyd's telegram from Shanghai states that the first two steamers have left Hankow for London, with full cargoes of the new teas. The race this year is between the new iron steamer Stirling Castle, of Glasgow, 4,500 tons register and 1,200 horse power nomi- nal, which ran 18 knots an hour on her voyage out, and the , fine steamer Glenfruin, 3,500 ton a register, which won the race last year. Great interest is taken in both steamers, and the run home is expected to be made in about 35 days. , TIIE HATTON-GARDEN ROBBERY.—In the Queen's Bench Division on Monday, Mr. Baron Pollock and a special jury had before them a case in which a firm of diamond mer- chants carrying on business in , London sued a firm of insurance brokers to recover.X3oo, the value of the insurance of two parcels of sapphires which were stolen in the robbery at the Hatton-garden Post Office in November last. The‘ deflandants had resisted payment of the c'aim on the ground that the jewels were not actualy insured bsfore the robbery • , and the jury found in their favour. , The death is reported at Sheffield of Samuel Ccookes whose deeds, as revealed by himself and his lecomplices before the Trade Outrage,Commission in 1807, tilled England with wonder and shame. Crookes was the principal lieuten- ant of the infamous William Broadhead, and on his own con- fession lie was guilty of at least one deliberate murder, and - of many deeperate outrages upon the property of manufac- turer who had rendered themselves obnoxious to the seceet tribunal which for many years enforced its decrees by the bullet or the " infernal machine." Penalties of £lO 17s, £4 18,e, and £23 Os were on Saturday imposed by the West Riding magistrates at Halifax, on the manager, underground viewer, and deputy underground viewer respectively, of a colliery at South° wram for neglect of the•provisioni of the Mince Regulation 'Act, owing to which neglect, a fatal explosion recently occurred. The prosecuting solicitor said it was desired to correct the errone- ous impression that the coal measures in that district did not generate gas like the softer seams, and also to Make it known that it was the determation of the authorities to en. s force the law.

NARROW ESCAPE OF A CLERICAL FARM—A heavy thunderstorm, accompanied by hail, lightnincr, and rain, broke over Wolverhampton at two o'clock on Tuesday after- noon. The storm lasted half an hour, and rain fell in torten's. While the storm was at its height the electric fluid struck the chimney of the Peacock Hotel, and a portion of the brickwork fell into a room where a numbn. of clergy and churchwardens were dining with Archdeacon Iles, who had been making his annual visitation. Considerable alarm was caused, but fortunately no one was hurt. THE ATTACK uPOtsT A GUARDSMAN.—At the Westminster Police Court, on Monday, William O'Connell, who said he was a labourer, and lived at 3, Regent-street, Chelsea, was charged on remand with unlawfully cutting and wounding John Pulling, a private of the let Battalion of Grenadier Guards, at the Union Tavern, Pimlico-road, on Saturday week. The previous evidence showed that a quarrel arose over the Phcenix Park assassinations' and the prisoner pro- duced a dagger-knife, with which he stabbed Pulling, in- flicting a superficial wound. The prisoner was committed for trial at the Central Criminal Court. FALL OF A WALL IN LIVERPOOL: Two CHILDREN IN- JURED.—ShortIy after nine o'clock on Tuesday evening, a wall in 8 Court, Richmond-row, which had been propped up ,by planks owing to the adjoining house being taken down, gave way, and two boys who were near it at the time were , serhously injured. The names of the children are Christo- pher M‘Dermott, fourteen years of age, living at 12 house, 8 Court, Richmond-row, and Hugh Watson, ten years of age, who resides at 2 house, 3 Court, Thurlow-street. Beth boys have sustained serious injuries from the falling dObris, and immediately after the occurrence they were taken to the East Dispensary, where their injuries were dressed. They were afterwards removed to their homes. _

THE QUEEN'S BIRTHDAY.—Her Majesty on Thursday completed her sixty-third year, an age which has been ex- ceeded by eleven only'or the Sovereigns of England, dating , Irma the Norman Conquest, viz. :—Henry 1., who lived to the age of 67 veers; Henry 111., who attained 65 years; Edward 1., who lived 67 yt.ars; Edward 111., •65 years; Queen Elizabeth, who reached the age of 69; James lI who was 68 at the time of his death; -Geore-e 1., who lived 67 veers; George 11., 77 years; George 111, 82 years; George IV., 68 years; and William IV., 72 years. Oaths 20th of June next Her Majesty will have reigned over the United Kingdom for a period of 45 years, a length of reign which has been exceeded by three only of the Kings of England, viz. :—Henr.v*lll., who reigned for 50 yeers ; Edward 111., whose reign lasted 50 years; and George 111 , whose reign extended over the long period of 60 years. EXECUTION OF CAPTAIN BRAND.—At eight o'clock, on Tuesday, Osmond Otto Brand, of Hull, expiated, in Arinley GaolvLeeds, his dreadful crime of murdering his fisher ap- prentice, Popper, tfuder circumstances of almost unexampled ferocity. His last few days had a great effect on him, the final interview with his wife having greatly affected him. He paid earnest note to the exhortations of the chaplain. When Marwood pinioned him he was terribly startled, but seemed by a great effort to regain his composure. On the way to the gallows he was evidently suffering keen mental anguish, though he attempted to control it. A long drop was allowed, and death was very speedy, there being very little struggling. On Monday Brand wrote a final letter to his wife, and made a confession bearing out what he had pteviously stated—viz., that'lle had not intended to murder the boy. DEATH OF THE DUKE OF GRAFTON.—TIJO DI11“2 Of Grafton died at his town residence, 4, Grosvenor Place, London, W.C., early on Sunday morning. His Grace had only been occupying his town residence for the last three weeks, and on Saturday week last was stricken with typhoid fever. He was attended by Sir William Jenner and Mr. Sibley, and, though the symptoms were pronounced, they were not at first considered to be serious, and nothing dangerous was apprehended till Saturday last, when the symptoms became alarming. Sir Wm. Jenner and Mr. Sibley were in constant attendance upon the Duke through- out the day ; but, notwithstanding their efforts, his Grace sank, and death ensued about an hour after midnight. His Grace, who was 63 years of age, was born in 1819, and married the third daughter of Lord Ashburton. He leaves no issue, and is consequently succeeded by his brother, Lord Charles Fitzroy. His Grace was a Liberal in politics, and was formerly attaché to the British legation at Naples. A HOT-TEMPERED BRITON.—At the Middlesex Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Jones, aged sixty-two, hawker, was in- dicted for committing damage to six panes of plate-glass, value £3O, the property of Edwin Dwyer Gray, Esq., M.P. At half-past ten o'clock on the night of May 17, while Mr. Tuohy, reporter, and Messrs. Callan, Dillon, and Gray were in the editorial rooms of the offices of the Freeman's Journal, at 211, Strand, they heard a series of crashes of glass down- stairs, and on going there found the defendant in the cus- tody of a police-constable, who had a large stone in his hand, and he said he had seen the prisoner throw it away. When the policeman apprehended him he said, "You have no right to be writing letters about Englishmen." On the way to the station-house he said, "I shall lose nothing by this; I shall get well paid for this." The prisoner, in answer to the charge, said he had been drinking. He was sentenced to hard labour for three months.

EXECUTION AT NORWICIL—On Monday Morning, William George Abigale, aged 19, was executed by Marwood inside Norwich Castle for the murder of Jane Plunkett, his sweet- heart, at Norwich, on the 25th of April last. At three minutes to eight, the culprit, looking haggard and worn, was presented to Marwood, who proceeded to pinion him while the chaplain read, not thg funeral service, but such passages of Scripture as he would read to a dying person. The prisoner responded fervently, now and then with difficulty. There was a nine-feet drop. He bad been accustomed to the use of firearms, and having been dis Charged from his situation as a waiter, he appears to have murdered his unhappy victim, with whom he was living, in a moment of despair. He maintained a stolid indifference from his trial until Sunday, when in the midst of the service he broke down, and afterwards made a full confession.

THREE LADIES BURNT TO DEATII.—A sad accident was reported on Sunday from Maybole, a weaving village in Ayrshire, by which at least three persons have lost their lives. Between two and three o'clock on Sunday morning a fire broke out in a dwelling-house at Balleny, and before assistance could be rendered the building was in flames, and the inmates unable to find an exit. Great exertions were made by the inhabitants, and one old lady named Campbell was rescued, but is seriously injured. Three others were burned to death—namely, Widow Campbell, aged 90, and two sisters (single women), named Marion and Helen Byron, both of whom were cripples. The fire was confined to the building in which it originated, but the block was completely destroyed. No water was to be had in the immediate neigh- bourhood, and it had to be conveyed in bucketsa considerable distance. The melancholy affair has caused great excitement in the district ; and the property destroyed amounts to several thousands of pounds.

ALLEGED BRUTAL CONDUCT OF A CLERGYILAN.—AC Salisbury, in answer to a plaint issued by Frank Read, a schoolboy, for the recovery of £5O, for damages alleged to have been sustained byea violent, unprovoked, and unjusti- fiable assault, the Rev. J. Lee-Warner' the incumbent of Tarrant Gunville, near Salisbury, has had to appeal in the district County Court. The case for the plaintiff was that he was left at home in charge of his sick brother, and that during the absence of the mother the defendant sent his man-servant to tell the lad to come to school. The boy declined, after which Mr. Lee-Warner went himself to the house' and, taking the plaintiff by the collar, dragged him to school, where, in the class-room, having partially un- dressed him, he gave him about thirty strokes with the birch rod, causing blood to flow. The defence was that only nine strokes were administered, and that the lad had behaved im- properly to one of the schoolgirls. The defendant, however, admitted that he had no right to go to the house and drag the plaintiff from home. The jury awarded Read is., and his Honour disallowed his costs. CONFERENCE ON THE NEW EDUCATION CODE.—An im- portant conference on the new education code took place on Tuesday, in the committee room of the House of Commons, between about 90 members of Parliament and a deputation from the National Union of Elementary Teachers. Professor Thor°ld Rogers, M.P., presided. The views of the represen- tatives of the national union were represented by Mr. A. Sykes, president, and Mr. Hellier, secretary, who explained that their modifications of the new code were chiefly with a view to relieve the existing over pressure on teachers and scholars, and to secure more liberty of classification and methods. Among their chief proposals were that managers of schools be allowed discretionary power to withhold from examination not more than 10 per cent, of the scholars qualified for presentation ; that the inspectors should state in their reports the grounds upon which the merit grant Was assessed ; that an assistant teacher count on the school staff for 40 instead of for 60 scholars; that 30 be substituted for 25 hours in the memorandum of agreement with pupil teachers, and that the needlework scheme be amended with a view to reducing the dem Ind OR girls' and infants' schools. The Chairman promised that these suggestions would be duly considered by the members. DISASTROUS FlRES.—Several disastrous fires are reported. Thirty houses have been burnt down in the village of Thornicombe, Dorset, and a large number of persons ren- dered homeless. At Queensborongh, the London, Chatham, and Dover Company's pier has been totally- destroyed by fire, one of the Flushing mail boats. which was lying along- side having a narrow escape. The Albion Art Cabinet Works at Bath were totally destroyed by fire on Saturday night, an adjoining malthouse being considerably injured. The damage is estimated at £lO,OOO. About nine o'clock on Sunday mording an alarm was given of fire at the York Workhouse, containing about 600 inmates. On the arrival of the steam fire engine it was found that the workhouse officials, by means of a hydrant, had kept the flames in check, and the brigade extinguished the fire before any serious damage was done to the building. THE ENRAGHT APPEAL: JUDGMENT.—JUdgMeIIt Was given on Monday in the House of Lords in the case of the Rev. P. R. Enraght v. Lord Penzance. Their lordships pre- sent were the Lord Chancellor, Lord Blackburn, Lord Bram- well, Lord Watson, and Lord O'Hagad. The appellant, the Rev. Richard William Enraght, vicar of Holy Trinity, Bordesley, Warwrickshire, sought to appeal from a judgment of the Court of Appeal Confirming a decision of the Queen's Bench refusing to grant a prohibition restraining Lord Pen- z ince from further proceeding in the suit,his lordship having issued an inhibition against Mr. Enraght for ritualistic prac- tices.—Lord Blackburn, in delivering judgment, held that Lord Penzance had jurisdiction under the Public Worship Regulation Act in issuing the monition against the appellant for unlawful practices, in using the alb, chasuble, biretta, and causing a procession with acolytes to be formed in the church.—Lord Watson and Lord Bramwell concurred.--The appeal was therefore dismissed, with costs.

FIGHT WITH AN OWL.—A son of a farmer of Marham- church has been admitted into Stratton Hospital, near Ply- mouth, suffering from severe injuries inflicted upon him by an owl. A pair of ewls had made their home in an elm tree, and made raids on the farmer's chickens to supply the wants of a numerous family of young owls. One of the farmer's sons ascended the tree and secured two of the young ones, and kept them for some days, feeding them by hand. He had one of the young ones in his hand showing it to a friend, when one of the parent birds suddenly pouncal upon him and struck him heavily on the head. He dropped the fledgling and defended himself with a stick, but the owl savagely renewed the attack and wounded the unfortunate boy in the eye so sericusly that the sight will be entirely destroyed. The father, who witnessed the attack, imme- diately killed the two young birds, whereupon the parent owl attacked him and another of his sons, inflicting wounds in the necks of both. The farmer went for his gun but the owl escaped. DISTRESSING BOAT ACCIDENT ON THE SCOTCH COAST.— Particulars of a melancholy boat accident have been- re- ceived from Arisaig on the extreme west coast of Inverness- shire. Angus Gillies, aged 61, Ann Gillies, his sister, aged 63, and Duncan Gillies and Angus Gillies, aged 21 and 17 years respectively, were returning from an island with a 12,atload of seaweed when the boat swamped. All held on by the boat till it drifted towards the rocks. Angus, the younger, got on to a rock and kept hold of his father, who ' was quite exhausted. Duncan reached the same rock, re- taining hold of his aunt, who was by this time dead. The rock is nearly a mile from the shore, and when assistance arrived, the old man was found to bo dead and the son Duncan was in an unconscious state, but still clinging to the rock and retaining his hold of tLe body of his aunt. Angus was also in a state of insensibility, but still kept bold of the body of his father. They were conveyed ashore, where the two young men after a time recovered conscious- ness, but only Angus was able to give an account of the melancholy death of his father and aunt. The other son re- mains in a precarious state.

DESPERATE ATTACK ON Two POLICEMEN IN GLASGOW. —A seious case of stabbing took place in Glasgow en Satur- day night, whereby the life of at least one man has been placed in imminent danger. Two constables, named James Anderson and Neil Darroch, apprehended, about ten o'clock, a woman named Doylan, the wife of a shoemaker, on a charge of being disorderly. Her husband urged the con- stables to let her go home; but she was so outrageous that they were obliged to decline. About an hour afterwards the policemen were passing a dark entry, when Dolan sprang suddenly out upon them, armed with a shoemaker's knife. Holding the knife daggerwise, he struck Anderson first upon the right side of the neck, then upon the left, inflicting with the second blow a severe transverse wound. Both men were taken by surprise ; but on recovering himself, Darroch rushed to the assistance of his companion. Doylan thereupon 'turned upon him and strnck him twice on the left side in the region of the breast. The first blow was fortunately diverted by the knife coming in contact with a brass buckle in ths constable's brace, so that only a flesh wound was sustained. The second struck the large wooden button of the overcoat, and caused the highly-tempered knife to snap near the handle. The ruffian was thu2 partially disarmed, but with the broken ' knife he inflicted two severe contused wound 3 on the brow of the constable, who succeeded in maintaining his bold until assistance arrived, and Doylan was taken to the police office. Anderson, who was greatly enfeebled from loss of blood, was sent to the Royal Infirmary, but the other con- stable, having had the wounds dressed, was able to go home. Doylan lean old soldier, and has been frequently convicted of assault.

"The Powersilon't or won't understand the critical position of affairs. The Arabs understand nothing but force. Soft words are no remedy here. The fleet has now been to Alexandria nearly a week, and the solution of the crisis is further off than ever. The optimist opinion of the Foreign Office that the presence of a small fleet at Alexandria will ensure without recourse to force the authority of the Khedive and the liberties of the nation is probably by this time dispelled."_

The -Journal de Si. Petersbdury, replying to a recent artic.de of the Republique Fre-mem-se, disputes 'the assertion of that paper that the Egyptian Question lies outside the jurisdiction of the European concert, and that since the Congress of Berlin, the control of Egyptian aff4irs has been officially reserved to France and England, this being the express condition of the participation of France in the Con- gress. The journal rega.ds such a view on the part of the organ of the former minister of foreign affairs as surprising.
MR. -MICHAEL DAVITT AT MAN- CHESTER

Presiding on Sunday at a Land League meeting in the Manchester Free Trade Hall, Mr. Micllael Davitt, who was enthusiastically received by the large audience, pointed to the great change which had come over public opinion upon the subject of land reform during his incarceration in Port- land, and defended the movement by the aid of which such a revolution in the popular mind bad been effected. No one lamented more than be did the recent outrages in Ireland, but it was blindly unjust to charge their cernmiesion to the Land League, whose cause they had greatly injured. The asertion that landlordism was essential to the supremacy of English authority in Ireland was an utter fallacy, the truth being that it presented the weakest point of attack of all the instutions or laws bearing an English complexion in Ireland. It had always been the most obnoxious faction of English rule, and it was not worth the trouble and expense which it caused to England and the misery that it entailed on Ireland, and if blind Conservatiye 'stubborness continued to disre- gard the consequences that had invariably followed un- bmding opposition to the just and popular demands of the people, the continuance of Irish landlordism by English statesmen might prove a more costly blunder on this side of the Atlantic than did the imposition of unpopular taxes a century ago on the other side. It was for Englishmen to make up their mind what course to pursue in furtherance e f English political interests. The people of Ireland had fully made up theirs as to what was their just demands, and what sentence must be passed on Irish landlordistn. Mr. Glad- stone's temporary expedient of tixing rent, backed by the undisguised despotism with which he meant to combat Irish land reformers, might satisfy Some Irishmen and frighten others from further efforts to eff ct a complete settlement of the Irish social problem ; but the Prime Minister deceived himself egregiously if he believed that the Land League movement was about to efface itself all the world over, because he had been converted to Mr. Parnell's views upon the arrears question, and had accepted the ser- vices of Mr. O'Shea in the Treaty of Kilinainham. The Land League movement as organized to effect a comrlete abolition of Irish landlordism. and-until th it work was fully and completely accomplished, there could be no alliance between the people of Ireland and the Whig p trty of this country. (Cheers.) Mr. Gladetone wanted Ireland to give a trial to his second attempt to settle the land question. The people of Ireland would refese to give any further trial to Irish 14ndlordism. Instead of having grappled with this pestering socal cancer-in a courageous and effective man- ner, Mr. Gladstone had proce,ded upon the lines of his pre- vious mistake, and had produced another cxpqrimental • measure by which landlords and tenants, instead of 'being legally divorced, were turned over to the lawyers, the coun- try b-ing asked to place all its proFpncts of peace and pros- perity in universal litigation. Even this much of legislation could not be given to Ireland without-being spiced with the customary vindictiveness by which Irishmen were deprived of their liberty and. their country -was flooded with troops. The concession Upon the arrears question was -offered side by side with a Bill which was realty mended to arrest the further public aclen of the people of Ireland towards the abolition of landlordism. Had Mr. Gladstone been in the confidence-of the secret secicies he could not have more completely played into their hands. (Cheers.)

DAY, MAY 27, 1882.
T?

have been devoted to the debate on the second read- ing, very little, if any, new light has been thrown upon the measure, and members might as well have voted upon it at the commencement as at the close of the debate. The necessity for the bill has, however, been amply demonstrated. In consequence of these arrears, which hang like a millstone round the neck of the Irish tenants, evictions are on the increase. In 1880, we learn, the average number of evictions per quarter in Ireland amounted to 473, certainly a great deal too many; but in the following year they had increased to 805. In the first quarter of the present year these evictions reached the startling total of 1299; and they are on the increase still, for in April alone they numbered 512 equal to 1536 per quarter—the highest number yet recorded. In three days no less than 150 families, numbering 750 persons, were evicted in Connemara simply because it was impossible for them to do that which they were requested liquidate their arrears, and that unhappily at the present time is the condition of many thousands. It is not pretended that these persons in Connemara were able to pay, or that they had been intimidated from so doing; it is not hinted, either, that they were a bad class of tenants, on the contrary they are spoken of as being highly respectable, but unfortu- nately they were poor; and in consequence of their eviction they are, as may be expected, at the point of starvation. Another instance of the necessity for the bill may be given. The bill proposes to deal with the arrears of tenants, the value of whose holdings is not more than £3O. The num- ber of such small tenants is estimated at 585,000, and of these it is computed one-third will be found to be behind. That means that about 200,000 tenants are in arrear, and by the mere fact of being so in arrear they are in a great degree excluded from the benefits of the Land Act, whilst they are likewise held at the mercy of the landlords, and many of them we know are not prone to be particularly merciful. The statistics we have quoted prove, we think, the necessity there exists for the arrears question being got out of the way; and Parliament by having la,t year adopted without question the arrears clause in the Land Act sanctioned S4a,te interference for the settlement of these private engagements. The Prime Minister describes, and very properly so, the interference " as excep- tional and extraordinary," and it can only be justified on " exceptional and extraordinary grounds ;" but such a step having been once taken, Parliament would stultify itself were it to atternpt to recede from it. It is consequently the more necessary that the inter- ference when made should be effectual. The step of last year was not as has been proved by experience effectual; but the present bill, which is in reality only an extension of the principle of the arrears clause in the Land Act, is designed to make up for the short- comings of last year. If it is justifiable to interfere at all in such a matter, and Parliament has affirmed that it is, then in our opinion we may as well inter- fere by means of a gift as by a loan, while at the same time we are convinced the one mode is sure to be more effectual than the other. It is only a question of degree. By a loan the tenant would never feel free, but if there is a general clearance of old scores and each tenant starts with a clean sheet and a fair rent, then we may have some reason for hoping that each and all will in the future endeavour to keep a-head and discharge all their liabilities.. At the present time there is no possibility that without aid they can ever lift themselves over their difficulties. Mr. Smith argues that if there is to be relief, the re- lief must be "complete and absolute," that we believe can only be secured by means of a gift from the public purse, and it is not likely to be accomplished by any scheme of emigration such as was hinted at by Mr. Smith. The bill has the cordial support of the late 'Chief Secretary for Ireland (11r. Forster), who, how- ever, suggested that the provision limiting the opera- tion of the Act to Sr tenancies should be reviewed so as to admit holdings of a higher value. Lord George Hamilton, in the course of the debate, likewise ex- pressed an opinion that the £3O limitation was too low, so also did Mr. Parnell, and if this should be raised in committee we doubt not it will meet with general approval. It is also worth while to consider whether the Land Commission has not already suffi- cient work on hand without having thrust upon them the necessity of ascertaining whether tenants arc or are not able to pay their arrears. Such an inquiry will be a tedious, it ought to be a searching one, and it is questionable whether with the work the Commis- sioners have already to do they could safely under- take this additional duty. Mr. Forster has suggested there should be a separate Commission, and if such is resolved upon in Committee so much the better. A nice point for decision will be whether the tenant can or can not be compelled to sell his tenant right in order to discharge his obligations in respect of arrears before he can demand assistance from the State, and an expression of opinion from the Government on this question would remove many difficulties. As it stands, however, the bill will be powerful for good, and prove, we hope, in the words of its sponsor, "equitable, safe, and effectual."

VOLUNTEER FUNERAL AT RUNCORN. Robert Bradley, a late volunteer, was honoured by a military funeral at Runcorn, on Sunday afternoon. The local volun- teers and the WidneS Company of the 21st LAIN., and a considerable number of the members of the Shepherds' Star Lodge (Ashton Uaity) were in attendance. The procession formed in Church-street, and was 'headed by the volunteer band, who played the Dead March. The body was borne by a number of men belonging to the Widnes Company, and the firing party was composed of 13 men of the 2nd C.R.V. The Rev. Canon Barclay officiated, and there was present a large number of spectators.s.

TELE LITE MR, RIGBY, OF RUNCORN: REFERENCE BY THE VICAR.—On Sunday morning, the Rev. Canon Barclay preached at the Runcorn Parish Church, and briefly referfed to the death of Mr. John Rigby, which was recorded in last week's Examiner. The Vicar said lie had recently committed to the grave an old and respected parishioner, the last resident member of a family which kad been more or less identified with the rise and progress of the town. When Mr. Rigby first knew Runcorn, it was merely a village hamlet, but he lived to see it 'grow into a populous and prosperous community. The deceased pursued in early and mddle life a career of honest industry. and contributed to the prosperity of Runcorn by serving in those various offices which uo good citizen ought to shirk. Mr. Rigby had been spared to a very ripe old age—having lived nearly 20 years niore than the space allotted to man's existence by the Psalmist, but had at length been gathered to his fathers, reminding us that "though a man live long and see not the grave, yet that wise men also die, as well as the ignorant and foolish, and leave their riches for others."

A HALTON CATTLE DEALER CHAROED WIWI FRAUD,. —William Padwick, cattle dealer, Halton, near Runcorn, was on Monday brought up on a serious charge at the Sale Petty Sessions. It was alleged that he had obtained from the London and North-Western Railway Company, by false pretences, 29 bags of manure, of the value of £2l 15s. The company were represented by Mr. Preston, and Mr. G. Moore defended the prisoner. From the evidence it ap- peared that Robert Brooks, farmer, Cambsley-lane, Lymm, had consigned to him at Thelwall station, on the 4th April, the 29 bags of manure in question, which he refused on account of the price. On the 14th April the prisoner, whom he knew as "Billy go-faster," callel at his house, and in the course ef conversation the manure was mentioned. Brooks. to convince the prisoner that the manure was priced at ten guineas a.ton, showed him the invoice, which he missed when the prisoner had departed. The same after- noon the prisoner went to Thelwall station, and gave the stationmaster, Mr. J. Kite, to understand that he came from the senders, producing the invoice relating to the manure. The prisoner said as Brooks refused to receive it, he wiahed to re-consign it to William Grace, Upton Rocks, Rainhill, which he did. Subsequently the prisoner received £22 is. in payment for the manure from Grace, who, in evidence, said he was unaware the manure had been obtained by the prisoner under false pretences. On the 19th inst., when these circumstances came to the knowledge of the police, the prisoner was apprehended. He informed his custodian he could "not see much fraud" in the transaction, as he had bought the material honestly, and could produce the bills. Brooks denied that he had sold the manure to the prisoner, nor had he given him any instructions with regard to its disposal. The Bench considered there was a prunes fade case, and committed the prisoner to take his trial at the nent Knutsford Quarter Sessions. •
WIDNES AND TILE SUNDAY CLOSING MOVEMENT.— A canvass of the inhabitants of Widnes on the question of Sunday closing is being made by the members of the 1.0.G.T.
-•-- - RUNCORNIAN S AND TUE QUEEN'S BIRTHDLY. —0 n the Queen's birthday, the ringers at the Parish Church) Runcorn, rang a merry peal, and flags were also displayed from most of the public buildings.

ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN SAILOR.—On Thursday afternoon, whilst Thomas Mc Grath, a seaman, was scraping the topsail yard of the schooner Psyche, he missed his foot- ing, and fell on the deck of an adjoining vessel. His thigh was fractured, and he was taken to Dr. Monti, z's surgery. He was afterwards removed to Liverpool Royal lufimary. WIDNES ST. MA.RY'S CITHOLIC CHURCH. -Oa Sunday, the annual sermons in connection with this school, were preached. At High Mass, the Rev. Father Clare, S.J., was the preacher ; and the afternoon sermon was by Father Doherty, S.J., formerly of Canada. RUNCORN PRIMITIVE METHODIST SCHOOL SERMONS. —These annual sermons were preached on Sunday, by the Rev. W. Rowe; and in the afternoon the choir and children gave a service of song, entitled "Song memories of Bible scenes." The reader was the Rev. J. Pickwell, and Mr. Billingsley presided at the organ. The collections amounted to £2B. Mr. David Lewis acted as conductor. We understand that this is the first time that this gentleman has held the baton, and we congratulate him upon his success.

SINGULAR AND FATAL ACCIDENT TO A CHILD AT WIDNES.—On Wednesday, an inquest was held at the Nor- ton Arms public-house, on the body of Anne Ellis, aged 12 months, the daughter of a labourer named Simnel Ellis, of 42, Oxford-street, Widnes Evidence was given to the effect that a fortnight since the mother of the child took a hot potato-pie out of the oven and placed it upon the floor. The little one fell against it and was so badly burned that it died on Sunday last The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

. PROPERTY SALE.—On Wednesday evening Messrs. T. and J. L. Tunstall offered for sale at the Golden Grove Inn, Warrington, two lots of freehold property, at Hatton. The attendanee was not large. The auctioneer intimated that he would offer the whole of the property in one lot, but as the bidding did not reach a satisfactory figure, it was withdrawn. The property was then offered in two lots, and after a fair amount of competition both lots were sold to Mr. Parr, of Hatton.

NEW WESLEYAN CHAPEL AT WIDNES.—TiIe plans of a new Wesleyan Methodist Chapel in Oakland-street, Widnes, have just been submitted for inspection by the contractors. The new building will face Irwell-street, and will be 50 feet by 58 feet, and built in the style known as mixed Italian. There will be two entrances from Irwell-st., one on each side of the front. The entrances will be arranged so as to- form transepts. From the transepts two commodious vestries will be constructed. The exterior will be of patent bricks, and the stone used will be from the Appleton quarries. It is expected that the foundation stone will be laid early in Jun', and that the structure will be completed about November. • THE SEWERAGE WORKS AT WIDNES.—Owing to a mis- understanding with the contractor, the whole of the contrac- tor's men engaged on the Wridnes sewerage scheme, were, on Monday, discharged from work. A meeting of the Board to consider this difficulty was held on Thursday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. Kershaw. Our representative, on presenting himself at the meeting, was informed that the proceedings were private, but, the chairman added, the matter would come before the public in the ordinary way. The Board, however, we are enabled to state, decided to place the matter in the hands of their legal adviser.

WHIT-MONDAY LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT KNOWS- LEY PARK.—Know9ley Park, the seat of the Earl of Derby, will on Whit-Monday be the seen of a united Liberal demonstration and athletic festival, under the auspices of the Liverpool Reform Clubs. Prizes to the amount of £125 will be competed for, and during the afternoon a political meeting will be held, under the presidency of Mr. E. K. Muspratt, and addresses will be delivered by Mr. W. E. Briggs, M.P., and a number of the leading Liberals in South- west Lancashire. Apart from the demonstration many persons will doubtless avail themselves of this opportunity of visiting on account of its associations, the seat of one of the most popular noblemen in the country, which is situated in the midst of a very picturesque domain. A LOCAL ARTIST AT THE ROYAL ACADEMY.---It is sincerely to be hoped that Mr. Luke Fildes, A.R.A., has some large and important pictorial drama on hand, or that be is absorbed in the 2tudy of some abstruse theory of the art in which he excels ; for from his gifted hand we have this year only a single picture, modest in dimensions, and unobtrusive in subject. It is (263) " Nina," a delicious little portrait study of an Italian ragazza, of the type Mr. Luke Fides knows so well how to paint—a graceful little damsel, with a " touzled " head of dark hair, with mutinous eyes, and osculatory lips—in mien decidedly coquettish, and as decidedly slatternly, and looking for all the world as though a little warm water and a modicum of old brown Windsor soap would do her a " power "of good. Yet is Nina delicious, for the reason that in his des% tints and his draperies mt. Fildes has revelled in that rich and mellow colour with , which his palette is, to all appearance, in- exhaustibly supplied.--licri!.y Telegraph.
