Pearson, Broad-street, Pendleton, nurseryman. BREWTNALL7S PATENT COUPLINGS rOR ELECTRICAL

PURPOSES.—The. Engineer of Saturday last contained an Illustrated description of a very neat coupling for electrical purposes, invented and patented by Mr. Arthur W. Brewtnall seta of Mr. Brewtnall, of Thelwall. We are unable to give the engravings, ha.; we copy the description, which was as follows :—" The accompanying engravings illustrate a new and simple coupling, invented and patented in England and abroad by Mr. A. W. Brewtnall, for connecting branch wires with main electric light leads, which will be of especial Use in fitting incandescent lamps. The couplings consist of a small brass cylinder, one end of which is solid and the other fitted with a broad screw or nut. A slot is cut in the side at an angle of about 45 deg. to the length to receive the main wire or cable. Intersecting this a hole is drilled, either longitudinally or transve: sely, to receive the branch wire. When the wires are put in their respective positions, and the screw or nut is tightened up, the main wire or cable is jammed forcibly against the branch wire and against the solid end of the slot. This gives a very firm and endearing contact between the two wires or conductors, and the surface contact is large, thus ensuring perfect electrical conductivity. A fusible portion can also very easily be combined with this form of connector, which is an obvious advantage. These couplings furnish a rapid, easy, and absolutely reliable means of connecting up-wires, and entirely supersede the old method of soldering'. No tool or material of any kind is required, save a screwdriver and the usual knife or instru- molt for cleaning the insulating matter off the wires. They are supplied at a very moderate cost by Messrs. Farady and Son, Berners-street. A new form of ball-and-socket joint to be used with electrical chandeliers, or electroliers,' has been also introduced by Mr. A. W. Brewtnall. In this only one wire need be used for the lead, and the return can be made through the.outer•tube without any chance of short circuit- ing, however much the electrolier ' may swing. The con- tact surfaces are large, and are so arranged as to do away with all possibility of 'parking' or corrosion."

LECTTJEE ON VEGETARIANISM AT WARRINTON. Under the auspices of the Warrington Vegetarian Society, Mr. Peter Foxcroft, of Manchester, delivered a lecture on "Science and experience," on the new Fair Ground, on Monday evening. A lurry was improvised as a platform, and Mr. W. H. Chapman presided. There was a moderate attendance. In introducing Mr. Foxeroft, the chairman re- marked that his experience as a vegetarian had shown him that there was one common cure for a great many ailments,. and one, too, which entailed no expense, that was starva- tion. Englishmen, it had been stated, ate three times as much food as was necessary to sustain them in good health and strength, and by abstaining from food for a short period many ills could be cured. The lecturer observed that a vegetarian was a man who abstained from eating flesh, fish, or fowl. These substances, he said, did not contain that amount of nutriment generally supposed, from 65 to 70 per cent. being water. Cerials, such as wheat, corn, beans, lentils, &c., he pointed out, contained about 86 per cent. of solid matter, and consequently contained greater nutriment. In addition to this increased nutriment, a vegetable diet was more healthful, a fact which was demonstrated in his own case, he never having had the assistance of a doctor for 30 years, whilst previously he bad seldom been free from his (the medical gentleman's) attendance. He explained the reason why vegetarians were generally eo thin by stating they had become converts to vegetarianism, as a rule, in consequence of bad health, and in almost every case had derived much benefit. At the conclusion of the lecture, Mr. Foxcroft answered a number of queetions, erei he was accorded a hearty vote of thanks.
About five o'clock on Tuesday afternoon a thunder- storm broke over Warrington. Rain fell heavily, and the lightning flashes were very vivid, but the storm was of brief duration.
In the House of Commons, on Tuesday, Mr. J. G. McMinnies, the member for Warrington, voted against Mr. Sclater Booth's amendment, and with the Government on the Arrears Bill.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST MISSION, LATCHFORD.—The Sun- day school anniversary of this mission was celebrated on Sunday, when sermons were preached, morning and evening by Mr. Councillor Allman, of Crewe. Mr. T. Rollaston, o Widnes, in the afternoon, addressed the scholars, who sang several special hymns for the occasion. The collections for the day amounted to £5 03. id. POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR WHIT-MONDAY.—On Monday (Bank Holiday), there will be only one delivery by letter carriers in Warringtor, namely, at 7 a.m. The money order and savings bank business will cease at 12 noon, and the receiving-offices will close altogether at the same time, the only evening collection of letters being from the pillar and wall boxes. •

WARRINGTON' COUNTY COUET.—At this court on Thursday, before the judge, Mr. W. Wynne Ffouikes, and the registrar, Mr. E. J. Nicholson, there were heard 361 original plaints, 6 adjourned plaints, and 40 judgment sum- monses. The cases Were devoid of public interest.

DETERMINED ATTEMPr AT SUICIDE —COURAGEOUS REscuE.—On Tuesday, at Whines Police Court, a middle- aged woman, named Bridget Oates, was brought up charged. with attempting to take away her life, at Farnworth. Pri- soner, on the evening of the previous day, went to a deep pit full of water, near the Cheshire Lines Railway, and about 300 yards from her own house; at lees skirt on the bank, and jumped into the water, shoeless. Luckily a Farnworth labourer, named Cunningham, happened to be passing, saw the poor creature struggling in the pit, and, without a moment's hesitation, jumped in, and succeeded in bringing her to the surface. In answer to his enquiries, the prisoner said she had jumped in because she wished to take her life, "and she would do it yet." She was taken to the police station. Prisoner, in reply to the charge, did not say a word, and had to be supported whilst standing in the dock. On the application of Inspector Barnett, she was remanded for eight days. THE WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS', AT ST. HELEItS.— Should the weather keep tine the Whitsuntide holidays this year will be taken advantage of by the peop'.e in this dis- trict. Several trips are advertised, and there is every reason to believe that these will carry to their destinations large cargoes of human freight. St. Thomas' Church have their trip this year to Morecambe, where the bay and the rustic surroundings will no doubt prove attractive. The Rainford Mutual Improvement Society have their trip, as usual, to that now fashionable watering place, Llandudno. The train will call at St. Helens to pick up passengers. There are in addition several trips by the Railway Company to Glasgow, Manchester, Blackpool, and oth(r places. The people who choose to remain at home will find enjoyment in the Band of Hope demonstration. The principal streets of the town will be paraded in the usual fashion, and the usual games will take place on the field. CLAIM AGAINST A WARRINGTON CONTRACTOR.— On Thursday, at the Warrington County Court, John Buckley, contractor, Church-street, was sued by Richard Farrington, of 34, Mersey-street, for £l. 198. 4d. The defendant, it ap- peared, was under an engagement with the Corporation to convey gas water to the chemical works of Mr. Knight, at Farnworth. He, in his turn, employed the plaintiff to per- form part of the work, and on the 24th October, 1881, the plaintiff took several loads of the water to Farnworth. Shortly afterwards Knight failed, and it was alleged by the defendant that he ordered the plaintiff to stop carting pre- vious to taking the loads for which he now claimed payment. After hearing the evidence, his honour said the defendant was trying to shirk an honest liability because he thought he should be unable to recover his own debt, and gave judg- ment for the plaintiff.

FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.—About a quarter to 11, on Tuesday morning, an Accident occurred on the London and North-Western Railway, near Arplev Station, to a shunter named John Hunt, which terminated fatally. A goods train was at that time shunting. Hunt detached six wagons. and whilst these were running into the siding he stood on the buffer of the first wagon. From this position he was seen to fall by some men in the vicinity, and the whole of the wagons, which were loaded, passed over him, severing his right leg and right arm from his body. He also received a severe scalp wound. He was placed on a stretcher and conveyed to the Infirmary, where Dr. Richmond proaosnced life to be extinct. The deceased was 32 years of age, and resided at 148, Pierpoint-street. Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, held an inquest yester- day, at the White Hart Inn; Sankey-street, when evidence bearing out the above was given, and a verdict of "Acciden- tal death" was. returned.

ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT.—At this court on Wednesday, before Mr. Thompson, Judge, and Mr. Tyrer, registrar, a man named Danial Meldon, provision dealer, Parr, for whom Mr. Riley appeared, sought to recover up- wards of £5 from Adam Knowles, labourer, formerly under- keeper for Ccl. Gambles The plaintiff's case was that de- fendant's wife obtained the goods, which were groceries and other necessaries, front him on credit, and whenever he sup- plied her he marked the amount down in figures, although he could not write, and whenever his wife supplied defend- ant's wife with anything she made certain hieroglyphics which they both nnderstood, and which he afterwards entered into the book. Plaintiff said there was a 'compact amongst the ne!ghbours round about to swindle him out of his money and goods, because he was a hardworking man, and tried "to save a bit." Mr. Swift said defendant had forbidden his wife to get anything from the plaintiff, and during his illness his wife received £1 a week from two clubs, which was as much as he earned by working. *ome two years ago, in 1880, defendant was sued for a very large amount, about LSI, by a shopkeeper. He consented to judgment, because up to that time he never had forbidden his wife to get goods on credit. He, however, as he had great reason to do so, did so then. The hesitancy which cbaracteriged defendant's wife's evidence caused his Honour to remark that he should have given evidence against the plaintiff, but he could not believe Mrs. Knowles. He had not the slightea reason for doubting the perfect honesty of the plaintiff and his wife, who aploarently had l.tert victimised by such people as de- fendant's wife. He would make an order of 4s. a month. —William Gaskell, collier, was sued by the same plaintiff for f.,3 ss. 7d., goods supplied during the colliers' strike a year and five months ago. Judgment for the plaintiff.

DISTIHONIAL TO MIL. S. BRADSHAW, ST. HELENS.— On Wednesday evening a meeting was held in the school- room adjoining the Parish Church, for the purpose of pre- senting Mr. Samuel Bradshaw, who has occupied the post of a scripture reader in the town for about nine years,— between three and four years of which he has been in col!- ' nection with the St. Helens Parish Church—and who is now leaving the town, with a testimonial as a slight token of the esteem in which he is held in the town and neighbour- hood, and in recognition of his valuable services both in the : parish where his kind and agreeable disposition have en- deared him to the hearts of all with whom he came in Con- tact, and particularly to the poorer class amongst whom his labours have chic fly been, and by whom he will long be remembered as a kind and genial friend, whose aim whilst among them was ever to promote their welfare and hap- piness both in time and eternity; and in the Sunday school where he has been the teacher of the Young Men's Bible Class, and where his courteous manners have as in the parish generally attached him both to his fellow teachers and to the members of his own class by whom his removal from them is cl(eply regretted, as his kindness and the warm affectionate interest he always showed in them, will cause him to be thought of in years to come, and remembered both as a teacher whose aim was ever to show to them the truth of God's Word, and impress those truths upon their hearts and minds, and also as a personal friend to each one of them. The testimonial consisted of an illuminated address, and a parse of gold containing £2O. :The address was designed and illuminated by Mr. S. 0. Lees, of St. Helens, and reflects great credit upon him for the artistic manner in which he has executed it.—The Rev. W. T. Noble, curate of the parish, presided, and apologised for the absence of the Rev. Canon Carr, who was unable to be present, owing to bcing out of town ; and after explaining the object of the meetimg and expressing sorrow at being only able to speak himself of a few months' acquaintance with Mr. Bradshaw and the good work in which he had been occupied in the town of St. Helens, called upon the Revs. W. Chaplin and G. Lakeman, who both bore testimony to the high esteem in which Mr. Brad- shaw was held, and of Iris valuable services in the neigh- bourhood.—Mr. P. Lea, superintendent of the Sunday school., and several members of the Bible class supported what had been said.—The Rev. W. T. Noble then made the presentation, and Mr. Bradshaw replied at considerable length to the remarks made by the gentlemen present, and expressed his hearty thanks for the kind feelings and re- gards that had been expressed towards him and for the kind manner in which he had always been received by all with whom he had come in contact during the time ha had been in St. lielens.—After a vote of thanks to the chairman for the ab!e manner in which he had performed the duty put upon him, the meeting was at his request brought to a close by the singing of the Nation 4 Anthem on account of its being the anniversary of the birth of Her Most Gracious Majesty the Queen. The following is a copy of the address :—" Ts Mr. Samuel Bradshaw.—The Bible class, teachers, and friends of the Helens Parish Church Sunday School have great pleasure m presenting you on the occasion of your leaving the town with the accompanying purse of gold containing twenty pounds in token of the high esteem in which you are held in St. Helens, and as a grateful acknowledgment of your valuable services as scripture reader of the St Helens Parish Church. Your courteous, kind, and agreeable manners have made you respected by all who have come in contact with you, and it will always be a source of pleasure to us to hear of your future success in life, and we hope that your health may long be spared to enable you to carry on the good work as successfully as you have done in this town.—We remain, on behalf of the subscribers, yours faithfully, Pam, LEA, superintendent; ISAAC ECCLEBTON, sccretary.—St. Helens, May 24th, 1882."
THE ELECTION OF RUNCORN GUARDIANS. IMPORTANT DECISION OF THE LOCAL GOVERN-
MEN I' BOARD.

Yesterday, a letter was received by the Runcorn overseers from the Local Government Board, dated Thursday, stating that they have acceded to the resolution passed at a late ratepayers' meeting, and decided to issue an order for the filling up of the three vacancies in the representation of, Runcorn on the Board of Guardians. The decision has given general satisfaction.

div.head: WIDNES PATENT CASE.
div.p: A WIDNES PATENT CASE.

At the Liverpool Court of Chancery, yesterday, Vice- Chancellor Bristowe resumed the hearing of the action of Parnell and Simpson v. Mort, Liddell, ST, Co., which was commenced on Monlay last, and bas occupied the whole of the week. The question at issue is the right to manufacture alkalies by a certain process which the plaintiffs allege to be their property protected by patent. The parties are all chemical manufacturers of Widnes, and the questions in- volved are of, considerable importance to the trade. The plaintiff's case closed yesterday, when his Honour Intimated that he would adjourn to take time to consider whether any case bad been established for the defendants to answer, and would apprise the solicitors of the day upon which he would be prepared to give judgment or proceed with the further hearing. Mr. Ralph Neville and Mr. Valentino Browne, instructed by Messrs. H. W. Collins, Robinson, & Co., were counsel for the plaintiffs; Mr. Aston, Q.C., and Mr. T. M. Goode:ye. instructed by Mr. Walter Weld, being specially retained for the defendants.
MEETING OF WIDNES RATEPAYERS.

A meeting of the ratepayers of Widnes was held on Wed- nesday afternoon, at the Overseers' Offices, Victoria-road, for the purpose of considering the desirability of appointing an assistant collector, the township being in arrears with its call to a very considerable sum. There were present Messrs. F. H. Pankhurst (in the chair), J. W. Garble, J. W. Ware- ing, J. Matthews, J. Farrant, T. Sadler, and Goff. After some introductory conversation, Mr. CAIILILE said he thought that neither the Local Government Board nor the Prescot Board of Guardians had anything to do with the matter to be considered by the meeting. If certain money had to be paid out of certain rates, the overseers would have the power to draw a cheque. " They " had nothing to do with it. Some said that the auditor had power to surcharge the ove:s2ers, but he did not think they had power to do any- thing of the kind. Mr. I,VAREING (deprecatingly) : Excuse me, Mr. Carlile, but we cannot go upon what this person or the other save. It is too late to consider such statements when we find we have to pay the money, and it is no good finding that one person had said we should have to do so in the end, and that others said we should not

Mr. Fennesr said he remembered that some four or five years ago, when Mr. Fearing was the assistant overseer for Widnes, be used to collect the poors' rate for £OO a year, and he believed that the cost of that work had now risen to £1.50 a year. Mr. Fearing had also other townships to col- lect fer, but though this was the case, lie kept the rate "pretty well straight." He believed that souse short time ago, it was reported that Mr. Rigby, the late assistant over- seer for the township, on being asked what the arrears were when he came into office, replied XS 000. He (the speaker) believed that the Guardians were to a greal extent, respon- sible for the position in which the township now was. He certainly sympathised with the overseers, who were placed in a very awkward position. Be did not think they ought to pay any more money for collection of the rate, as the work was not any more difficult than it was at the time when Mr. Rigby took the situation years ago. Mr. SADLER thought it would scarcely be fair to tax the assistant overseer with a negligence which might be the result of the work not having been properly looked to by previous collectors. He was of opinion that the overseers were quite entitled, under the present circumstances to claim the sympathy of the ratepayers. Mr. Flame:sr : Both the present and the late assistant overseer have complained of the way in which the work has been done in the past. Mr. CARLTLE : Perhaps von are not exactly acquainted with tte state of affairs in Widnes. Mr. FARRANT replied that he thought he understood the difficulties which had to be contended with.

Mr. CARLILE said the after the present rate had been dealt with, it would be the duty of the assistant overseer (Mr. Goff) to gc) from house to house and get the exact numbers of the dwellings. Mr. FARRANT: That is just what Mr. Fearing and the other assistant overseers did when they were in office—they went from street to street, and from house to house. Mr. CARLILE: Y4S, bat many years have elapsed since that was done. Mr. FARRANT : Then it should not have been allowed to elapse. Mr. MATTHEws: But what is done and what should be done are very different things. Mr. WAREING : Gentlemen, are not we wasting time? Mr. CARLILE considered it would be better to first decide ' whether they would have assistance, and afterwards deal with the question of remuneration. Mr. WARRING: I think so ; but I shall object to the • question of remuneration being raised at this part of the proceedings. It was for himself and his fellow overseer to consider whether it was necessary or not to forward the reso- lution to the Local Government Board. He, as an overseer, was not going to stand by and be quietly surcharged. Mr. SADLER said that when at the fate audit, he made ,1 some enquiry of the auditor in respect to the position of the overseers, and that official said that the overseers would cer- tainly be charged with the assistant collector's &any, if they appointed one themselves, and the on!y way of freeing themselves from the liAbility was to call a vestry meeting. • Mr. FARnAN r was in favour of taking the bull by the horns, and sending the resolutiou to the Local Government Board. • Mr. CARLILE replied that the Local Government Board had nothing to do with the matter, which was purely and simply a township charge. He begged to propose that the vestry meeting then assembled give the requi&te authority to the overseers to appoint an assistant collector to the assistant overseer for the township, for a term not exceeding six months to collect and aid in the ordinary business of the township. Mr. MATTHEWS : I will second that. The CHAIIMAN: Is there any amendment ? Mr. FARRANT: No, I shall make no amendment. The CHAIRMAN: Those in favot:r of the resolution, signify it in the usual way. The motion was carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. CARLILE, seconded by Mr. FAR- RANT, it was resolved that the remuneration of the assistant be fixed at 30s. weekly; after which the proceedings termi- nated with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: STARR-BOWKETT APPROPRIATION AT RUNCORN,
div.p: STARR-BOWKETT APPROPRIATION AT RUNCORN,

On Wednesday evening, a meeting was held in Bethesda Congregational schoolroom, Runcorn, under the auspices of the local Starr-Bowkett Society, for the purpose of making another appropriation. Mr. Archibald Campbell, one of the trustees, was voted to the chair. The minutes of the last meeting were ready by M. HANDLEY, and confirmed. Mr. Pownall and Mr. Bisbrown were appointed scrutineers for the ballot, on the motion of Mr. ARTHUR RILEY, seconded by Mr. BOOTH. Miss Bessie Speakman, aged 12, daughter of Mr. J. J. Speakman, was selected to draw the ballot balls. The CHAIRMAN said that the members had in the course of two months risen from 190 to 221, which was certainly a matter of considerable gratification to all connected with the society. He felt convinced that after the next appropria- tion had taken place, a still more satisfactory increase would occur in the number of those associated with them. The 221 members held 478 shares, being over an average of two shares per member. (Applause.) All they required was that each friend of the movement should put his shoulder to the wheel, and they would soon find that they would have the full number of members allowed in one society. It would be perfectly useless for him to say anything that evening in favour of Starr-Bowkett Societies, after the excellent lecture delivered on the last occasion of their meeting together by their friend Mr. Barcroft. Indeed, the advantages of their organisation were apparent to every one, and they had proved one of the greatest inducements of modern times for the working classes to cultivate a spirit of thrift. Savings banks and old stockings had their uses, and so had Perma- nent Benefit Building Societies, but, after a careful con- sideration of the subject, be had come to the conclusion that none of these was to be compared to the Starr-Bowkptt move- ment. (Applause.) There was another important point which they must not forget, viz ,that the greater the number of members the more the working expenses of the society were increased. The balloting was then gone through, and much laughter was caused by it resulting in the winner's number being re- presented by 000. It was then proceeded with again, and won by No. 158. Mr. Wm. HANDLEY said the number was held by a num- ber who was several weeks in arrear with his subscriptions. (Loud laukhter.) He sent the person word about his arrears on Saturday, and asked him to complete his payments by Wednesday, but he had neglected to do so. The CHAIRMAN: Well, it will have to be gone over again. The winner of the next ballot was declared to be Mr. Arthur Riley—(loud applause),—who Ilolds two shares, entitling him to receive an advance of £2OO. There were at present £240 in the bank, so that the gentleman could have the money advanced at any moment: (Applause.) The Cnernatart made a remark to thri effect that it was always alike; "to him that bath shall be given, and he shall have abundantly." (Laughter.) A vote of thanks was then passed to the Chairman, who said he trusted that their future meetings would he provo- cative of the same good feeling as had marked their gather- ing that evening. He certainly thought that was one of the most extraordinary ballots which had ever taken place in connection with the proceedings of any such society. The meeting then terminated.

We (Daily News) understat—d that Mr. Justice Bowen will succeed the late Lord Justice Holker in the Court of Appeal. ! Mr. Justice Bowen. who ia the youngest judge on theßench, was appointed in June, 1879.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOAIID.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOAIID.

The monthly meeting took place on Thursday afternoon. Mr. Bradshaw presided, and there were also present the Revs. Thomas Finegan, James Clarke, and Messrs. Shaw, Brock, Davis, O'Keeffe, and Danby (clerk).

div.head: SCHOOL FOR TRUANTS.
div.p: A SCHOOL FOR TRUANTS.

The District Education Committee reported that during April, 375 persons had been before them, 78 of whom were applicants for payment of fees, and 297 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in 59 cases, and 19 applications were refused. There had been 13 prosecutions before the magistrates. The committee also recommended as follow :--" That the Board, subject to the Board reserving to themselves a power of inspection' do make towards the maintenance of children committed to industrial schools under the 14th or 15th section of the Industrial Schools Act, 1866, upon the application, or with the sanction of the Board, a contribution not exceeding one shilling and sixpence per head per week daring the period of the children's detention." Also" That the Board, subject to the Board reserving to themselves a power of inspection, do make towards the maintenance of children committed to industrial schools under the Elementary Education Act, 1876, or under the 16th section of the Industrial Schools Act, 1866, upon the application of the Board, a contribution as will, with the Treasury allowance, amount to 88. 6d. per week in each case during the period of the children' detention."

Mr. DEACON moved the adoption of the committee's report, and remuked that the charge in the case of the truant school was 85. 6d. per week, and towards this the Government made a grant of 2s. per week. The charge would prove a heavy item to the Board, were it not that a child was generally only sent to the school for a few motths, and no children had, as yet, been committed to the school. The report was adopted.
SCHOOL MANAGEIENT COMMITTEE.-A HIND OFFER FROM THE CHAIRMAN OF THE BOARD.-IMPORTANT 'ALTERA- TION IN TEACHERS' SALARIES. •

The School Management Committee's report was read by the Rev. THOMAS:FINEGAN. and stated that they had re- ceived the following (copy) letter from the Chairman of the Board:—" Widnes, May 6th, 1882.—With the consent of the School Management Committee, I shall be glad for the present school year, also for the following school year, to pay the school fees Of every child who shall make attendance every time the several board schools may be open: on'e half the money robe paid to the parents. the other half to be de- posited in the. Post Office Savings' Bank in the names of the children, and subject to the same regulations as are now in force-for deposits made at the board schools." They recom- mended that the best.thanka of the Board be given to the Chairman, and that his offer be accepted. It was also' recommended that schedule C. regulating the salaries of' teachers be rescinded, and the following substituted from September Ist, 1882. viz :—Salaries of teachers—head teachers. Class I.—Teachers who have received theie cer- tificates of first class: Masters, cemmencing £l7O, advancing.. per annum subject to favourable reports from managers, £5, to £200; girls' mistress, Commencing at £lO5, advancing per annum subject to favourable reports from managers, £3, to £120; juniors', £95, advancing per annum subject to favourable reports from managers, £3, to £110; infants', commencing at £B5, advancing perannum subject to favour- able reports from managers 43, to rlOO. Class 11.--Teachers who have received their certificates of the second class: Masters, commencing at £l3O, advancing per annum sub- ject to favourable reports from managers, £4, to £166; girls' mistress, commencing at £B5, advancing ner annum subject to favourable reports from managers, £2, to £103; juniors', commencing at £75, advancing per annum subject to favoarable reports from managers, £2, to £93; infants', commencing at £65, advancing per annum subject to favour- able reports from managers, -£2, to £B3. Class Teacherk who are under probation, not having received their parchment: Masters, commencing at £124, advancing per annum subject to favourable reports from managers, £3; to £127; girls' mistress, commencing at 'rBo, advancing per annum subject to favourable reports from minagers, £2, to £B2; juniors', commencing at ,E7O, advancing per annum subject to favourable reports from managers, £2, to £72; infants', commencing at £6O, advancing per annum subject to favourable reports from managers, £2, to £62. I.—ltararr SCHOOLS ONLY.—A bonus of 5 per cent. on the year's salary if a good report be obtained from Her Majesty's Inspector, and 10 per cent. if an excellent report is obtained. _

2.—(a)—SENIOR AND JUNIOR SCHOOLS.-If the passes average 85 per cent. (Junior Schools 90 per cent.) of the number of scholars presented, a bonus of 5 per cent. on the amount of the year's salary will be given; if the passes average 80 per cent. a bonus of 221 per cent.—kb) On Class Subjects: If the grant is earned for two subjects a bonus of 5 per cent. on the year's salary; if for one subject a bonus of 2k per cent.--(c) Specific Subjects: 23 per cent, of the drawing grant earned by the scholars.—(d) Portion f Drawing Grant: 25 per cent, of the drawing grant earned by the scholars. _ _

N.B.—The increase will date from January Ist in each year. AsstsraYr TRACI-MRS.—Boys : Certificated—Not ex- ceeding £75 per annum, rising by £5 annually to £lOO, sub- ject to favourable reports from managers..Uncartificated— Not exceeding £45 per annum, rising by £5 annually to £7O, subject to favourable reports from manigers.—Girls, Juniors, ami Infants: Certificated—Not exceeding £5O per annum, thing by £5 annually to £7O, subject to favourable reports from managers. Unnertificated—Not exceeding £35 Iper annum, rising.ts annually to £5O, subject to favourable reports from managers. STIPRNDIARY MONITORS.—MaIes, £6; females, a. PUPIL TEACITERS.—MaI -!s : Frst year, £l5; second year, £18; third year, £2l ; fourth yesi-, £24. Females: First year, £l3; second year, £l6; third year, £l9; fourth year, £22. And to each pupil teacher who passes Her Majsty's Inspector's ex oninition well £1 10e, fairly 153. Mr. FINEGAN, in moving the adoption of tho report, said the members were aware that a long time had elapsed since the question first came before them whether the present system of paying salaries was the best which they could follow, or not. Re was aware that it was the decided opinion of several gentlemen upon the Beard that the present plan was not the best. He believed there was a general consensus of opinion that the plan now adopted did not work satisfac- torily. Under it junior teachers without parchments could have almost as large a salary as these who possessed parch- ments. The system was also faulty in this respect—that teachers in infant schools had, practically, always received higher saleries than those teacning in a school where the education was of a higher grade, and where more labour and a superior kind of instruction was required from the teachers. It was only right, and according to the laws of common justice, that a teacher in a higher grade school shculd receive a larger salary than one who instructed in- fants. It was the object of the new scale to remedy this ' state of things. ' The committee also considered it jot that the master or mistress who had obtained a first-class certifi- cate should command a larger salary than the one upon probation, who had not received his parchment, and who was merely allowed to follow his occupation under a certain amount of restriction. There was a further reason why he thought the new scale of salaries should commend itself to the Board. viz., that they gave a progressive increase every year, which increase varied according to the department in which the teacher was employed. This proposal would prove an inducement to masters and mistresses to remain in the employ of the Board when they saw that the scale was more satisfactory. The object of the committee had not, upon the whole, been so much to reduce the salaries as to equalize them. Whether the Board adopted the scheme or not, was to him a matter of little moment, but he certainly considered it an honest effort to meet the difficulties in which they were at present placed; and he believed that if it was approved it would not only give satisfaction to the members but the teaehers generally. In conclusion, he might say that it was the opinion Of all acquainted with educational matters, that the grant would be less in the future, under the working of the new code, and in that way the &aeries of the teachers would be lessened. The CHAIRMAN seconded the motion.

DEAMN said that at present the Board paid by re- sults, and a large proportion of the Government grant; but the proposed new scale of payment was upon an entirely different basis, for the teachers would get a large standing salary, and a very small percmtage of the Government grant. The payment by results had worked very sitia- factorily in Widnes. As a matter of fact, they would lind on enquiry, as to what had taken place in the past, that their teachers remained with them under the present scale. There was, however, one point on which be certainly considered Father Finegan bad made out his case, that it was entirely unjust to pay the infant school mis- tresses according to the rates they at present received, (Hear, hear.) As to the new code, he must say that he thought it Impossible to exactly say at present what its effect would be upon the salaries. Mr. SUAW was strongly in favour of payment by resu'ts and he suggested that the committee -might take the re- commendation back.

Ihe Rev. T. FINEGAN replied that the scale, or one similar to it, was brought before the Board 12 months ago, by the Rev. G. Holloway, so that no member could say it was a matter of yesterday. He (the speaker) was certainly not prepared to take the scheme back, as far as he was con- cerned. He then briefly recapitulated the arguments he had advanced in its favour during his opening speech. The scale was adopted by six to two votes. The only members voting against it were Mr. Dstacen and Mr. Shan,. The general recommendations of the committee were also passed. HUNTER.

Tan GOOD SAMLRITANS."--An Irishman named Joke Mitchell was charged with being drunk in Bank-street on the previous night, and also with assaulting Patrick Higgins. —l'he nrosccator said that at h quarter to ten on the previous night he was standing in Batik-street, waiting for his brother who was in a public-house. Spinks said at eleven o'clock on the previous morning the prisoner was in charge of a horse and cart laden with provender and a live pig. Whilst the) cart was proceeding up Sankey-street, the prisoner was try- ing to quieten the straggling pig, but being drunk, the animal broke from his grasp and fell to the grourel, alighting on its snout. The pig bled profusely, and made its way into the yard of the Co-operative Stores. Here it was captured by the Sergeant, who took it to the Eagle and Child. Re then followed the prisoner, and took him into custody.— Councillor Fairclough said carters wanted teaching a lesson with regard to drutirenness, and the prisoner was fined 10s. and 4 ad. costs, or in default, 14 days' imprisonment.; A Isnamp's TRlCE.—James Barns, a tramp, was charged that, being a casual inmate of the Warrington Workhouse, he unlawfully reused to perform Eta task of work.—The prisoner was admitted into the house at midnight on Mori- day.
