div.head: Pitt to tW gditor.
div.p: Pitt to tW gditor.

WALKING DAY. Sir,—l should like ta know whether the two gentle- men who organised the meeting on Tuesday think that the people of Warrington have gone wrong, or what do they think ?—that they are the only two who know when to have the Walking Day ! I think that the meeting the May.or called settled that it should be on the 7th of July, and I further think that the gentlemen I refer to are to blame for all the bitterness that is going on in the '.7town at present. Mr. Morris says that the teache7s have no right to settle what day they shall walk. Now, Sir, I coptend that because a few men who ar€, fond of gambling, and want all their own . _

;, LT, should not be tiie, man to settle it. I also hope • that the Sulllay school people and the manufacturers will stick to the 7th July, and let the Doctor see they can do the thing that is riot to the majority without the aid of men who don't know their own minds five minutes. Warrington, May 25. W. W.

Sir,—After reading the report of the meetir'ns on Tuesday night with respect to Walking Day, as a Sunelav school teacher, I cannot help expressing my surprise that Dr. Mackie and Mr. Morris should continue the agitation on this vexed question. They speak as though all the blame rested upon us as Sunday school teachers, and hoping that even yet, we may be induced to alter our decision. Let me ask and answer a few questions that the public may judge fairly of our position. First: Who requested the gayer to call the meeting that was held under his presidency in the Town Hall, to reconsider the question ? The request was from certain manufacturers who found the third Friday in June (the then appointed day), an inconvenience and a.loss because: of repeated stoppages. ' Who proposed the first Friday in July? Not the teachers, but the manufacturere, who said it would be more convenient on that day, as it would come in the stocktaking week. Who were the manu- facturers as represented? Were they of such standing and importance as would make it desirable to consider their in- terests? I think even Mr. Morris will admit that Messrs. Rylands Brothers, White Cross Co, Monks, Hall, and Co. are worthy of our consideration. As far as I could gather the views and feelings of the teachers, they would have preferred the third Friday in June, but they unanimously felt it to be their duty to have respect to the wishes of the manufacturers, and gave way for them in favour of the first Friday in July. Mr. Morris, also representing an important works (perhaps the most important taken singly), says it does not suit them. As the Mayor said it would be difficult to fix upon a day without causing ieconvenience to someone, I, or one, would be glad to meet Mr. Morris, if I could do so consistently with my principles, but I could never allow myself to vote a general holiday on the same day that horse races are being held in the neighbourhood. God knows our young people are subject tr, temptations numerous and powerful enough without Sunday school teachers as a body voting them another. I confess Ido not find it quite so easy to become all things to all men as to speak of my being a Sunday scheol teacher at one meeting, and recommend men to go to horse races at another, lest they should be melancholy at home, baying no one to cook for them. I could do anything to save men, but not to please them. Let the manufac- turers help us in this matter and show themselves to be the real and true friends of the men, the women, and the chil- dren, by not closing their works on that day, and so helping to make it easy to do right and difficult to do wrong.—l am, &c.. A SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHER. Warrington, May 26, 1882.

div.head: BAZAAR AT LITTLE LEIGH.
div.p: BAZAAR AT LITTLE LEIGH.

lathe history of Nonconformity, the part taken in the movement by the county of. Chester will occupy a con- spicuous niece. It was Cheshire that gave birth to Primi- tive Methodism, and in Cheshire was established the first Baptist Chapel in this district. From the latter has sprung numerous communions, and amongst others is that of Little Leigh. The chapel, an exceedngly plain structure, is situated in the heart of the county, and in the midst of the be dairy farms whence the neighbouring city of Liverpool draws one of its chief milk supplies; but with the sparse population of a farming district it was impossible for the congregation to be very large. Latterly, however, it has been found necessary to alter and extend the.chapel and, school, and a circular in which this is set forth by the deacons gives some interesting particulars. They state that "The church celebrated its jubilee anniversary a short time since. Like many of our rural churches, this one began with a very small nucleus, but it had a most interesting origin and has had a most blessed history. In the year 1816 two young married couples reanoved into the neighbourhood and commenced the work. They had been membera of the church at Hill Cliffe. Thus the church- at Little Legh is the daughter of the most ancient Baptist Communion in our land. • For thirteen years the meetings were held in a farm- house and many conversions resulted from the preaching. The farm- house, chapel was built in 1830,,but proved in a few years to be inadequate, so that it was enlarged. A school-room was subsequently built, and this is much too small for the requirements of the useful and growing work that is going en. There are promising adult classes, which should be taught alone, but there are no vestries or class-rooms what- ever." Since this circular was issued the schOol has been enlarged, two class-rooms have bees added, and preparations are now being made for re-seating the chapel. The cost of these alterations is estimated at £.300, and on Thursday and Friday a bazaar was held for the purpose of raising the money. Iwo stalls had been erected in the chapel, from which the seats had been. removed, and they wqe laden with a large collection of goods of an excellent desaaiption. The first stall was presided over by Mrs, Davidson, Mrs. James Rigby, Mrs. Bentley, Miss Rath Smith, Miss Mad- dock, Miss Howarth (Bacap), Miss Rigby, and,Miss Massey. The most attractive articles on the stall were a silver tea and coffee service, handsome beaded and wool-worked tea oosies (one of which was made by the Mayoress of Crewe), beautiful brackets, some in crewel work and others com- posed of cork and nuts, a variety of rich cushions, a splendid assortment of antimacassars in crewel work, lace, &c. worked by ladies in various parts of the country, a num- , ber of lamps and clocks, pictures and texts, toilet tidies, gents' ties and scarves, .card baskets, scrap books, umbrellas, a variety of mats, a large quantity of pin cushions, an extensive assortment of underclothing, well-made counterpanes, china toilet service and jugs papier mache pin trays, cuff box, and brackets, several Cooks, including Mr. Beamont's "Journey in the East," toys, and other articles. On the second stall were a crewel-worked gipsy table, a walnut what-not and work table, crewel-worked brackets, several beautifully beaded footstools, splendidly worked tea cosies, black satin aprons, china tea service, a large quantity of majolica ware, several glass jugs engraved with a view of the original Hill Cliffe Chapel, towel rails, child's chair, a variety of cushions, wool wcirked slippers, hand- , painted placques, picture frames, toilet tidies, an excellent oil painting of sea shells and weed, which possessed addi- tional attraction as being the work of a gentleman 80 years ef age, a coantitv of wool work by a lady in her 87th year, and curtains knitted by a lady 72 years of age, a magnifi- cent collection of antimacassars and bed covers, a patchwork bed cover ornamented with temperance texts, work boxes, baskets, umbrellas, timepiece, toys, scents, and other goods, besides a table laden with infantile wearing apparel. The stall was in charge of Mrs. Hough, Mrs. Clarke, Mrs. Fletcher, Miss Clarke, and 31ise Hough. There was also a refreshment stall, replete with delicacies, under the superin- tendence of Mrs. Rigby, Mrs. Maddock, Mrs. Grounds, Miss Worrall, and Miss Smith, and a "fish pond" in charge of Miss Hough. Besides the above, able assistance was ren- dered by the scholars and members of the congregation. In one of the class rooms was an excellent art exhibition by Mr. J. S. Greenhalgh, of Rochdale. There were several oil paintings, the most interesting being one of Mr. Gladstone resting at the foot of a tree at which he has been labouring with his axe, and a large collection of photographs of places of interest in the Holy Land, arc. The chapel bad been nicely decorated with flags and mottoes, such as "Welcome to our bazaar," "Work and win," "Nothing without labour," dr.c. Mr. Thomas Rigby, of Sutton Weaver, opened the hazaaar on Thursday morning, when there was a good attendance, amongst those present being the Rev. W. Pilling (Hill Cliffe), Rev. F. Carter (Northwich), Mr. and Mrs. Davidson, Mr. and Mrs. Barber, Mr. and Mrs. Jackson (Sutton Weaver), Mr. and Mrs. Houg4, Mr. and Mrs. W. Fletcher (Whitley), Mr. and Mrs. John Rigby, Mr. and Mrs. James Rigby, the Misses Rigby, Mr. George Arrowsmith, Mr. Wyley, (tc Letters of apology for non-attendance had been received from Mr. J. G. Mc3linnies, M.P. ; the Mayor of Crewe (Alderman McNeill), the Rev. W. Durban, Chester; Mr. F. J. Green, Crewe; Rev. Joseph Rigby, Malton ; Rev. A. Roe- buck, Rev. T. Naylor, Northwich.

Mr. DAVIDSON- briefly introduced Mr. Rigby, who he said was always ready to go where duty called. Mr. RIC4BY said he wa,s obliged to his friends for tho honour they had done him in asking him to open the bazaar, although he would have preferred listening to another doing so. They had laid a table and spread it abundantly with varied fruits of their industry in a skilful and most attractive manner, and they now wished to dispose of them for money to d;scharge the obligation they had incurred in enlarging and improving that building. They had bs4ividually said by their contributions and the interest they had manifested in the work, what they now wished by that ceremony to say unitedly—" Now, therefore, our God, we thank Thee, and praise Thy glorious name. But who am I, and who is my people that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things come of Thee, and of Thine own have we given Thee." It was well that it was in their hearts t 3 do it, and it was well that it was done bo well and so abundantly. He wished them "God speed" most sincerely, and said with all honest commenda- tion, "You have done well by this ministry;" and might their utmost desires be realised. He craved for them now the generous acknowledgment of their visitors in speedily purchasing those beautiful specimens of their handiwork, and in making them the adornment of their own homes, or the useful servants of their many requhTments. He craved it for them for their works' sake, and for the purpose they had it in view to accomplish. They were the inheritors of a faithful and use- ful work which had been pursued there for more than fifty years, and they wished to continue it and carry it on with at least equal efficiency and fidelity, until they in their turn gave it up into the hands of their children. They wanted chiefly, as he understood, to make the place a centre of attraction to the young, and of holy influence to all around, the abode of a living power to draw out the best purposes of the will, and to educate and influence them wisely. They desired to instruct and inspire the mind with faith in God, and to strengthen and confirm the life in every good word and work. Their object was the same as that of their fathers—to preach Christ's Gospel as they understood and

experienced it. and to preach it as they did simply but faithfully and earnestly, and in the spirit of love and meek- ness. They honoured them for this, and they wished that - morning to honour the memory of the faith and patience and self-denial of their predecessors. Our beloved country owed much more of its liberty and its high moral and re- ligious life to Nonconformist village !churches than was generally allowed. Their very existence as self-sustaining centres of spiritual power testified to an earnest purpose of benevolence, and of desire to serve their fellow men. Their original object was to unite as believers in the Gospel, and to provide for a due observance of the ordinances of religion for their own eelificatien, in such simple form as seemed best to their own minds; but the opposition to which they were subjected, more than town or city churches in earlier days, added to their duties and responsibilities. It cam; pelied them to examine closely .into the teachings of the Divine Word, and led them whol.y to dissent from the polity of the National Church, and separate themselves from her communion. This developed strong decision of character and begot a sturdy independence of spirit that feared nought but God, and had been a potent element, as he thought, in the formation of our national character, and that led at the same time to a purity of life which acted as a standing rebuke to the immorality and ungodliness of the age. In reproach they were called Puritans, but in truth both as men and as maidens, and as fathers and mothers, they honoured the name. (Hear, hear.) No period of our history as a nation had been more fertile in manly men and in virtuous woman than this age. Their piety was first pure and then practical, and their church life partook of their own individuality. The revival of religion in the days of Wesley and Whitfield deepened their spiritual life, and those of them who remembered the old men and women who were members of Nonconformist churches in their youth thought of them for the most part as the best type of Chris- tian character they had ever known. If religion was ever a reality with any men it was with these. It was the life of their soul. They loved the truth, and were only concerned to be in harmony with it. They were not educated men, but they were fairly intelligent; not relined in manner, but chaste in feeling; not rich, except in faith and in good works, and in humanity, in prayerfulness, and in goodness. At the same time they were men of ctecision, not half-hearted or ! almost persuaded Christians; bat thorough, altogether be- lievers, having the courage of their convictions, and ready to testify or suffer for the faith that was in them. Although often reproached they were never ashamed of the Gospel, and never grudged attendance to its duties, nor sacrifice for its principles. He knew some such men in his early life, and their faith and assurance had often by remembrance confirmed his own belief in the reality of Divine truth. That place had known such men too. Ile had heard one of its pastors spoken of with the highest respect because of his humanity, and another because of his spiritual power as a teacher and a preacher of the Word, although only a farm servant; and he had a friend who told him frequently of the simple but beautiful and affecting prayers she remembered as a child hearing from the lips of a third, a man of remark- ably mild spirit and consistent life. These churches, too, had always been the sanctuary of all that was just and merciful, and liberal in politics. The freedom of the slave, the Reform Bill, the abolition of the Corn Laws, the repeal of the tests and disabilities, and the equitable administration of justice had always had their consistent and steady ad- vocacy ; so also had hospitals, missionary enterprise , and benevolent work of all kinds. Religious questions, too, in which there was difference of opinion, had always found them on the side of liberty of conscience and homage to truth. Their views of the sovereignty of Christ, and of the spiritual character of His kingdom had committed them to many conflicts with the National Church in most of which they had won, and in all of which, as he thought, they must inevitably win. Time will make it plain, and "The day will declare it." Meanwhile let them say— ! Let Cmsar's due be ever paid ' To Car and his throne, But consciences and souls weie wade
To be the loid's alone,

_They found it necessary yet to stir one mother up to liberality and to consecration ts His service; but when He ' comes whose right it is to reign. He will find a people so fall of love and devotion that they will vie with each other which can do most to honour Hirw, and the latter days shall be more glorious than when kings and statesmen thought it necessary to support or to patronise the Church of Christ; and none would have done more to. 'accomplish this than such institutions: They aspired to a part in this service; and were offering that bazaar 'and its 'proceeds towards , its accomplishment, and again they. said "May your best wishes be accomplished." Be it theirs to be true to the best 'epirit and the best tradition , of their fathers.. Take the children whom God sent to their school and nurse them forilim. "For the promise is unto you and to your children." Be helpers of each other'a. joy, and consolers of each other's sorrow. Let no root of bitter- ness spring up to trouble them. Be patient towards all men, support the weak, and ever follow that which was good both in the sight of Ged and man, and, "the God of Peace be with you;" and when the books were opened at last might it be found written of that little hill of Zion, "This and that man were born in her," and of them and him, and all the redeented, might the commendation of the humble disciple be recorded "She bath done what she could." (Ap- plause.) In • conclusion, he declared the bazaar open, remarking that the first purchasers would have the greatest choice—(laughter)—and the largest buyers would be the greatest helpers. (Applause.) On the proposition of , Mr. WILEy, secondal by Mr. , Titomls flAnnEn a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Rigby, and the sales were at once proceeded with.

div.head: LYME
div.p: LYME

. David William Davies, fustian cutter, Lymm, was tined 103. and. costs or 14 days' imprisonment, at the Sale Petty Sessions, on Monday, for stealing a couple of pigeons, the property of Andrew Day, at Sale, on the 4th February. Met. T. E. MunnTy AT LYMM.—The teetotallers of Lymm were gratified on Sunday by a visit to their picturesque village of Mr. T. E. Murphy, of the Blue Ribbon Army. The popular temperance advocate was accompanied by the Rev. T. Rippon, and both gentlemen addressed an out-door meeting in the afternoon, and afterwards Mr. Murphy gave an address in the Wesleyan Chapel.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

On Satulday last the district coroner, E. Driffield, Esq., held an iquest on the body of Mary Blackmore, late of Brynn, who died suddenly the previous Thursday, as reported in the Examiner of last week. The inquest was held at the Brickmakers' Arms, Bank-street. A verdict was returned " Death from natural causes."

SUNDAY Scnoor. ANNITERSAHY.—OH Sunday last two sermons were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Edge Green, Golborne, by the Rev. E. Mather, of Northwich. The services during the day were—an address in the morn- ing at 10-30 by the above gentleman to scholars, teachers, parents, and friends; and services in the afternoon at 2-30, and evening at 6 o'clock. All the services were well attended and much appreciated. The singing also was very good. The anniversary altogether was a great success. The col- lections realised during the day £2l 9s id, and the donations received since 12s, making a total of £22 is id. ST. THOMAS'S SCHOOLS.—The scholars attending St. Thomas's Day Schools have passed a most satisfactory ex- amination in religious knowledge, as will be seen from the subjoined report :—" Diocese of Liverpool Inspection of Schools in Religious Knowledge, May 20, 1882,—Dear Sir, —I beg leave to send you the report of your schools, which is also submitted to the bishop.—Yours faithfully, JOHN WATSON WATSON." " Golborne School: Inspected 19th April, 1882.—The children in the infants' school passed a very fair examination; the repetition was well said, and the scripture answering very fair. Present, 96. The girls' school has been fairly instructed, and the general results of the examination are creditable to the teachers. The repe- tition is well said, and the slate and paper work good. The , younger children have made a decided advance. Present' 102. The boys' school throughout passed a very creditable lexamination ; but group one took up too much work in the Old Testament subject. Considering the amount they took the answering was good. The work throughout the school was very praiseworthy. Group three did specially well. Present. 97." Both teachers and scholars will doubtless appreciate the congratulatory sentiments contained in the report.
MID-CHESHIRE ITEMS.

It was resolved at last Friday's meeting of the Altrin- cham Local Board that a rate of 25. in the pound be laid for the year, to be collected in two instalments. The Rev. H. I. Blackburne has been re-elected chairman of the Nantwich Union School Attendance Committee for the current year. _ _

It has been decided to hold this year's show of the Church Coppenhall Horticultural Society on the 28th August next, near the Cross Green, Coppenhall. At the last meeting of the Nantwich Guardians a member gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board he would move "That in future the election of Guardians take place triennially, and that the Clerk take the necessary steps to carry out the same."

The third and final competition for the right to represent the Northwich Volunteer Company at Wimbledon, county and battalion prize meetings took place on Saturday last. Private Musgrave and Sergeant E. Musgrave head the list, and are consequently entitled to represent the company at Wimbledon.

PAROCHIAL APPOINTMENTS AT ALTRINCIIA3I.—At the meeting of the Altrincham Board of Guardians, on Wed- nesday morning, Mr. Joseph Toft, of Lymm was appointed assistant-nlerk, in place of Mr. Tom Cutter, appointed to the clerkship of thh Chesterfield Uuion. Mr. William Moore, the librarian of the Manchester Mechanics' Institu- tion was appointed relieving officer for the Lymm district, the emoluments of which office are worth £l6O a-year. There were over a hundred applicants. BURGLARIES IN CEIESIIIRE.—There have been during the Last month two entries made_ into the house of Mrs. E. C. Prosser, widow of a former curate of Tarporley. Only a ! short time ago, a man was seen by a neighbour endeavour- ing to force his way into the house of Mrs. Prosser, at Church Minshull. The prisoner, a tramp, was then com- mitted for two months' hard labour. The hoetse was left un- tenanted while the lady was on a visit to some friends in London. A second raid on the house has been more success- ful, for it has been discovered that a valuable timepiece, pre- sented to the late Mr. Prosser on leaving Tarporlev, has dis- appeared, as well as an electro-plated service, consisting of coffee-pot, teapot, sugar bowl, and cream jug, all richly chased. POACHING AFFRAY IN CHESHIRE.—On Tuesday a gang of poachers was surprised by three keepers in the employ- ment of Captain Tomkinson, the Earl of Haddington, and

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 27, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 27, 1882.

two other gentlemen, who have the right of shooting over Delarcere Forest. The estates in the neighbourhood of Tar- porley having been poached over by a large gang for several weeks past the keepers determined to make a raid on them, and endeavour, if possible, to capture them. At one o'clock on Tuesday morning they came across the poachers at a place known as the Duck Bank, in the occupation of Mr. Charles Newport, of Wilkington. After a severe melee, the keepers succeeded in securing two poachers named Thomas Astburn and Aaron Walker, and har.ded them over in charge of the'county constabulary at Kelsall. On returning the keepers came on two more of the gang named Enoch Astbury and Robert Astbury. Three large nets, some hags, bludgeons, and stones, together with a stick furnished with a spear at the end, were taken by the keepers from the poachers. The latter fought desperately, and in the encounter a son of Mr. Tomkinson's keeper, a youth named Jones, had his head badly Cut. TIIE CIIESHIRE YEOMANRY.—The competition for prizes offered by the Duks of Westminster for the first ancPsecond best swordsmen in the regiment took place on Saturday, on the Roodee, at chester, in the presence of several thousand , spectators. After a spirited contest between two picked men from each troop, Captain Pope, the judge, awarded the sil- ver cup to Sergeant W. Owen, of the Arley troop, and second prize of £5 to Corporal R. Mullock, of the Eaton troop. On the result being announced, the band played "See the con- etuering hero comes." The regiment was inspected on Mon- day, by Colonel the Hon. C. Thesigei, GB., Inspector- General of the Auxiliary Forces, Northern. District. The number of men present (375) was about 50 short of the average—two troops, Cholmondeley and Peckforton, being entirely absent owing to political feeling, according to some accounts, and to agricultural depression, according to others. The tenantry of Lord Rocksavage and Lord Tollemache form the bulk of the absent troops. The inspecting officer congratulated the Duke of Westminster, as colonel com- manding, and the other officers, on the general appearance both of the horses and men, and expressed himself as satisfied on the whole with the days proceedings.—The Duke of Westminster expressed himself pleased with the manner in which the orders had been obeyed. Alluding to the ab- sence of the two troops, he said he did not know what might be the matter with them; he could hardly imagine that they , were so ruined either in circumstances or in spirit as not to be able to attend the annual training of the Cheshire Yeo- manry. For his own part, he had been supported through- out all the twelve years he bad been in command of the regiment by the officers and by the landlords in the county, and it was rather late at his time of life, and considering the number of years he had been connected with the regiment, to speak in a disparaging tone of the landlords failing in their support.

teetotal hospital, that was, intoxicating liquor was not used in the treatment of the patients, and a far greater majority recovered than in an hospital where drink was used. (Hear, hear.) It was a fact that those persons who abstained from drink had less illnesses, lived longer, and when taken ill had a much better chance of recovering than those who took strong drink. He appealed to them for their own sake, and for their children's ache to become teetotal. In England at present there were some 600,000 drunkards, and all these in 20 or 30 years would be dead. Did they think there would be another 600,000 to take their places? He was afraid there would. • He asked trim for toe sake of the children, for those who were helpless in this matter, to resolve to have nothing more to do with drink, and that God helping them they would do what they could to make England a sober nation. Another hymn was now smile-, and the meeting separated. At seven o'clock a public heeting was held in the Wes- leyan school, under the pre_sidency of Bro. Bebbington, and there was a large audience. The members of the order wore their badges. During the evening the choir, under the leadership of Bro. Geo. Clarke, sang in good style a number of temperance melodies, which included "Make the song," "The Templar Army," "See our ranks," and" Come, come, my friends." Bro. John Warburton gave a reading entitled "Drink's doings." Sister Becket, of Liverpool, recited, with cansiderable elocutionary power, a poem "The drink demon dethroned," and she was heartily applauded. Prayer having been offered by Bro. Passmore, The. Calla-NUN give a few interesting facts with regard to the Order. Their organisation, he observed, was a perma- nent aril successful temperance society. They had been established in this country some 12 or 14 years, and to-day numbered nearly 100,000 Good Templars. In South-West Lancashire, which contained Liverpool, St. Helens, Wigan, and Warrington, they had a membership of about 5,000 !adults, besides 3,000 juveniles. Good Templars were men and women banded together to help one another to resist the evils of drink, and he knew families whose homes had once been scenes of wretchedness and misery, but now they were Good Templars had bright and happy Lmes. The advan- tage of the Order was that its members were enabled to help each other from ever falling again under the temptation of this drink; and they. also had to promote the temperance cause, which could be done much better banded together than separately. The promotion of temperance they esteemed of great and high importance. Bro. J. B. Commeess, P.G.W., Conn., Liverpool, remarked that he would ask them a straightforward question : Were they for the cause of temperance, morality, and religion, or were they for the cause of drunkenness ? Perhaps they would answer that they took a little occasionally, but syni- pathised with the temperance movement .and had great esteem for those who were engaged in the work. There was a time, lie supposed, when they would have liked the sym- pathy of those who drank' but they were not now in that ' position. (Hear, hear.) The temperance cause was quite able to stand apart from anybody who used intoxicating liquor. (Hear, hear.) They wanted sympathy, but their sympathy without themselves was of very little use. "How to stop drunkenness" was a rather strange title for a book written by a brewer. Mr. Charles Buckstone, the author, spoke of the fearful evils that resulted from intemperance, and then he said in one sentence, which would live for years to come, that the struggle of the school, the library, and the church on the one side, against the public-house and the gin palace on the other, was but one development of the war between heaven and hell. He fancied if the teetotal- lers had said that, some newspapers would have said it was like the teetotallers, something very extreme. But this was the fight they were engaged in—of heaven against hell. There could be no neutrality on this question; those present that night were in one of two classes—those who drank and those who did not. Those who drank moderately were in great danger. Dr. Andrew Clarke speaking of moderate drinking, said "I say to men and women, allowing a little more for men than women, if they go beyond what would be represented by half a pint of beer at dinner or sup- per; or one glass of ordinary wine, or one tablespoonful of spirits well diluted wills water, they are doingethemselves harm ; they are passing beyond the physiological point of innocent gratification to that of wicked indulgence." (Ap- plause.) That was a defination of moderate drinking of which the teetotallers-had no cause tO complain. (Hear, hear.) It did not say that taking the quantity named did any good. (Hear, hear.) - The speaker then touched on the desirability of Sunday—closing, remarking that the responsibility of lreep-ing them open rested upon the moderate drinkers. (Applause.) Sister GREEN, R.W.S.J.T., a, Liverpool, who the Chair- man said had been actively engaged in juvenile temperance work, was then called upon to address the meeting. In the course of an earnest speech, she spoke of the importance of coming to an immediate decision with regard to the tem- perance question, and narrated two instances v. hich had come under her own observation in Liverpool, to show tile danger of delay. She depicted, in eloquent terms, the evils arising float drunkenness, and appealed to those present to escape them by joining the Earlestown lodize. She did not think it possible that any man or woman could .keep a publichousa when they saw the Fin and 'misery their bueiness was doing. The teetotallers did not hate the publicans; they hated the traffic. How could they help hating it when it was making their sons and daughters lose their manhood and woman- hcod ; when it was blighting the light in their • homes and its inmates miserable wrecks; how could they help hating it when it was destroying flue handsome young men and women that could be put to healthy work for the Master ; how could they help hating it when it was keeping their churches and chapels empty and filling the ale houses and jails, making them lead lives not fit for slaves nor human beings. .(Applause.) They must hate it, and they wished these present to hate it with them. If they would join the Order they would show them how to hate it heartily. If some strong steps were not taken the women of England would become quite as fond of drink as men if not more so. If there was anything more repulsive on the face of this earth than a drunken man it was a drunken woman. • She would sooner die than live with one. (Hear, hear.) Brother Monrits JONES moved a petition, to be signed by the Chairman, and forwarded to the House of Commons, with reference to Sunday Closing. It stated "That your petitioners believe that the sale cf intoxicating liquor on Sunday is a fruitful source of intemperance, immorality, and crime, and wherever such sale has been prohibited by law great benefits have followed. Your petitioners, there- fore, pray Your honourable house to pass a bill stopping such sale during the whole of that day." The motion was seconded by Brother R. W. KIRICUS, and adopted unanimously. ' A vote of thanks was accorded to the speakers, visitors, &c,, on the motion of Brother GEORGE WARBURTON, senior, seconded by Brother JOHN LITTLE, and the meeting ter- minated.
A RIGHT OF WAY QUESTION AT NEWTON AND
EARLESTOWN.

After Father Lennon's passage at arms with "the School Board man," with sharp points, has been duly disposed of, as we foresee it will, he may enjoy a friendly tilt with his near neighbour, as to the right of way of his flock, and other residents of Newton, through Mr. Clarke's farm yard to his and other places of worship. In former years, and long be- fore St. Mary's was built, or thought of, there was a foot- path from between Worsley's and Critchley's cottages, near this farm house in Crow-lane, through the fields into the Mains. A right of way not then disputed • for many of the present inhabitants have travelled it hundreds of times, and the cottagers still live to'attest the fact. Some dozen years ago the path was ploughed up, the stile was taken away and the hedge made up, by the present occupier, and the road through his farm-yard substituted so far as the portion en- closed was concerned, although, even them, he had an objec- tion to allowing pedestrians to go through his yard, for they went to the east of his barns at first. This was considered an equitable arrangement by many, but a few knowing the precariousness of any such arrangement continued to go by the old pathway at least once a year, in order to maintain the public right, and with what reason appears now. On Sunday last, a traveller by this road, and who had used the pathway on Sundays constantly for all these years, to his ease and comfort, was informed by the farmer that he would really have to forbid the road to all and sundry, because the gates had been left open and his cattle had gone out a few Sundays ago, and since which he had nailed up his gates. In fact he would look upon all passing that way as trespassers as indeed they are so far as his farm-yard is concerned, But no further, for the question arises whether the right to the original pathway should not revive when the accommo- dation road is stopped. It behoves the Town Commission- ers, who represent the ratepayers, to see that no further con- cessions be made on any pretext whatever. - But the imme- diate cause assigned is the greatly increased number of travellers to and from the Roman Catholic Chanel, who, it is said, could find a nearer way home than by this footpath. But we should say there is all the more reason for the corn- missioners looking after this particular pathway, which has been brought before them long ere now, with what result this may show. Not that there is any disposition to blame the commissioners, only to admonish them as gently as possible to attend to this business at once. They may,how- ever, suddenly make up their minds to open up the new road so long contemplated between the railway bridge in Wargrove-road and St. Mary's schools. If this were done there would be little to be said, except that there would be one the less pleasant field path. But, as matters stand at present, it seems somewhat arbitrary and a breach of faith to talk of stopping up this particular road, the only one in fact between Park-road and Cross-lane, a mile apart, if we except the diagonal road over the Mains—and which con- nects Newton and Earlestcwn on the one side as Crow-lane does On the other. Although this pathway of which we speak existed before there was any Crow-lane from the Tan House (Clarke's Farm) to the- bridge below the Congrega- tional Church, as the making ef Crow-lane is within the memory of living men, and in the part spoken of, which looks like adamant, it was a mere bog and waste with a trottoir, as was proved when the continuation of the main sewer was lately made, and which is a further proof of ,t; the antiquity of thia road in question, which doubtless led off the domains to these cottages presumably occupied by tanners. It has even been gravely stated that Cross-lane was intended as an equivalent for this very field road, but that seems like nonsense to those who have travelled both roads in the same day many a time and oft. But if true, it is an additional proof that a right of way did exist. It is much more likely to have been made as the nearest cut to Jones and Potts' foundry (where the Waggon Works now stand). But, to return to this pathway. It is conveniently left out of sight that a simple stile-at each end of the premises would obviate the difficulty complained of, and keep the cattle from straying. It would also be more convenient to females, who, at present, to save ten or fifteen minutes walk in a half-hour's journey, have to clamber over two, if not three, five-barred gates; a picturesque proceeding no doubt to those not engaged in doing it, but highly inconveuient to those who are, and are

pressed for time in attending the many services of the Roman Catholic Church, not to speak of the Congrega- tionalists on Sundays. For both, and lately all three, were locked or nailed fast; that in the Mains without warrant, as we think, although there is a board to say that trespassers, will be prosecuted. Should a prosecution at any time en- sue, it is to be hoped that the grateful public will not leave the victims to pay their own law expenses, as was the case in a late public matter where the defendants had the satis- faction of paying each his own lawyer, and no doubt would do so again, only for the forces arrayed against them, although right is might. But it is to be hoped nothing of the kind will be done, for although the common bas slipped out of their grasp, we trust no cajollery will whistle away any present rights and privileges the inhabitants of Newton and 14:arlestown may at present enjoy. We beg Mr. Len- non's pardon for using his name in this connection, but he uses his pen so deftly, that we think he could not do better than save some of his people from doing unnecessary penance by putting the matter properly to the authorities with his accustomed vigour, force, and fertility.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

1.0,G.T. HOPE OF EAULESTOWN LODGE. - On Monday evening the usual weekly session of the above lodge was held. One candidate was restored to membership, and several proposed. Amongst other business it was unani- mously and most heartily resolved that the thanks of the lodge be tendered to the Mr. T. J. Gilmour for accompany- ing the lodge choir on the harmonium at the public meeting on Saturday, and at other times. A special vote of thanks was also accorded to the choir for their services. It was re- solved to postpone the lodge from Whit-Monday to Tuesday in order to give the members an opportunity of taking part in the Band of Hope Demonstration at St. Helens on Whit Monday. There was a very good attendance of members.

NEWTON CONSERVATIVE CLUB—For the purpose of adopting new rules for the efficient working of the club, on Thursday evening a meeting of the !timbers of the Newton Conservative Club was held in Newton Town Hall. Mr. Thomas Camber presided, and amongst those present were Messrs. Samuel Brewis, Golborne ; Gillispie, J.P., Newton; and Mr. Thomas Sutton, of Warrington. The new rules were read by the ste:etary and unanimously confirmed. An address was then delivered by the Chairman on the present political position of the country. Mr. Thomas Sutton, Con- servative agent for Newton polling district, also made a few remrrks, in which he urged the desirability of constantly attending to the register, and expressed his gratification tlfat a Conservative Club had been formal in the district, as he considered it was calculated to assist their cause more than anything else.-- A vote of thanks to the chairman, passed or. the proposal of Mr. Brewis, concluded the proceedings. GOOD TEMPLARISNI AT EARLESTOWN. DISTIIICT MEETINGS.

The quarterly meeting of the South-West Lancashire Dis- trict Lodge of Good Templars was he!d in the Wesleyan school-room, Earlestown, on Saturday. Upwards of 70 representative.?, besides a good number of ..,sitors from all parts of the district were present, including lodgegin Liver- pool, Bootle, Southport, Wigan, Leigh, Tyldesler, Warring- ton, Widnes, G-arstori, St. Helens, aud Ashton. The session was opened at two o'clock by Bro. N. Bbbington, D.C.T.,of Garston, most of the other officers being also,present. Bro. senr., of Newton-le-Willows, was appointed Assistant Guard.

The report of the D.C.T. showed a good amount of work had been accomplished. He had attended 41 meetings and written nearly 200 letters during the quartkr, besides paying visits to individual members. From a general survey he found the lodges working steAily. In some towns, as in Warrington, where the Blue Ribbon movement had been oi.ened, or active public work taken up, the lodges had in- creased in membership, and he trusted the members present would note that fact, and Would make up their minds for more active and earnest effort amongst the public, and good must result. Brother R. W. Kirkus, district secretary, reported the members:4 in November to be 4,600, and in February 4,640, which was a decrease of about GO, but the returns already received seetned to indicate that the numbers were improving, and he was expecting to report an increase for the May term. There were 87 lodges in the district, 70 having already reported. The report of the worthy district treasurer (Brother Stephen Pugh, Liverpool) showed the finances to be in a fair position. The report of the D. Executive was tendered by Brother Kirkus, and stated that arrangements were being made for conferences to be held throughout the district for the good of the order and to carry on united mission work. Brother R. Anders, D.S.J.T., reported for the juveniles, and was gratified to be able to report favourably on the juvenile order. There were now 40 juvenile temples in the district, with a membership of about 1800, being an increase on the quarter of 49. There were also 169 adult members who bad taken the juvenile pledge as honorary members, which included abstinence from strong drink, tobacco, and gambling, the number being an increase on last term. The district council were arrang- ing for a sale of work during the aatumn to raise a fund for the more extensive and effectually carrying on the work among the young; and he urged the adnits to assist in making this successful. All the reports were adopted, be- sides several resolutions bearing chiefly on the internal working of the Order, which were disposed of. It was ' unanimously resolved that the annual Good Templar demonstration be held in St. George's Hall, Liverpool, in October next, a committee being appointed to arrange for the same. It was also decided to arrange for special mis- sion work during the summer months throughout the dis- trict. Brother Bebbington gave a practical sketch of how the work Could be done. It was I agreed to send a vote of sympathy with the relatives of the late Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke in their heavy and sudden bereavement, Brother Kirkus to formulate and send through proper channel such expression. The next session of D.L. will be held in Southport at the end of August. The session being concluded the representatives proceeded to the lower school-roorn, where tea had been provided. This part of the proceedings was then thrown open to the public, and about 150 persons were present. The following presided at the tables: Sisters Mrs. Howard, Harriman, Allison, Taylor, Dillow, Bell, Mrs. G. Warburton, Mrs. H. Warburton, Miss G. Harriman, Miss M. J. Howarth, A. Howard, M. E. Barrett, Hughes, and Whitty, assisted by Brothers John Taylor, G. Little, J. W. Broomhall, J. H. Barrett, W. Andrews, W. B. Foden, 11. Watts, and Edward Newman. An adjournment was afterwards made to the market ground, where art open-air meeting was held. A small cart was improvised as a platform, which Brother M. Bebbington, D.C.T., of Garston, ascended. The members of the order gathered round, and commenced to sing the hymn "Dare to be a Daniel." By this means a. large crowa of, men, with a few women and children, was quickly collected, and they appeared to give earnest attention to each speaker. Bro. BEBBINGTON, in a short address, said he did not know whether it was possible for anybody in that company who were not Good Templars, to be ignorant of the existence and principal object which the Good Templars had in view, and I it would be unnecessary to explain. He might say however, that a Good Templar was a teetotaller who was very much in earnest and very desirous of making other people teetotal as well as himself—(hear, hear)—and they that afternoon wished the people of Earlestown to consider the claims and importance of the question of total abstinence from drink, especially with relation •.o their habits. The habit of not taking intoxicants at all, was, the Templars believed, by far I the safest and most sensible thing for men and women to do. At one time it would have been necessary to prove that a man could live without drinking intoxic ints, but it needed no argument to prove Oa; he could do everything required of him without their aid. He had all his life existed without drink, and his life had proved that man could live without intoxicating drink, and enjoy good health as well. (Hear, hear.) He concluded by appealing to those present to be- come teetotallers, and then to join the Good Templar Order to promote by every endeavour the temperance cause. Bro. MORRIS JONES, of Liverpool, after another hymn had been sung, then delivered a short speech. He observed that the Templar Order aimed at the moral, social, and spiritual well-being of humanity at large. He had come there to ad- vocate its principles, which were total abstinence (or the in- dividual, and prohibition for the State. They regarded this as afvery loyal business to be engaged in, and as such felt it to be their duty, as far as might be, to persuade all the friends outside the pale of the organisation to give their co- operation in one of the greatest struggles for freedom the world had ever seen. There was no slavery so bad, no habit, and no tyranny so evil as the bad habit of drinking strong liquor, and they wanted if possible their co-operation to re- move this terrible sin. It was a fast well known to most of them, perhaps, that in Liverpool there were 2,500 public- houses to tempt man astray, whilst there were only 200 places of worship te teach man duty to God. In Liver- pool alone each week there was spent £58,000 for strong drink. When they—" teetotal fanatics," so called, or "Good Templar lunatics "—told these facts, and wished for some restriction upon the sale, the publicans said they intended to rob the poor man of his beer. The fact was the poor maR was robbed by his beer, and the Good Templars Nvished to I save him from his ruin. In addressing the meeting, Bro. J. B. COLLINGS, P.G.W.C., of Liverpool, pointed out the physical advantages derived by being a total abstainer. In London, he said, there was a

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

A BURIAL SCANDAL.—Yesterday week, at the meeting of the Wigan Board of Guardians, Mr. John Lowe, the governor of the workhouse, submitted the following report : —"I have to report that the body of one Julia Gray, late a Boman Catholic inmate of the workhouse, was sent to the cemetery on Monday last for interment, but as there was no officiating priest in attendance, the body was placed in the grave without the performan3a of any funeral ceremony. Yesterday (May 17th) the body of one Edward Edwards, late a Nonconformist inmate, was also sent for interment, and no minister of that persuasion being present, the burial service was read over the body by the sexton, and left in the chapel. I communicated with the registrar on the subject, and have received from him his explanation, which I have handed oser to the clerk."—The Clerk said the'explanation ran as follows :—"The body of Julia Gray was placed in the grave on Monday afternoon, and the burial service read over her on Wedaesday afternoon, by the Rev. J. Johnson. In the case of Edward Edwards. the Nonconformist sexton did read the burial service over the body, awl hear- ing nothing more I thought it might be perhaps a week before another funeral took place in that ground. We had no Church of England minister yesterday (May 17), and the body has remained in the church all night. Things like that are occurring pretty often here lately. Yours re- spectfully, TllomAs Y. BYROM."—Mr. Strickland suggested that the report of the governor, together with the letter of the registrar, should be sent to the Wigan Burial Board with a request for an explanation.—This was agreed to.

div.head: HAYDOCK.
div.p: HAYDOCK.

HAYDOCK PARK COMPANY, LIMITED.—This company proposes to acquire a 21 years' lease of the Haydock Park Farm, situate at Newton-le-Willows, Lancaster, and to lay out the same for preserving and coursing bares, rabbits, dx., and also to construct a racecourse. It woe registered on the 10th instant with a capital of £20,000, in £lO shares, with the following as first subscribers :—Thomas Stone, Newton- le-Willows, 1 share: L. Pilkington, Widnes, chemical manufacturer, 1; Cr. F. Fawcett, 2, Exchange-street East, Liverpool, stockbroker, 1; G. O. Sharpe, 17, Castle-street, Liverpool, timber merchant, 1; G. Alexander, Dublin, mer- chant, 1; Alfred Briscoe, 15, Arlington-street, London, 1; N. Dunn, Union Club, Newcastle-on-Tyne, I.—lnvestors' Guardian.

A BATCH OF DEFENDANTS.-At Newton, on Saturday, James Swain, James Pilling, Thomas Pilling, James Hayes, John Gleaves, Robert Williams, Daniel Deardone, William Banner, and William Williams were all charged with play- ing at pitch and toss on a highway at Haydock on the 7th Inst., or with aiding and abetting. All defendants pleaded not guilty, through Mr. Moore, who defended. P.C. 364 stated that he saw all the defendants playing on a road lead- ing to the canal. Mr. Moore submitted that the road was a private one, and did not come under the title of a public highway. He also held there was no evidence to prove the ofbiace had been committed. Fines of 103-and costs and 5s and costs were inflicted.

div.head: F RODS HAL
div.p: F RODS HAL

STREET OBSTRUCTIONS.—The memorial presented to the West Eddisbury Highway Board, complaining' of the in- blerable nuisanCe, caused by swings, roundabstits, standings, shows, Jic , being erected in the Main-street, Frodsham, has been followed up by a memorial in somewhat singular terms which has been addressed to the Marquis of Cholmondeley, as lord of the manor, and has elicited a very favourable reply in which, while expressing an opirdon that the police have power to interfere, his lordseip promised to co-operate with the inhabitants of Frodsbam in removing the nuisance corm:dallied M.

CHURCH PARADE AT KINGSLEY.—On Sunday the Frod- sham Volunteer Corps attended divine servie.7: at Kingsley Church, under the command of Captain Robert Ashton, the other officers pres2nt being Captain. C. W. Hazlehurst (Runcorn), and Lieutenants R. G. Henry and H. Harrison. The rank and file, including the band, mustered 40. Hymns had been selected appropriate to the occasion, and a suitable sermon was preached by the vicar (Rev. Samuel Hague) horn 2 Timothy, ii c., 3v. "Thou therefore, endure hard- ness as a good .goldier of Jesus Christ." We understand that it is intended to have frequent volunteer church parades at Frodsham, Helsbv, and Kingsley, and although it is a new feature in the volunteer programme, it cannot fail to have a good efLct, and has much to commend it. . MISSIONARY SERMONS AND ANNUAL MEETING.—The They. Henry Linton, M.A., lion. Canon of Christ Church, Oxford, preached two sermons in the Iron Church, Fred- sham, on Sunday, in aid of the funds of the Church Mis- sionary Society. The annual meeting was held in the Town Hall, on Monday evening, when the vicar, H. B. Blogg, pre- sided, and there was a good attendance. The meeting having been opened with singing and prayer, Dr. Weaver read the statement of accounts, from which it appeared that £43 3s. 31., had been contributed to the society from the parish of Frodsham during the year 1881, and the sum of £l3 had been received at the collections on Sunday, being a con- siderable increase of last year. At Os. GI had also been con- tributed through the medium of missionary boxes. The Rev. Canon Linton gave an excellent address, in which he demon- strated the spirit in which our missionaries enter the field, and related some touching incidents in his experience, of the sacrifice which his friends had made to devote their lives to the cause of foreign missions. The Chairman gave a very, interesting address, and explained that the Rev. A. S. Grenfell who had been announced to speak, was prevented by the storm from making his intended visit. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the speakers on the motion of Mr. E. A. Wright, Esq., J.P., and a collection was made at the close of the meeting which amounted to £7.

div.head: LATE LORD JUSTICE HOLKER.
div.p: THE LATE LORD JUSTICE HOLKER.

Just at the time when the judicial bench needed streng- thening, and when the legal knowledge, great experience, and acuteness of Lard Justice Holker would have been invaluable in the High Court of Appeal, that distinguished lawyer has been taken away. After a brief illness, his lordship expired on Wednesday morning, and his loss will not only be felt by the legal profession, but by the people of Lancashire, particularly those of Liverpool and Man- chester, by whom he was well known and held in high regard. Lord Justice Holker possessed the personal gifts— rarely combined—which make up a successful lawyer, and which also secure popularity with all classes of people; and among the many brilliant careers of men who have attained judicial eminence few have been more remarkable than those of the man who, without influence or family connec- tions, fought his way from the position of a humble lawyer's clerk in an obscure Westmoreland market town to that of one of the Lord Justices of Appeal. The Holkers are an old Lancashire family. The late Lord Justice, the son of Mr. Samuel Holker, a Bury manufac- turer, was born in that town in 1828, and was educated at the Grammar School there. He was, when quite a young man, articled to a firm of solicitors at Kirby Lonsdale, and had for a fellow clerk Mr. Barker, a gentleman in practice as a solicitor at Southport, and who is the deputy coroner for this division of the county. The firm to which young Holker was articled held the position of clerks to the justices for Kirby Lonsdale; and at the bar dinner at the recent assizes a learned gentleman—although now grown grey in the profession is yet a stuff gownsman—related that when he was a junior on the great northern circuit "Jack Holker," as he was familiarly known at the bar, used to ride over (for in those days there was no railway communication between the two places) from Kirby Lonsdale to Appleby with briefs and instructions from his employers' office to those members of the bir who were employed in prosecutions. Some of the gentlemen thus instructed are still in practice here, and they speak with much kindliness of their young "instruc- tor," who afterwards attained so great an eminence in his profession. After completing his articles Mr. Holker practised but a short time as a solicitor. He studied for the bar, and was "called" at Gray's Inn in 1854, and chose the northern circuit. He took up his residence at Manchester, and for some time his chambers were in Queen's-r,quare in that city. Having the reputation of being a sound lawyer, he soon obtained a good practice, some of the earliest of his briefs 'being given to him by Messrs. Cobbett and Wheeler and Mr. Thomas Bellringer (one of the regis- trars of the Liverpool County Court). He frequently ap- peared as counsel at the Kirkdale Quarter Sessions, and conducted several important appeals before the Earl of Derby, Sir R. A. Cross, Mr. Edward Gibbon, Mr. G. Winter- Moss, and other magistrates. While a stuff gownsman his practice at the assizes, especially at nisi prius, was very large, there being scarcely a commercial case of moment in which he was not retainea as junior. He had for his confreres Messrs. Littler, Crompton, Addison, Ambrose, Cottingham, Torr, Jordan, and other names well known in the circuit. Although not a brilliant speaker, he was a successful advo- cate. His style of oratory had nothing in common with:that of James, Bliss, Temple, Slice, or Russell ; and in his career no great forsenic triumphs on his part can be pointed to. But he was rightly called by the solicitors a " winner of verdicts ;" and his practical, plain way of stating a case, his skill in cross-examination, and his knowledge of law, obtained for him great success with juries, and thus enabled him to gain more cases perhaps than any other man at the bar during his time. In 1868 he was appointed Queen's counsel ; was, in the Tory interest, elected M.P. for Preston in September, 1872; was appointed, on December 12, 1874, Solicitor-General in the Disraeli Government; and Attorney- General in November, 1875. On the nomination of Mr. Gladstone he was appointed a Lord Justice of Appeal, and during the brief period be held that distinguished office gave further evidence of his legal ability, his decisions being markcd by all that soundness of law and common sense

which always characterised his career. The news of his death was received in Liverpool with the greatest sorrow, and in the various courts regret was expressed that so learned a lawyer and so kindly and courteous a gentleman should have been taken from among us at a comparatively early age.

At the meeting of the Preston Town Council on Thursday morning, after votes of condolence had been passed with the Devonshire family and Miss Burke, a vote of condolence was passed to Lady biker on the death of her husband, and lengthy eulogisms were passed on his lordship. It was announced that the funeral would take place at Lytham next Monday.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

_ The fitters turners, smiths, and pattern makers of Kirk- caldy have demanded an increase of wages to the extent of one half-penny per hour, to take effect on Saturday next. All the cabmen of Bury are on strike in consequence of an attempt on the part of the Corporation to enforce by-laws requiring all licensed cabdrivers to wear a brass badge on which inscribed the number of their license.

A strike occurred on Monday at Easton Steel Works, Middlesborough, whereby the whole Bessemer department is laid idle. It was brought about by about 150 enginemen re- fusing to work on account of a stoppage of Sunday work. Several hundred men are affected. THE NORTH STAFFORDSHIRE IRON TRADE. A mass meeting of puddlers, shinglers, and forge rollers employed at all the iron works in North Staffordshire was held at Burslem on Monday, to discuss the demand for an increase of ed. per ton on a branch of the work called "doubling," which demand the employers had refused to submit to the South Staffordshire Arbitration Board, which hitherto ruled their wages. The meeting resolved to ask the employers to submit the question to an independent arbitrator, failing which it is feared a strike will be resorted to. THE ENGINEERING TRADE IN LANCASHIRE.—The en- gineering departments at the Lancashire Wagon Works have given a week's notice of a demand of 2s. per week increase of wages. If the request be not acceded to it is believed a strike will be resorted to. About two years ago the men's wages were reduced by this amount, on the understanding that it would be returned when trade was more favourable. The concession has been granted in many places, and the above demand, we believe, has been made at the instigation of the executive of the Society of Amalgamated Engineers. If so it will effect the mechanics working in the different mills in the town.

THE CORN TRADE.—The Hark-lane Express says :—Dur- ing the past week the weather has been brilliantly fine and dry, with strong easterly winds and cold frosty nights. On Sunday the air was more southerly and softer, as it was yes- terday morning. Very little progress has been made by vegetation as compared with the previous week, and the ten- dency of the week's weather on the wheat crop is distinctly in the direction of forcing plant into ear on the stunted growth of straw. The spring corn wants rain and warmer nights, and none of the cereals are in a better position than they were a week ago. The trade for native wheat remains dull and languid, but rates have not declined for good mil- ling samples. Country flour has become weaker in value, and occisionally less money has been accepted. In other descriptions of home-grown grain there has been no change during the week. Foreign wheat off stands in London has met a very laborious sale during the past week, whilst in Liver- pool values declined id. per cental all round on Friday. Flour at the close of the week must be written decidedly easier to buy, Australian makes being relatively cheaper than Australian wheat. Maize has met a languid demand, and prices are easier.

THE LABOUR MARKET.-The labour market is again somewhat more settled owing to the conclusion of the iron- workers' strike in the north, but in several large branches of industry, though employment is good, profits are reported to be small, and barely 'remunerative. Building in and about some of the great industrial centres, especially Middlesborough and Newcsstle-on-Tyne, is again better, and in the South Plymouth also shows some signs of improved activity in the same direction. At Wolverhampton the works are well off for orders, and prospects are on the whole good. At Birmingham and Sheffield the tool manufacturers in the several departments are well engaged, and, most of the great trade societies report comparatively few hands out of em- povment. One of the more important new works recently sanctioned by 'Parliament is the Forth Midge, which will involve a large expenditure of labour and capital. New ' docks at Tilbury are also approved. In Weardale the lead- miners remain poorly off for work, and in North Wales the quarrymen are still somewhat unsettled. On the Clyde the ship engineers have secured an advance in wages, and at all the leading parts shipbuiders and marine engineers remain very busy. Emigration from all parts of tlie. country con- iinues very high, and serviceable labour is rapidly absorbed in the United States. At Winnipeg, Manitoba, domestic servants are in keen demand. Departures to Natal have again been less ntnnerous.-Labortr News. THE NORTH-WALES STraxsts-The unfortunate dispute in the North Wales mining district has now lasted upwards of five weeks, and as yet shows no signs of a peaceful termina- tion. A number of men have resumed work at the old rate of wages, and others have gone in at the 5 per cent, reduc- tion insisted on by the masters. But the great majority are still 'out," refusing to return to work at the reduced terms which the masters say they are compelled to offer in conse- quence of the depressed state of trade. The distress throughout the district is daily increasing, and it has been decided to form a central relief committee at Wrexham.- On Thursday at the tneeting of the Wrexham Board of Guardians, a letter .:was read from the Local Government Board, complaining that out-door relief had been granted to able-bodied strike hands, and pointing out that relief should only be given to such paupers in the workhouse, if the workhouse was full, then the guardians ought to impose a labour task in return for the relief granted.-Mr. Wm. Lester said he knew for a fact that if the house was offered to the colliers on strike they would come there on masse, and that meant that they might perhaps find themselves in the position of having to deal with 7,000 .persons at one time. He would propose that the clerk inform the Local Government Board that the workhouse was full, that the guardians found it necessary to continue out-door relief to the strike hands in the form of bread, and that the question 9f adopting a labour task had been referred to the visiting committee for their consideration.-Mr. Edward Rowland seconded the motion, and it was agreed to unanimously. The men resumed work at the Grosvenor Collery, three miles from Wrexham, on Thursday morning, on terms which are highly satisfactory to tbe men and their leaders, the new rate of wages being, practically, an advance upon those paid when the strike began. This is the third colliery that has resumed work, the other two being the Ffrwd and Brynkindllt. THE LANCASHIRE COAL AND IRCp TRADE: Manchester, Wednesday.-The coal trade generally continues quiet, and pits, as a rule, are not working more than four to five days a week. House-fire coals move off very slowly. Engine fuel is only in moderate demand, and both burgy and slack are plentiful, with stocks of the latter accumulating. Quoted prices are without material alteration, but there is a great deal of pushing in the market, with Yorkshire and Derby- shire coals coining in at very low figures, and in the Man- chester district there is a tendency towards some reduction in ilst rates with the close of the month. At the pit mouth the average prices are about as under : House coals of the better qualities, Bs. to Bs. 6d. ; seconds, 6s. to 75.; common round coals 45. 9d. to ss. 6d. ; burgy, 4s. 3d. to 4s. 9d.; good slack, 6d. to 3s. 9d.; and common sorts about 3s. per ton. With the commencement of the usual season for placing out gas coal contracts inquiries are coming in for this class of fuel, and a few transactions have taken place on the basis of 6s. 31. to Os. 9d. per ton for good screened qualities at the pit mouth. For shipment a fair demand is maintained, but prices continue low, steam coal averaging 6s. 6d. to 75., and better sorts, suitable for house-fire pur- poses, 7s. 9d. to Bs. per ton, delivered at the high level, Liverpool, or at the Gerstein Docks. Coke continues in tolerably good demand, at about late rates. In the iron trade there have been a few more inquiries stirring during the week for forge pigs, but the offers made by buyers are at very low figures. For local brands of pig iron makers are asking 455. 6d. for No. 4 forge, and 465. 6d. for No. 3 foundry, less 2, delivered equal to Manchester, but they are unaale to do business on these terms. In the finished-iron trade there has been a moderate inquiry for sheets and plates at comparatively low figures, but otherwise business is very quiet, and bar makers report new business coming forward only in extremely limited quantities. For delivery into the Manchester district the average price now ruling for local bars may be taken at .£6 7s. 61 to £6 103. per ton. The engineering branches of trade continue as a rule well sup- plied with work, and preparatory to the usual Whitsuntide 'holidays some of the large local establishments have been put on overtime.

PAUL'S C.C.—This match was played at Crewe on Saturday last, and after a pleasant game resulted in a victory for the home team, which was a good one Owing to the train leaving so early, the Wesley Hail were only able to raise nine men, out of whom only five belonged to the first team. 12, Hargreaves-street, Oldham, Nov. 17th, 1881. Dear Sir,—Ever since I was four years of age, my parents in- form me that I have suffered from great weakness. At the present time, I am 21 years of age, and if the paTticulars of my ease will be of any service to you, I shall be only too happy to give them to you. For a great many years I have been under different doctors, and the last doctor I visited told me he could do no more for me; so he sent me to the Southport Hospital, but after remaining there some time without finding any benefit, I returned home. I have been treated as a consump- tive patient. I have earned very little money for my parents, seldom being able to work through being so weak, and most of the time I have been under the dector's treatment. About three weeks ago I commenced wearing your " Magnetaire," and in a week's time I felt so strong that I began work, and have never been off work one hour since. I assure you I should never have thought it possible that I should feel so strong as I d, now, and you may depend upon it both I and my parents shall always recommend your Appliances. Yours faithfully, Mr. Lonsdale ELIZABETH HULLEY.

div.head: SCIATICA.
div.p: SCIATICA.
Blacon Point, Saugball-road, near Chester, 21st December, 1881.

Dear Sir—Hearing of the numerous cures effected by the use of your Ati,hmetaire Appliances, i was induced to give them a trial. I had been suffering 18 mou'lrs from sciatica. The pains in my hip and leg were very severe, and got so bad that I was afraid I sh.uld be c‘unpe;led to leave my work. Had tried all sorts of remedies, but was unable to obtain any relief until I tried your Appliances. Since wearing same I have found the greatest benefit, can sleep well, use my leg with ease, and am entirely free from pain. -For the good of others I feel It my duty to make it known, and shall be happy to amwer any inquiries, feeling sure the Magnetaire only requires to be better known to be generally worn.—Yours faithfully, Mr. R. Lonsdale, AIAGNUS WATT.

SCROFULA AND PARALYSIS. 11, Broom-street, Hanley, Jan. 4th, 1882. Dear Sir,—When I came to you four months ago; I had been paralysed in one leg for ten years, the limb being perfectly cold and stiffened. I also suffered from scrofula badly, and was troubled with a very severe cough. I have worn the belt and soles you recommended ever since, with the following result : I can now walk very well with the leg that was previously stiff and numb, and can bend the joints, the circulation too is quite restored through my body, have lost the cough entirely and my face is very much better, the skin now being dry and much lighter in colour than before. We are all very highly satisfied with what your Appliances have done, and shall al- ways recommend them with confidence in any similar case. My spirits and appetite are also much better.—Yours truly, Mr. It. Lonsdsle. JNO. GRIFFIT EIS.

TESTIMONIAL FROM THE HON. AND BIN. A. C. TALBOT. Rectory. Church Eaton, Stafford, December 26th, 1881 Si r,—ln behalf of my fellow-sufferers, and in justice to you, I give you my experience of your " Magtietaire." Some seven years ago I had a severe pAralytic attack which had left me with a stiff shoulder and arm, with little use in my hand. I used the electric remedies, then invented, for three years with benefit, and after that time, as I was convinced that I could not expect any further relief from them at my age (now 76), I discontinued them. Hearing from Mi. Clendinnen of your Appliances (though without much faith in them), I purchased one of your Invigorators, and, to my surprise, in ten days I found my arm much more supple and useful, but the benefit I have received is very marked, and I have but little doubt that my limb, though very weak, will continue to improve under your Appliances. I wish you to send me a Magnetaire Friction clove, as I think friction will complete the cure.— Yours, die., Mr. R. Lcasdale. A. C. TALBOT.
