• PU.NCORN POLICE COURT. moNDAy.—Beforo Mr. C. W. Ilazle'nurst (chairman) an,l

Mr. S. B. Chadwick. REZUDR..IT ForaL.—A married man, named Richard Clench,' was summoned for using threats to Ellen Clay, shopkeeper, of Percival-lane.—Complainant said she wished to with— draw the case, and the Beach granted the application. TUIT.3DAY.—Before Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst. CAUGHT RED•HINDED.—Henry 1101115 was charged with having, on the same morning, stolen a brass buckle and a strap, the property of Charles Arnold, a boatinan,,Prosecu- tor said he had been in the habit of putting up his horse at Mr. Hayward's stable, Top Locks, and at six o'clock that morning he left the harness hanging behind his horse. In oonsequence of what was said to him, about half-past nine I be went to the place, and found that the buckle and the strap were miming, and the strap had been cut.—A lad named Benjamin Traeman said that at about a quarter-past nine he was in the stable, and saw the prisoner cut the buckle prodaced from a strap belongin to Arnold's ,horse. He told Cha ostler.—P.C. Mellor stated that be apprehended the prisoner at the stable, and found upon him the buckle pro- duced. He made no reply to the charge.—Prisoner now pleaded guilty, and elected to be tried samularily.—The Chairman said he would be scot to gaol 14 days, and he hoped the imprisonment would be a warning to him. WRDNESDAL—Befbre Messrs. John Brundrit (chairman)
and S. B. Chathvick.

A SALUTARY HINT TO VILLAGE ROUGIIS.—Joseph Caw- ley, or Frodsham, a chemical works labourer, was charged with having on the 20:h inst. assaulted a watercress seller, named John Smith, of Rock Savage.—Complainant said that on Saturday be was at Frodsharn, which is about a mile from Rock Savage, and before going into a public- house on the Frodsham side of the bridge, he put his basket nontaining watercress on the road. On afterwards going out he saw that some one had taken some of the contents of the basket, and he asked the prisoner, who was standing near, if he knew anything about the watercress, or who it was that had taken it. Cawley threatened what he would do to him if he spoke to him about the matter. He (witness) then went on the road to Rock Savage, and when near the turn bridge, the prisoner and three other men overtook him. Cawley, withontwteing a word, struck him a violent blow, seriously injuring his face.—A woman named Lucy Barri- son,who lives at Clifton, corroborated complainant's state- ment. Though she was a hundred yards off complainant at the lime he was assaulted, she heard his screams, and she then noticed Cawley kicking him violently. Prisoner had to be pulled off by another man before he would desist.— The Chairman said the prisoner would be sect to gaol for two months with bard labour, and he hoped this would prow a caution to men who were like minded, that they could not be permitted to go about the country assaulting; any one with whom they might happen to meet.—The pri- soner's wife, who was in court at the time the sentence was delivered, wept bitterly; and also threw her arms round her husband's neck, kissing him tenderly.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT. SkrußD.l.Y.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun..
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT. SkrußD.l.Y.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun..

ONE Ti; 711-13—ACM-4- or COAL •STEALERS. —The prisoner Mary Daly was again brought up, charged with stealing 73 lbs of coal, value 2d., the property of Messrs. Burns and Robinson' on the previous day, from a wagon at West Bank. She was fined 21s. and costs, and given time in which to pay the morpy. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. John Brock.

A SAD CASE.—John Robinson, and his wife Eliza (who appeared with a child in her arms), were charged with begging. Evidence was give] to the effect that the pri- soners were seen to enter several shops in Victoria-road, on Monday night, and beg.—lnspector Barnett said the begging nuisance was becoming an intolerable nuisance, and the police had received strict instructions to look very sharply after such offenders, as their number in the district was legicn.—Prisoners said they had been looking for work, but were unable to find it.—The magistrate remarked that if they had no means of subsistence they ought to apply to the workhouse authorities.—They were each sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour, and the child was ordered to be taken to the workhouse _
W&DNESDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun.

A LICENSED VICTUALLER PERMITTING DRUNKENNESS Mr. Charles Harrison, licensed victualler, was summoned for permitting drunkenness on his premises, and also with selling beer to an intoxicated person. Patrick Murray and Christopher Kerley were charged with having been found drunk in the house.—Sergeant McGregor gave evidence to the effect that on Saturday night, the 13th just, about half- past nine, he and Sergeant Strickland went to the Ram's Head public house, kept by the defendant Harrison. On going into the vaults, he found six men there, amongst whom were the two defendants, Murray and Kerley, who were very drunk. A half-pint glass of beer was in front of Kerley, and a quart bottle full of freshly drawn ale on the bar counter, before Murray, who afterwards put it under his coat, in the presene, of the barman, and walked out. Strick- land then asbedtl barman if he had supplied Kerley with the beer, and he replied, "I have." He next asked the bar- , man if he considered the man fit to be supplied with beer, and he said "He is not very bad." He next enquired if he considered Kerley quite sober, and be said "I don't think he is drunk." He told the barman that he should report him, , and he went for the landlord. He and Strickland then left the house, but remained in the doorway. The landlord after- wards came to them, and said he did not consider the ,nan very drunk. At this time Murray again returned, carrying an empty quart bottle. He drew the landlord's attention to what he had seen in the house, as to the beer upon the counter, on which he remarked "He is drunk, but it is a question whether he was supplied with the beer here or not." The landlord followel. Murray inside, and refused to fill him any beer. Next Murray and the landlord came outside to him and the other sergeant, and the former said to him (wit- ness) "Do you consider me drunk and unfit to be supplied ' with beer ?" He replied "you are quite drunk." Kerley gave a wrong Christian name and a wrong address. , —Sergeant Strickland gave corroborative evidence.--Mr. Bartlett, for the defence, said that Kerley was in the opinion of every one in the house at the time of the occurrence, quite sober. His client was prepared to admit that Murray was drunk. In order to show that Kerley could not have been drunk, he might state that after visiting defendant's, he went to another public-house, kept by a Mr. Tyrer, and he called the manager's attention to the fact that the police- men considered him drunk. The manager then supplied him with two pints of ale.—.Ackroyd Rogers, barman to Mr. Harrison, said he supplied Kerley with drink, and consi- dered him perfectly sober. After the police had spoken to him, the manager made Kerley walk from one part of the bar to the other, and he did so straightly, and seemed perfectly sober. When Murray came in, be said that he was not sober, and refused to serve him. Murray had a bottle, but he did not get it in that house.—Nicholas Kerley, labourer, said he was served with a glass of beer in the public- house, and he was drinking it when the police came in. The police said be (witness) was drunk, but he was not.— Patrick Murray, another defendant, said that when he went into the Ram's Head the barman refused to serve him. Ho afterwards went out, and sent for a pint of beer, which he wanted for Sunday morning. His daughter went to Mrs. Price's for the beer, and as she was going home with it, he met her, took it from her, and went to the Ram's Head with it in his hand.—Janees Spruce and Thomas Beasley, labourers, were also called for the defence.—The Bench said they were satisfied that the case bad been proved, and the landlord would be fined 20s. and costs, and the two other men 7s. 6d. and costs each.

DisTrasEus OF THE PUBLIC PEacz.—Thomas Kennedy was charged with a breach of the peace in Lug,sdale-road, on the 13th instant.—P.C. Ormerod gave evidence in the case, and defendant was ordered to enter into sureties to preserve the peace for three months, himself in £lO, and one surety of £5.--John Brock was convicted of having fought with a man named William Leather, and caused a disturbance in the publie street, eu the 10th instant, and was oidered to find sureties in a similar amount, and for a like period. :•SCtIOOL BOARD CASES.—A number of tilse should have come up for hearing, but were adjourned. SUNDAY GAMBLINO.—CATTORT IN THE ACT.—Three youths named John Davitt, Peter Roberts, and Thomas Whalley were summoned for gambling on the footpath at Moss Bank, on the 14th instant.—P.C. AlmAnd stated that he stw the defendants playing cards on the footpath .—Each of them was fined 23. 61. mind 10s. costs. A DEAR Toss-up—James Clare and Patrick Ford were prayed to have played at pitch and toss in Liigsdale-lane.— P.C. Almond proved the case, and defln.lauts were each fi.ned ss. and 53. costs.

A CARELESS DatvErt.—Satauel Butterfield was °barged, under the Highway Act, with permitting his horse and cart to stand in Waterloo-road for a considerable time, on the 3111 a March, without anyone in charge of them.—lt was stated thbt defendant drives for Greenall's, of St. Helens.— He was fined ss. and 4s. 61. costs. Dunwx ON LICENSED PREMISES —Catherine Coyne was brought up, on remand, charged with having been found drunk on the licensed premises knotvn as the King's Arms, Anne-street, Widnes, on Monday.—She was fined 10s. 6d. and costs. ASSAULTING A WOMAN WITH A GINGER BEER BOTTLE. —Catherine Cannon was charged wit!' lowing, on the 22nd instant, assaulted Elizabeth Ogden.—lt appeared that the prisoner, at the previous Petty Session? wa.s fined 203. and costs. Complainant went cut on Monday for the purpose of buying some necessary articles, and met Cannon, who had a ginger beer bbttle in her hand. Before complainant Could offer any resistance, the prisoner struck . her on the head several times with the bottle, so that she was covered with blood, and beaune senseleFs. I'risoner denied the truth of Ogden's statement. and said her conduct was dictated by revenge—Cannon was ordered to enter into sureties, herself in £lO and one in X. 5 to keep the peace three months, or, in default, be sent to gaol 14 days. - I A SWINDLER SENT TO GAOL—THE Br:AGAR AND DIS MYSTERIOUS STEED.—JrAn Brown was charged with having, ' on the previous evening, been guilty of begging in Victoria- road.—An officer statA that by saw the prisoner go into several shops in Victoria-road, and band one of the people whom he solicited. a book, in which the following statement was written :—" This is to c-..,rtity that the latarer bas lost his horse through gripes. It Iris been a great loss to him. Hoping that the readers of this will kintily assist him. (Signed) R. John Brown." The hook showed that several subscriptions had been received.—lnspeciorßaz'nett was put in the witness-box, and said he bad askul the prisoner what he had done with the money be had collected. He replied "I have spent it in eating. It has just kept me out of the workhouse ! " Several of the signatures appear,d to be in the prisoner's own handwriting.—Brown was sent to gaol one month with hard labour.--An elderly wcaan, named Mary Jones, was charged with begging in Caroline-Street.—

A policeman stated that on Tuesday afternoon he caught the prisoner begging in the street named, after watchiug her about two bours.—Superintlndent Barker said it was the custom of beggars to ask for bread, and afterwards sell it to the lodging house keepers, who fed their pigs upon it.—The Chairman 9iid the Bench could not allow begging in the town, and the prisoner would be sent to gaol seven days. A PP.DLAII WITHOUT A CERTIFICA.TE.—ThOIIIRS Maguire was charged with pedling without a certificate.—The pri- soner, who said he had not a farthing, was fined ss. and 63. 6d. costs. ASSAULT CASE.—Mary Daley was summoned for assault- ing Catherine Roberts and Elizabeth McGee, of Lliztbeth- street.—lt was proved that defendant struck one of the com- plainants on the forehead, and also gave the other a blow.— She was fined ss. and costs in each case. TRESPASSING IN A. FlELD.—James Dwerryhouse was summoned for trespassing in a field at Widnes.—The game- keeper to Mr. Lidney Young gave evidence to the effect that he cautioned defendant, who, however, said he did not care, as even if he were summoned there would not be much to pay.—Defendant was fined is. and costs, and the damage, making Os. A DISORDERLY Womax.—Hannah Conlon was convicted of having caused a disturbance in Wellington-street, on the 7th inst., and she was ordered to be committed 14 days, in default of finding sureties to keep the peace three months, herself in £lO, and one surety in £5. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. H. S. Hall. _

THE BEGGAR. AND THE POLICE SERGEANT. - Charles Becker was charged with begging that morning.—Sergeant Strickland said that about a quarter past nine the prisoner came to his house in Charles-street, Simm's Cross, and asked if he had any bread or coppers to spare! He im- mediately took him into custody.—Prisoner was sent to gaol seven days.--A man named John Thompson was charged with a similar offence.—P.C. Worthington stated that he saw the prisoner go into the West Bank Hotel for several coppers.—Thompson pleaded guilty, and was sent to gaol seven days.

div.head: BLUE RIBBON ARMY FMONST RATION.
div.p: THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY FMONST RATION.

The demonstration by the Warrington rne:nbers of the Blue Ribbon Army, took place on Saturday aftetnoon last in weather the reverse of that which resulted in the pro- cession being postponed. In place of the black sky and pitiless downpour of rain which prevailed about three weeks ago, the processionists were favoured on Saturday with a clear blue sky, from which tbesun shone brilliantly; and the only drawback in regard to the weather was the strong east wind which blew clouds of dust along the streets. The tendevotta was the vacant land in Bowsey-road, opposite St. Paul's Church, whence the processionists started on their journey through the town shortly after half-past two. Two mounted marshals preceded the procession which was headed by a three horsed brake, in which rode Mrs. Parker, president of the British Women's International Temperance Association, and a number of other ladies who wore the white badge of the Association in addition to the badge of blue. Then followed Wycliffe Sunday School brass band, under the leadership of Mr. R. Travis, and im- mediately behind walked the Revs. T. Rippon, J. Morton John Yonge and E. Moore, and succeeding them:came the female members of the army, the girls from the Workhouse schools, who had joined the corps, being last. The clean and tidy appearance of the latter provoked much favourable comment, as did the appearance of the boys from this school, who were accompanied by the band under the con- ductorship of Mr. H. M. Mines. The male members followed, and the rear of the procession was brought up by a trap driven by Mr. T. Weaver, and containing three teetotal patriarchs and Mr. W. Clarke. The venerable teetotallers were Mr. John Cassidy, who has reached the ad- vanced age of 92 years, and has been a total abstainer for 48 years; Mr. J. Broadhurst, 78 years of age, a teetotaller of 46 years' standing; and Mr. W. Mee, aged 76, who has also abandoned the use of intoxicating liquors for the period of 46 years. The number taking part in the procession has been variously estimated at from one to several thousands, but without committing ourselves to any particular figure, we may state that whatever the actual number was it would have been considerably greater but for the fact that the time fixed for the procassion to move off was very inconve- nient for many working people who would have been glad to be present. The great majority in the ranks were ado- lescents, and the assembly and start was witnessed by thousands of people—every coign of vantage in the vicinity of the rendezvous being occupied, and the streets traversed by the procession were thronged with spectators. The route taken was down Bewsey- road, along Tanners'-lane, through Winwick, Horse- market, Bridge, Mersey, Irlam, Buttermarket, Sankey, Legh, Edgeworth and Bewsey-streets, and again along Bewsey-road to the starting point. Here the brake was drawn up to serve as a platform, and from it brief addresses were delivered. The first speaker was the Rev. TlRippon, who observed that they had had what he regarded as a re- markable demonstration which must have appealed to everybody:that the temperance cause in Warrington had taken a new departure which meant the emphasising of the great principle of self sacrifice. The Rev. John Yonge thought all of the Blue Ribbon Army must rejoice at the success of the demonstration that day, and be trusted the movement which had begun so nobly, and carried with it the sympathies of the people, would continue, and progress during the coming years of the history of Warrington, so that there would be a public sentiment created which it would take a great deal to overcome. Mrs. Parker also spoke a few words, and the proceedings concluded, as they began, with singing and prayer. What may be described as the first field day of the Warrington corps of the Blue Ribbon Army was fairly successful, although it must be admitted considerable disappointment was felt at the absence of the leader, Mr. Murphy, who had promised to attend, but who, it was stated, was at Blackpool and had been misled in regard to the trains. However that gentleman arrived in time for the evening meeting at the Public Hall, and he wa.3 warmly cheered on making his appearance. The hall as usual was crowded. Mr. Murphy conducted, and ad- dresses were delivered by the Rev. J. Cullen, of Oughtring- ton, on "Nuts to crack," and the Rev. W. Reid, Levens- hulme, spoke on " Lessons from the condemned cell," the address bearing specially on the case of the man McDonald who was recently hung for the murder of his landlady at Burnley. On Sunday evening another service was held in the Public Hall, and addresses were delivered by Mr. Murphy, the Rev. John Yonge and the Rev. T. Rippon. The attendance was large, the hall being crowded, and the meeting was one of the best which has been held here in connection with the movement.

div.head: THREE MEN NEARLY SUFFOCATED AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: THREE MEN NEARLY SUFFOCATED AT ST. HELENS.

About the time this paper was published last week a serious accident occurred to three men named John Huyton, James Johnson, and Wm. Millighan, who were employed by the St. Helens Corporation cleaning out a sewer on Green- 'bank. About two o'clock Huyton descended a manhole to fill a bucket, and Johnson stood at the top, his duty being to draw the bucket up. While Huyton was engaged there ' was a sudden lush of gas along the sewer. This was in- haled by Huyton, and he fell down insensible. Seeing the situation Huyton was in, Johnson descended to his as- sistance, but he was overcome by the gas, and fell heavily upon Huyton at the bottom. Millighan, in the hope of saving his fellow workmen from suffocation, ventured down the ladder, but having got half way he also became partly unconscious, and was in immediafe danger of • falling when Thomas Lyon arrived on the scene, and seizing Millighan by the collar dragged him to the top. Haying placed Milli- ghan on the ground, he wrapped a shawl round his mouth and then descended for the other men. Being a person of considerable strength Lyon soon raised the men to the surface, where several people had collected. The men wero carried into houses near, and a messenger was despatched to the surgery of Drs. Twyford and Jamison. Medical aid was obtained and proved efficacious, but Huyton was so weak frora the effect of the gas, having been in the longest, that he had to be removed to Denton's Green, where he lived, in Ia cab. Our readers will remember that the ground in the vicinity of the Greenbank Alkali Works is saturated with acid, and efforts from time to time have been made to im- preve the drainage, which is very imperfect. The borough surveyor (Mr. Hart) has frequently brought schemes for its improvement before the Highways Committee of the Town Council, who had ordered the work in question to be done. To clean out these sewers, holes are made every thirty or forty yards, but notwithstanding the additional ventilation ehtained the work is very dangerous, and the men are obliged to proceed- with great caution. The Greenbank Alkali Company are' exerting themselves to remedy this state of things, which has existed for a long time, and machinery is now in satisfactory operation to effect an improvement. The men are now not much the worse for the incident, yet but for the timely assistance of Lyons there might have been fatal consequences.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 27, 1382.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MAY 27, 1382.
MR. G. W. LATHAM ON TENANT RIGHT.
CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE AND TENANT RIGHT.

The half-yearly meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture was held at the Town Hall, 7,Chester, on Satur- day. The chair was taken at the commencement of the meet- ing .by Mr. George Slater, of Northwich. _ _

—Alr: THOMAS IfiGnv (the secretary) read the report of the Council for the half-year, which contained the following recommendations on the tenant riAtt question : (L) That compensation should be made to outgoing tenants for improvements made by them during the tenawy. and which either in whole or in part are in existence at the expira- tion of the tenancy. That such compensation be measured by the increased agricultural value of the holding, which increase, has been caused either by actual money outlay or by the general condition and cleanliness of the soil, and is due to the expen- diture and skill of he tenant. That in case of dispute, the amount of compensation be settled by arbitrati ,n, or if neither landlord nor tenant should desire arbitration, by allowing the tenant to dispose of his interest in the holding to an eligible in- coming tenant, against whom there are no reasonable grounds of objection.
, (2.) That notice to quit an agricultural holding be extended to twelve montha.

(3 ) That to carry out the previous and other proposals. it will be ne,essary to establish a Land Court to settle matters in dispute between landlori and tenant expeditiously and econo- ml'ally, _ _ _

(4 ) That there should be granted full liberty of cultivation, cropping. and sale 0' pro .uce, subject to a power to be given to the Court to restrain any acts of the tenant which would be injurious to the landlord, and assess damages, if any, to the extent to which the acts complained of have reduced the letting value of the land.

(5,) That the law of distress beabolished, subject to a power to be given to the Court to allow, in case of non-payment of rent, the re-entry of the landlord, on such terms as it shall consider equitable, or to place the tenant under terms as to payment of rent.
A motion that the report should b 2 received was moved by the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Byrd (Tarporley), and carried.

The CLUBMAN, in calling attention to the recommenda- tions of the Council, said be was pleased to find at their last meeting in Chester, during a discussion on questions be- tween landlords and tenants, that there was a spirit of fairness which was very gratifying Co all. He was sure the tenant farmers of Cheshire had no wish whatever to infringe in the slightest degree upon the rights of the landlords. One's sympathies generally went with the tenant, because he was supposed to be on the weaker side; but he (Mr. Slater) hoped that in discussing the proposals which would be brought before the Chamber each one present would put sympathy on one side, and act on the broad principles of justice and fairness. (Hear, hear.) Mr. G. W. LATHAM said he was chairman at the meeting of the Council at which the resolutions (given aboye) were arrived at, and although they did not entirely commend themselves to his mind, being rather too much of a compro- mise to exactly suit him, yet he could assure the members of the Chamber that they were drawn up with the utmost desire to secure impartiality and fairness. The Council con- sidered that if the resolutions were carried there would be a perfect protection for the tenant farmer in all his agricul- tural pursuits, and that, at the same time, the landowner would be very much benefited. They might, he thought, take it for granted that there was an entire concensus of opinion among both landlords and tenants, that compensa- sation should be given for unexhausted improvements; the only difference of opinion was as to how that ccmpensation should be assessed. (Hear, hear.) There were many bills pro- posed for dealing with questions between landlowners and tenant farmers. In his opinion, continuity of tenure was the one sole remedy for meeting the difficulties which now arose, but that was not at the present time within the range of practical politics, though he believed there were some now living who would see it become the law of the land. After considering the various bills and schemes for dealing with agricultural questions, the Council came to the con- clusion that the fairest basis on which to give compensation was the improved letting value of a farm, but it did not very much matter how that improved value was arrived at, whether by the expenditure o 2 skill or the expenditure of money. They expressly excluded everything' in considering the basis of compensa- tion, that did not affect the farm ; their proposals were, therefore, not open to the charge brought against one bill that a man might, if it became law, build a public-house on his farm or turn his farm into a villa, and then come upon his landlord for compensation because the farm would let for more. They avoided that difficulty by declaring that the "improved letting value " must mean greater agricul- tural value. It would be a very easy thing, he believed, for an experienced local valuer to tell what was the letting value of a farm. If neither party desired to call in an arbi- trator, then the outgoing tenant, the Council thought, ought to be at liberty to sell his tenancy to someone else. His (Mr. Latham's) opinion was and always had been that a sale of the tenancy was the fairest thing for both sides, for then the landlord would, for the first time in the history of agri- culture, have the outgoing tenant assisting him to find a respectable tenant for his farm, and the outgoing tenant would be able to sell his tenancy in the open market. With reference to the second resolution, that the Council thought twelve months' notice to quit would be best, he himself thought two years would be desirablo. With regard to the third resolution they were of opinion that a court was re- quired which would settle, cheaply and expeditiously, dis- putes arising between landowners and tenant farmers, so that the liberty given to the tenant might at any time be stopped from degenerating into license. Mr. Latham briefly specified the reasons which had induced the Council to adopt the fourth and fifth recommendations, and explained that the object aimed at by the Council was to secure the rights of both parties. It was felt by them tbat unless tenant farmers were guaranteed compensation for the im- provements which they made, severe competition would crush them to the earth, in which case landowners would most certainly grievously suffer. (Applause.) In conclu- sion, Mr. Latham moved the adoption of the first resolution. The meeting then adjourned for luncheon, and on re- assembling, The Duke of WESTMINSTER, president of the Chamber, took the chair, and gave a general assent to the programme of the committee. As to the manner of assessing the amount of compensation for improvements, his grace said that the question was one of great difficulty, which would have to be faced by the Government, though it was highly improbable that they could deal with it this year. The duke, on the other band, dissented from a proposition to allow the tenant to dispose of his interest in his holding to an eligible incoming tenant. This, his grace, declared, would be bring- ing in the Ulster custom of tenant-right, which many main- tained had not given satisfaction in Ireland, and the introduction of which into England was undesirable. The
duke also doubted the econom-ii Of a land court, but as to the law of distress he was quite willing to see it abolished.

The VICE-PRESIDENT, the Hon. Wilbraham Egerten, was the next speaker. He said the resolutions were deserving of some comment, and he wished to criticise them in a friendly manner, and for the most part to support what his grace had said. He had always been in favour of compensation to outgoing tenants for bona-fide improvements—(hear, bear) —and it had been the practice on the estate with which he was connected. He therefore, thought he could approach this subject prepared to take a favourable view of the prin- ciple of resolution No. I—certainlr so far as the first para- graph was concerned. With regard to the second paragraph, he had always held that it was a- very great fallacy to estimate the improvements by the lottino• value, and he could not therefore support that paragraph'. As to the last clause of the first resolution, he asked how was a person who never saw the farm before, when the tenant left, to estimate the improvements, and to _determine whether they were _

_ caused by manuring, by skill, or by other causes! Because improvements were often due more to the seasons than to the skill or expenditure of the tenant. After briefly refer- ring to the second resolution, which, he said, contained a provision which already existed in the Agricultural Holdings Act the speaker proceeded to the third proposal. He thouglgt it was quite unnecessary to establish a land court. With regard to the fourth resolution, he did not think there should be unlimited liberty of cultivation, without some strong law to protect the landlord against the dishonest tenant. Referring to the law of distress, he said the question was now before a committee of the House of Commons, and his only objection to its being abolished was that it Would be very much against the small tenant farmer. He would like to see it amended, and begged to move that, pending the result of the examination of witnesses before thd committee now sitting in the House of Commons, this subject should be postponed until the report has been received.
Mr. T. BAXTER (a tenant farmer) said the best way, in his judgment, for farmers to secure the reforms which they desired was to take care that they were represented by proper men in Parliament.
Mr. Jourr ROBERTS stated that the members of the Chester Farmers' Club agreed entirely with the first two resolu- tions.

Mr. J. TomurrsoN, Rho was a candidate in the Liberal interest at the recent by-election in West Cheshire,expressed general approval of the resolutions. Other gentlemen having spoken' Mr. G. W. LATHAM thought that if the proposal of Mr. W. Egerton were adopted it would be just of as much value to agriculturists as passing a resolution declaring that two and two make four. After a few words from the Rev. C. WOLLEY DOD (Mal- pas), who supported Mr. Egerton s proposal,the amendment, which had been drafted as follows, was put to the meeting : "That comnensation by law, in the absence of agreement.to the same effect, should be paid to outgoing tenants for im- provements made by them during their tenancy, and which, either in whole or in part, are in existence at the expiration of the tenancy; and that in case of dispute the amount of compensation be settled by arbitration." Six voted in favour of the amendment, and 25 against it. The resolution was afterwards put to the meeting,and carried by 23 against 3. The second of the resolutions given above was adopted with, ut discussion. On the third resolution, The VICE-PRESIDENT (the hon. W. Egerton) moved that the resolution be struck out. If it should be the wish of the chamber to carry these resolutions •as they were, intact, he should with very much regret be obliged to reconsider entirely his position with regard to the chamber. He could not with any self-respect retain his position if the chamber passed a resolution which was contrary to the maintenance of any fair and just feelings between landlord and tenant; he could not remain a member of a chamber which permitted, t:y a side wind,the introduction of the principles of the Irish Land Act into the relations of landlord and tenant in this country. (Hear, hear.) Therefore, in moving the rejection of the third resolution, he begged very respectfully to say that if it was carried he must decline to sit any longer in the chair.

Mr. G. W. LATHAM said he could assure Mr. Egerton that he, as much as any member of the Chamber, would regret if Mr. Egerton resigned the position of vice-president, but 1 he thought the members of the Chamber were not to be dictated to by a threat like that, and prevented from taking ; what they believed to be the right course. (Hear, hear.) Words were very often used to create a wrong impression. He did not mean in the smallest degree to insinuate that Mr. Egerton wished to express what he meant wrongly, but when he said that the resolution brought in the Irish Land Act—and that was what Mr. Egerton was afraid of—(Mr. Egerton: The principles of that Act, I say)—he was en- tirely under a mistake from beginning to end. All that the proposed court was intended to do, and all it could do ac- cording to those resolutions, was to guard the interests of both landlord and tenant. It was perfectly clear that if the law of distress were abolished they would want in some cases the power of immediate re-entry giving to the land- lord. While allowing a man to ',cultivate his farm as be thought best, it would be necessary occasionally to restrain the tenant from doing a foolish, it might be a wicked, thing. At present the landlord had the power to go to the Court of Chancery or to the High Court; and what was proposed by the resolution under consideration was simply that a cheap and expeditious court should be substituted for the present cumbrous machinery. There was not one single idea in the minds of those who drafted the resolution that they were carrying out the system or the principles of the Irish Lard Act. (Hear, bear.) That explanation would, he hoped, in- duce Mr. Egerton to say that he really had mistaken the meaning of the resolution, the object of which was to settle at once matters between landlord and tenant. He hoped the meeting would not, because et the threatened resigna- tion of the vice-president, hesitate to do what was right and just within its own knowledge. (Applause.) Mr. BYRD supported the resolutions, and disclaimed any - intention to introduce the principles of the Irish Land Act. ' Mr. TOMKINSON said that after the explanations of Mr. Latham and Mr. Byrd he saw no objection whatever to the passing of the third resolution. But might it not be better to modify the wording in some way with regard to the land court? The VICE-PRESIDENT was understood to say that he wa sorry he had misconstrued the resolution. Mr. FAIR advocated the appointment of an umpire in lieu of a land court. (Hear, hear.) Mr. LATHAM was quite willing to agree to an alteration of the wording as follors:—"It will be necessary to instruct the county court assisted by competent valuers," Ice. After some discussion, the resolution, subject to Mr.' Latham's amendment, was agreed to by 24 votes to 2, and the chamber adjourned the consideration of the remaining clauses to their next meeting. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Instructions have been issued by the London Social Democrats to the Freikit Editorial Committee that thst journal should be continued on lines, if possible, even more revolutionary and extreme than heretofore.

Messrs. Howard and Bullough, machinists, Accrington, have recently erected a new foundry 240 feet in length and 180 feet in width. They are now about to erect a new fitting shop 70 yards in length, 20 in width, and four storeys high.

On Thursday two cottager! in a street at Bury, which had been undermined for the purpose of making cellars beneath, fell with a loud cra3h. The cottages were about to be included in some extensions of the Star Inn Brewery, and were consequently untenanted. No one was injuted.

A luggage train engaged in shunting was backed through the Turner-lane Crossing, Ashton-under-Lyne, on Thursday night, and the gates on both sides of the road were smashed. The crossing is a busy thoroughfare, three or four convey- ances being frequently blocked chen the gates are closed for passing trains.

It was announced in Liverpool yesterday that the new bishopric of Newcastle had been-offered to, and accepted by, the Rev. E. R. Wilberforce, Canon of Winchester, and formerly Vicar of Seaforth, near Liverpool. Canon Wilber- force is a son of the late Bishop Wilberforce. and was pre- sented to the vicarage of Seaforth and the canonry of Winchester by Mr. Gladstone. In the Chancery Division, yesterday, the proprietors of Punch obtained an injunction extending over next motion day restraining some persons at Bristol from selling copies of Punch for id. The defendants are a hosier and a firm of advertising agents, who buy Punch in quantities and inter- leave it with sheets of paid advertisements. Owing to the depression in trade the Whitsuntide holi- days at some of the mills of the Blackburn district will be longer than usual, but in general agreement has been made as to the duration of the stoppage. In most cases work will be resumed on Wednesday morning, but in others the holi- day will be a day longer, and some mills will be stopped the whole of the week.

Letters have been received from the Duchy of Lancaster Office by the gentlemen nominated by the Heywood Town Council for borough magistrates asking if they are prepared to accept the position if appointed and to devote the neces- sary time to the duties of the office. It is said that the county justices will have concurrent jurisdiction within the borough. __ _

div.head: NORTH WALES STRIKE.
div.p: THE NORTH WALES STRIKE.

The strike among the North Wales colliers now seems almost at an end. The atmosphere of the strike district looked much brighter yesterday morning. It is now thought a speedy settlement will be arrived at, as large numbers of miners have resume w°rk, while those who remain on strike have, after six weeks' delay, come to the conclusion that half a loaf is better than none. A mass meeting will be held on Monday.

THE AGRICULTURAL OUTLOOK IN CHESHIRE. The soft warm rains of the past three days have wrought an immense improvement in Cheshire pastures. The season is the earliest experienced for many years. In consequence of the luxuriant growth of grass cattle are yielding large quantities of milk. The make of cheese will be very large this season, prices being encouragingly firm. Potatoes, of which a largo acreage is sown, are rapidly recovering from the effect of the first frost nip last week. MORE FIGHTING IN THE BALKAN. PROVINCES.

On Thursday intelligence from Sophia states that deputa- tions have arrived there from Tirnova, Lovata, and Gabrovo to demand the immediate convocation of the National Assembly. Reports have reached Philippopolis of fighting between the military and the Christian inhabitants of Uskub-, in Which eight sokliers were killed and twety-four wounded. The losses of the Christians are not stated. THURSDAY'S NIGHT'S DIVISION.

Amongst the noes in the division on Mr. Cowen' s amend- ment, on Thursday night, were Messrs. Jacob Bright, Burt, Collings, Carbutt, Labouchere, Storey, and P. A. Taylor. Messrs. Sllgg, Arnold, and Armitage did not vote. Amongst the suiiporters of the Government were Messrs. Agnew, John Bright, Cheetham, Coddington, R. A. Cross, Fort, Grafton, Lord Hartington, Messrs. Hibbert, Leaks, Mason, Sir Stafford Northcote, Mr. Raikes, and Colonel Stanley.

div.head: FATAL BURNING ACCIDENTS.
div.p: FATAL BURNING ACCIDENTS.

Inquests were held on Thursday at the Blackburn In- firmary, on the bodies of Elizabeth Bennett, 51, wife of a labourer, living in Blackburn, and Ellen Farrell, a winder, of Accrington, who died on the previous morning from burns received on Saturday night. The clothes of Bennett were ignited by some hot coals falling from the fire when she was putting fuel on, and those of Farrell were ignited through the bottom of a paraffin lamp she was carrying fall- ing off. Verdicts of accidentally burned was returned.

div.head: TIIE DUBLIN MURDERS.
div.p: TIIE DUBLIN MURDERS.

At a recent meeting of the Social Democratic Working Men's Club, in London, a resolution was - unanimously adopted "highly approving of the courageous deed of the Irish r3bels, which act was especially well timed, inasmuch as it took place at a moment when certain chiefs of the Land League party were upon the point of entering into the shameful treaty with the English Government." Nothing further has transpired regarding this terrible travdy. Earl Spencer visited the grave of the murdered under-Secretary, Mr. Burke, on Thursday evening, and re- mained some time in silent contemplation. The grave is still guarded by police. THE LATE SIR JOHN HOLKER.

In the Court of Appeal, Westminster, yesterday, the judges present being Lord Coleridge and Lords Justices Brett and Cotton, the Lord Chief Justice of England paid a touching tribute to the memory of Sir John biker. He referred in graceful and eulogistic terms to the deceased's distinguished abilities, and remarked that his high minded and simple character would long dwell in the hearts of those who knew him. The Attorney-general made a suitable reply on behalf of the bar.
SEVERE EARTHQUAKE AT THE AZORES. GREAT DAMAGE TO PROPERTY.

A Lisbon telegram says intelligence from the island of Fayal, one of the Azores, states that a violent earthquake occurred there on the 3rd. The shocks continued an hour. Churches, public buildings and many houses were des- troyed.

div.head: LOCAL LAW CASE.
div.p: LOCAL LAW CASE.

In the Queen's Bench Division, Westminster, yesterday, the case of Jackson v. Savage was brought before Justices Grove and North, sitting in banco. The action was to recover damages for fraudulently misrepresenting the takings of a public-house. It was tried at the Liverpool Assizes, and resulted in a verdict for £5OO. That was the amount which the plaintiff gave for the house, and Mr. Russell, Q.C., now moved for a rule for a new trial. The learned counsel, although he did not complain of the verdict being

for the plaintiff, contended that the dama7es were obviously excessive, as he still retained possession of the house. Their lordships having consulted with Justice Cave, who tried the case at the assizes, reported that the learned judge did not at all consider the damages too high, as the house appeared to be worthless, a previous tenant having sworn that the takings were insufficient to defray the working expenses.— A rule was therefore refused. . END OF A MINERS' STRIKE.

The strike of colliers in the district of Andley, North Staffordshire, after lasting only a week has collapsed. Most of the men have already resumed work at a reduction of 5 per cent, and the remainder will go in on Monday. The employers have made a reduction in consequence of the price of coal having been reduced is per ton. The coal trade of the district is at present very unsettled.

AN OLDHAM MANUFACTURER'S MUNIFICENCE. Mr. William Richardson, J.P., of Messrs. Platt Brothers and Co. (Limited), Oldham, his offered to erect at his ex- pense an additional ward to the Oldham Infirmary. It appears Mr. Richardson visited the infirmary lately, and was so pleased with what he saw that he determined to increase its usefulness. Some years since Mr. Harry Clegg erected a ward in the infirmary, so that this will be the second gift of the kind by Oldham gentlemen.
A CHILD BURNT TO DEATH.-SHOCKTNG CASE.

An inquest was held yesterday on the body of Edith Watson, two and a half years old, the daughter of Mr. Chas. Watson, wine and spirit merchant, of Oxford-street, Liver- pool. On Monday morning the deceased was in the children's bedroom with her brothers and sisters, and in the absence of the nurse they were burning paper, Jrc., at the gas. The deceased ;it a linen collar, and this set fire to her nightdress. She was severely burnt, and though her injuries were promptly attended to, she died in great agony on Tues- day evening. A verdict of " Accidental death " was re- turned. No blame was attached to the nurse, who had only gone down stairs to bring the children's clothes.

div.head: THREATENING THE QUEEN.
div.p: THREATENING THE QUEEN.

At the Central Criminal Court, yesterday, Albert Young, 17, clerk, was indicted before Mr. Justice Lopes for sending to Sir Henry Ponsonby a letter threatening to murder the Queen and other persons. There was another indictment for demanding money with menaces. The Attorney-General, Mr. Poland, and Mr. A. L. Smith appeared for the prosecu- tion, and Mr. Grain and Mr. Cavendish Bentinck for the defence. The prisoner pleaded not guilty to all the charges. The prisoner presented a miserable appearance. The Attorney-General said he had no wish to exaggerate the importance of the case, but the letter—and he thought they would agree with him—was of a most disgraceful char- acter. He believed he should have no difficulty in proving that it was written by the prisoner. The letter was as follows " Madam,—l am a Roman Catholic priest, and I have 59 men in the parish who have been evicted by landlords. These men have banded themselves together for your destruction, as they blame you for being the cause of their misery. They, however, promise to leave the country on the receipt of £4O per man to defray the expenses of selves and families. This amount must hemn the hands of my dupe, through whom you receive this, in three weeks from now, or they will commence operations against your life. I know this is treason; that is why I shall make use of a person of standing and character in England for the dupe to transmit your reply to m's in Ireland. I strongly advise you to send me the money, as the men are desperate enough, and they will make a sties of attempts against your life and those of your sons and daughters which must succeed in more than one respect. Assuredly you will not hesitate to send what will be but a moiety out of each pocket if all the members of the Royal Family subscribe amongst themselves for the required amount, rather than endanger so many pre- cious lives. Ask Prince Leopold how he would like to have a bullet put through bins on his wedding day (of which I wish him many happy returns) and die a lingering death like Garfield? I may add if no notice is taken of this I shall absolve them of all their misdeeds, instead, as now, hold them in check by threats of excommunication.—A WELL-WISHER. P.S.—The name of my dupe is A. Y., M.S.L. Railway offices, Doncaster. No notice will be taken of cheque; must be in notes and gold." In addition to the foregoing there was the following enclosure :—"Sir,—Will you oblige by showing her Majesty the enclosed? May say that if you don't credit or comply with it now you may do so when you receive a message to say 'Prince— is as- sassinated. Have captured assissins.' " The letters were in a disguised handwriting, but there were peculiarities which would be referred to by experts, and, although it might be thought that the prisoner had only acted foolishly, such conduct could not pass unpunished. It was intolerable that actual attempts should he made upon her Majesty's life, and that immediately afterwards letters of this kind should be forwarded.

Sir Henry Ponsonby was then called, and deposed to receiving the letters read by the Attorney-General. Edward Baskill. agent to the Macnchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, said he knew the prisoner as a telegraph clerk in the service of the company. He had frequently seen him write, and identified a report produced as that of Young's. He also produced other books and docu- ments in the prisoner's handwriting. He had seen the threatening letters, and firmly believed them to be the prisoner's writing slightly disguised.—By the Judge: The prisoner was not at the office on the day the letter was dated, which was a Sunday. Richard Hoare, in the service of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, said he saw the pri- soner's writing daily, and firmly believed the letters were his.

George Henry Garrett, a fellow-clerk of the prisoner's, also identified the handwriting, particularly that upon the en- velope. Mr. Chabot, the expert in handwriting, said he was clearly and undoubtedly of opinion that the letter was written by the same person who wrote the other documents handed in. In support of this he mentioned peculiarities which oc- curred in both, and pointed them out to the jury.

div.head: MR. PARNELL'S INFLUENCE IN IRELAND.
div.p: MR. PARNELL'S INFLUENCE IN IRELAND.

TLe Times says :—The estimate that has been formed in this country of Mr. Parnell's influence is founded, it must be remembered, upon the popularity he acquired in Ireland while he was at the head of an agitation the power of which was consolidated and fortified by public and private crime. This, at least, was the conviction of the Government when Mr. Parnell and certain other leading organisers of the Land League were placed on their trial in Dublin. Whether Mr. Parnell will obtain any authority or influence as a moderate politician, or whether he will fall into the abyss of political impotence and oblivi.on, is a problem enly to be solved by experience. In the former ease lie may, if he pleases, assist in maintaining order; butt whether he will choose to do so, and, if so, on what conditions, is altogether uncertain. But, unfortunately or fortunately, it is far more probable that the Government will have no need to consider in what way or on what terms Mr. Parnell's co-operation in the cause of order is to be secured, for Mr. Parnell, like other moderates before him, will too probably see his power pass from him into the hands of more daring and uncompromis- ing men.. Mr. Redmond gave the House of Commons fair warning that no settlement of the land question. even of the most sweeping and radical character, will satisfy the dis- affected classes in Ireland until legislative independence be conceded. This is the answer to the protests of Radicals like Mr. Slagg and Mr. Collings. It is satisfactory to discover that there is an overwhelming preponderance of opinion on the side of the Government in its effort to grapple with Irish crime. The hearty and strenuous co-operation of the Conservative party, which Mr. Trevelyan frankly re- cognised, will not be wanting, as the speech of Sir Richard Cross indicated, during the debates in committee. No occa- sion for difference of opinion among the friends of law and order is likely to arise if the Government hold firmly to the main lines of the Bill as it was introduced by the Home Secretary and accepted by the House. The Stand trd remarks :—Mr. Parnell has escaped for a moment a serious blow to his authority as a leader of the Irish party. Mr. Hilton is the most formidable of his rivals in the affections of the Irish people, and in the present morbid condition of feeling Mr. Dillon, if he appealed to them as the apostle of a more violent and intractable policy, I would win away from him much popular support. On the other hand, if Mr. Dillon's teaching were suffered to pass as the doctrine of the Parnellite faction,most of those who have given the Land League whatever moral force it has to boast of would find that at last a moment had come when further fellowship with it was impossible. Thus in any case the disruption of the remnant of Mr. Parnell's following seemed certain. Mr. Trevelyan had an easy task in showing that the Bill proposed simply to protect Irishmen who were honest and quiet from violence of every kind. Noticing the various difficulties raised as to particular provisions, he pointed out how each was related to the whole. As to the clauses affecting the press and rights of public meeting, be afforded a manly assurance that the wide powers conferred on the Executive would not be abused. The assurance ought to make it easier for the Government to consent to such a modification of the terms as would render it im- possible for them to be put to improper use.

The Daily News observes :—ln spite of the excited in- tolerance which some Liberal members displayed after the delivery of Mr. Di:lon's speech on Wednesday, the severity of the Government Bill was by no means universally ap- proved last night. Mr. Collings and Mr. Slagg supported Mr. Cowen's amendment, and there was a general disposi- tion, which we welcome as a promising symptom, to dis- tinguish between open agitation and secret crime. The case against some clauses of the Prevention Bill is that they are not in the least calculated to deter from murder or other violence. Mr. Parnell spoke with great ez.pasis, and with every appearance of intense earnestness, \Olen lie entreated the Government not to play into the hands of the secret societies. Whatever may be thought of the quarter from which the advice comes, it cannot be too carefully con- sidered. We, at least, have never denied that some legisla- tion has been- made necessary by the deplorable prevalence in Ireland of offences which are not emcused by being agrarian or political.. But the object to which the efforts of Parliament should be directed is narrow though vital, and
to confound it with other matters is to throw away a great opportunity and risk a terrible failure. We trust that in committee. Ministers will show their appreciation of the truth. •

The Morning Post observes :—lt is true Mr. Parnell admitted that Mr. Dillon and he and Mr. Davitt were op- posed to landlordism, but they never looked forward to its extinction save on equitable terms. It was a mere question of purchase and sale, and all that the leaders of the Land League demanded was that landlords should be bought out, not exterminated. But he was compelled to say a grievous mistake was made by the Government in accompaning their remedial measure with one taking away the liberties of the Irish people by depriving them of existing guarantees fcr the administration of justice, and denying them those rights of combination for the advancement of class interests which are conceded to English workmen. This would neutralise the otherwise beneficial effects of the Arrears Bill, and con- sequently he could only foresee total failure and possibly a further deAelopment of that crime which it was the aim of Parliament to repress. In fact, the restriction of freedom of speech would foster secret societies, with their attendant conspiracies, and a state of things would arise which would render it impossible for honest independent politicians like himself and his friends to do theit duty to their country.

The Daily Telegeaph says :—lncreasing disposition con- siderably to alter, if not wholly reject, the Arrears Bill is said to be shown by those who are likely to lead the opposi- tion in the House of Lords, the speech made in the House of Commons by Mr. Dillon on Wednesday afternoon having, had the effect of greatly alarming many who would other- wise have supported the measure. We are not disposed to undervalue the importance of Mr. Parnell's statement so far as he is personally concerned. Yet, unless he can get all the Irish members who sit below the gangway on the Speaker's left to agree with him, and unless through them he can turn the hearts of the perpetrators of outrage in Ireland, and re- store order to that distracted country, we cannot accept his recantation as an argument sufficiently powerful to induce the withdrawal or even the serious modification of the Pre- vention of Crime Bill.
THE PHCENIX PARK TRAGEDY: CLUE TO THE MURDERERS.

The Central News is enabled to state that the Govern- ment are satisfied that they have obtained a definite clue to the murderers of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke, as well as to the identification of several parties who have been aiding and abetting them. It is not contemplated, however, that any arrest will be made for some days to come, as it is the intention of the authorities to secure evidence sufficient to warrant a conviction before actually laying hold of the suspected and watched men. The liberal reward offered has had the effect of putting the police in possession of a considerable amount of information respecting that and other resent crimes in Ireland.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIDIENT, HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIDIENT, HOUSE OF COMMONS.

EGYTT.—Sir C. DILKE, in replying to Sir W. Lawson, said, any discussion on the subject of Egypt at the present moment could not but be prejudicial to the public service. MICHAEL DAVITT.—Sir W. HARCOURT Said he had 110 knowledge that Michael Davitt had broken the terms of his ticket-of-leave, and therefore it was not necessary to take any steps. POLICE PATROL IN PHCF.NIX PARK.—Mr. TREVELYAN was not then in a position to give full information as to the withdrawal of the police patrol in Phcenix Park on the 6th May. He would make further inquiries. _ _

EGYPTIAN AFFAIRS: A SCENE.—Mr. ASHMEAD BARTLETT asked if the document appearing in that morning's papers on the subject of Egypt was accurate or not.—Sir C. DILLE said it was substantially a genuine document. Steps had been taken to protect British subjects in Egypt.—Sir W. LAWSON protested against withholding all information.— Sir Stafford Northcote and others addressed observations to the Prime Minister.—Mr. GLADSTONE said it was impossible he could communicate information on the subject. The matter was delicate, and other powers were engaged in the negotiations. He might however say that nothing had yet occurred to interfere with the hopeful view of affairs, which the foreign Under-Secretary had given the House a few days ago.—Mr. ASHMEAD BARTLETT and Mr. O'DONNELL ex- pressed their disapprobation at the observations of Mr. Glad- stone.—The subject afterwards dropped. EVICTIONS AT CLONCURRY.—Mr. DILLON said he had received a telegram from Limerick begging him to get per- mission to erect huts for 500 people evicted by Loud Clon- curry. He asked the Government to telegraph authority to do so, and so save them from going into the workhouse.— Mr. D. PLUNKETT said the evictions were not due to Lord Cloncurry, but to the "no rent" manifesto.—Mr. PluNEr.r. denied that was so. They had been evicted because they refused to pay rack rent. The "No rent" manifesto had not been issued when these proceedings commenced.—Mr. FORSTER admitted that was so' but said the present state of things had been brought about by the advice given by the Land League. The tenants had been told if they acted on the advice given by the Land League, they should not suffer. The tenants declined to take the advantage of buying in the property, and the Land League, he considered, had not carried out their promise. Cases had occurred where huts had been put up for purposes of intimidation, and he cautioned the Government to be careful how they interfered with magisterial action in the matter. He denied he had ever interfered with the erection of huts, except when it was for the purposes of intimidation, and he defended the action of Mr. Clifford Lloyd.—Mr. TREVELYAN said where huts were erected with a view of carrying on intimidation they would not be permitted, but where they were put up for legitimate purposes of shelter the Government would not interfere.—Mr. SEXTON defended the advice given to tendnts by the Land League.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE considered the Land League responsible for what had occurred.—After a few words from Sir W. HARCOURT, the matter dropped.

THE PREVENTION OF CRIME BILL-Mr. LAHOLTHERE and Mr. PARNELL asked that the committee on the Preven- tion of Crime might not be taken next Thursday.—Mr. GLADSTONE said in the absence of assurance that Thursday and Friday should be devoted to Supply, he oduld not con- sent to such arrangement.—The House then went into Committee on the Prevention of Crime (Ireland) Bill.—On Clause 1, which enacted a special commission court, com- posed of three judges, for the trial of capital offences and treason-felony, Mr. HEALY moved an amendment limiting the power of the Lord-Lieutenant to appoint a commission. —After a discussion progress was reported. The County Courts (Ireland) Bill was passed. The House adjourned at five minutes to seven until Thursday next.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER, CORN, THURSO &X.—Messrs. WiMain Warbur- ton and Co. retort as follows --The trade generally has been dull since last market day, with a slight tendency to lower prices. The weather has been sunny, but with low tempera- ture. Imports into Liverpool have been liberal of flair and peas, small of wheat, and moderwe of other produce. To-day's market was fairly attended, but the business pacsing was limited. The quotations of last week must be repeated for whEat, and corn also was steady with an average inquiry. Oats were dull. Oatmeal in better demand. Beans receded Id. to 2d. and peas Id. per cental. Maize also was purchase- abl- at a reducton of Id. to 21. per cental on the week.

LIVERPOOL CORN, FRIDAY.:-The market opens quiet for wheat without decided change. Indian corn rather easier than on last market day. LONDON PRODUCE, FRIDAY—Sugar: Market remains with- out change. Coffee firm at late values. Tea: No public sales will be held to-day. Rica quiet and unaltered. Cotton: Market firm. Jute remains quiet. Tallow: new braoked, 54s f3d spot. Oils: Rape, 27s 9d to 285; linseed, 24s to 24s 3d. Turpentine, 40s. Petroleum, 51,1 to sid spot.—The produce markets will be entirely closed next Monday. CLYDE CRUSHED SUGAR, FRIDAY.—The market opened with a good demand, and a large business was dcne at Wednesday's prices. The official report states that a fair business has been done at steady prices. A compositor named John Stroud, thirty-seven years of age, living at Walworth, London, committed suicide OD 'hgursday. On Wednesday night he told his wife he bad lost money over the Derby. On Thursdiy morning he got up early, for the purpose, he said, of making up his betting book, and \vent downstairs, here he hanged himself. The body of a man named Williams has been found in the Tame at Duliinfield. It is believed that he committed suicide, and that a widow whom he was courting was the cause of the act. Her husband recently put an end to his life, and another man is said to have hung himself through her.

At the London Criminal Court, on Wednesday, Thomas Aiken Smythe, said to be a medical student, was found •uilty of the manslaughter of the Rev. Matthew Campbell. .tnythe had been called in professionally, anti it was con- tended that the rev, gentleman might have recovered had he been properly attended to.
